definitions.definition: Suffering from supernatural or cosmic agencies: cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning (Gauḍapāda) or possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas and planets (Vācaspati).
Right view arising through instruction or study (TS 1.3); also 'understanding' of the realities through pramāṇa and naya (TS 1.6).
Realization, the Dharma as attained (the wings of awakening), the second aspect of the true Dharma.
The intercalary lunar month in which no solar ingress occurs; also called mala-māsa, it is unfit for sacraments and many rites, though prized for devotion (Kālamādhava; Nirṇayasindhu).

Eligibility for knowledge and scripture, in three grades (low, middle, highest) by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant devoted to Viṣṇu. Eligibility to Veda, Tantra or the Name is distinguished by class and gender.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.47: one's right or proper claim, which extends to action alone and never to its fruits.

The qualification of the agent entitled to perform a rite and enjoy its fruit: a human (MS 6.1.4–5), man or woman — husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17) — of the three higher varṇas, with Vedic learning (MS 6.1.25–38); the subject of adhyāya 6.

Fitness for a practice: the Śiva Saṃhitā assigns the four yogas to four grades of aspirant (5.10–14); the Jyotsnā holds the dispassionate alone properly eligible though Purāṇic verses grant yoga to all beings; the HYP and DYŚ say anyone who practises succeeds.
An injunction that conveys ownership (enjoyership) of the fruit of the act, e.g. 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'.
A topic-section of the sūtras treated in five steps: subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection.
The unit of Mīmāṃsā discussion, with five members: subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view and conclusion (Nyāyamālā).
Seven procedures for settling disputes.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The eligible agent of a rite, the one to whom the fruit belongs ('one desiring heaven').
The qualified student: purified by prescribed duties and endowed with the four means.
the highest of the three grades (YS 1.22; YBh 1.20)
In this text: the phrase "adhimātram" introducing the correspondence of quarters and measures.

Confidence in the supreme vehicle, the 'seed' of the buddha's children.
The training in higher wisdom: knowing the four truths as they are (AN 3.89).
The condition by which cognitions of different streams determine each other, explaining intersubjective and karmic effects without external objects.
The training in higher virtue: restraint by the Pātimokkha, seeing danger in the slightest fault (AN 3.89).
The need for a controller, a proof of puruṣa (SK 17); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
Substratum: the real on which something unreal is superimposed (the rope for the snake; Brahman for the world).
byin rlabs, blessing: the transforming influence that flows from the lineage through the guru to the devoted disciple, regarded as the decisive condition for realization of Mahāmudrā.

definitions.definition: The eighth perfection, unshakeable like a rocky mountain (Bv 2); the four foundations of MN 140 (wisdom, truth, relinquishment, peace).
Bhagavad Gītā 7.30; 8.2, 8.4: asked 'who and how is the adhiyajña here in this body?', the Lord answers: 'I myself, here in the body' (adhiyajño 'ham evātra dehe).
The Lord himself in the body (BhG 8.4).

The three time-paths (past, present, future) in which properties stand; past and future exist in their own form because of this difference (4.12).
The six 'paths' of the cosmos — letters, words, mantras, kalās, principles and worlds — purified in nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.
The six paths - letters, mantras, words; kalās, tattvas, worlds - contemplated from gross to supreme (VBT 56-57; TĀ 6-12).
Time-period (past, present, future); conditioned dharmas are themselves 'the times'; the times are distinguished by activity.

definitions.definition: Deliberate superimposition by scripture and teacher (creation, sheaths, attributes) as a provisional teaching device.

Superimposition: 'the appearance, of the nature of memory, of something previously seen in something else' — the mutual superimposition of self and not-self that is the basis of all empirical life, called avidyā.

Superimposition: the appearance of one thing as another through error, like a snake in a rope; ego is the first superimposition on the Self; jīva and witness appear mutually superimposed like fire and iron.
The sixth step of the seven-point instruction: the resolve to take upon oneself alone the responsibility of freeing all beings from suffering and establishing them in happiness.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the compound adhyātma-cetas (3.30): the mind directed to the self, with which one resigns all actions to Kṛṣṇa; commentators gloss it variously.
The own nature (svabhāva) of the Imperishable (BhG 8.3); the knowledge of the self is the best of sciences (10.32).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Concerning the self: the knowledge concerning the self (adhyātma-vidyā) is the Lord among the sciences (10.32); Arjuna calls the teaching he has received 'the supreme secret called adhyātma', through which his delusion is gone (11.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.12: constancy in knowledge of what pertains to the self is among the dispositions called knowledge; 15.5: those constantly intent on it (adhyātmanitya) go to the imperishable place.
With respect to the self/body, as opposed to adhidaivata, with respect to the gods: the two registers in which the Upaniṣads state correspondences (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4-5).
Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: Defined as own being (svabhāva) (8.3; the verse does not say whose); known 'in its entirety' by those who strive for release taking refuge in the Lord (7.29).

(1) In Haribhadra's Yogabindu the first yoga: study and contemplation of reality with friendliness etc. by one with vows; (2) in Yaśovijaya, pure activity centred on the self by one free of delusion (Adhyātmasāra 1.2); (3) the name of the seventeenth-century movement centred on the Samayasāra.
The study and direct experience of the pure self (śuddhātman) by the ultimate standpoint, as taught in the Samayasāra and its Hindi renderings.

Internal suffering, bodily (from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm) and mental (from desire, anger, separation from the dear, etc.) (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati on SK 1).
The nature of buddhi (SK 23); perception is determination concerning each object (SK 5), explained by Vācaspati as a predominance of sattva in buddhi.

The unseen cause of motions without visible cause and of the mind's passage at death and birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C).
The residue of past action that brings about the body (NS 3.2.60); set in motion by the Lord (NBh 4.1.21).

definitions.definition: The inclination toward non-duality, which arises only by the grace of the Lord.
That paired concepts — saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, defiled and pure, self and no-self — are not two; entry into non-duality is beyond words, shown by Vimalakīrti's silence.

Non-dual understanding (advaya-buddhi), free of the extremes of existence and non-existence, is with compassion and bodhicitta a cause of bodhisattvas (MA 1.1); the non-dual path to nirvāṇa (PsP 17.30).

definitions.definition: Non-dual gnosis: union, non-abiding nirvāṇa, buddhahood; words like 'unborn' point only to it (Pañcakrama 5.25–27).

definitions.definition: Kālī as the primordial Śakti and giver of nirvāṇa (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.41; Mahānirvāṇa 4.32).
Toxicology: signs and treatment of bites of snakes, insects, spiders, rodents and of combined poisons (Su Sū 1.8); 'daṃṣṭrā' in AHS Sū 1.5.
Faultless speech; above all the authorless Veda and the other true scriptures, the only means by which Viṣṇu is known.
Testimony: the activity arising in a hearer from the words of a reliable speaker who has seen or inferred the matter (YBh 1.7); it too reaches only the general (1.49).
The teaching that has come down through the succession of teachers from Maheśvara.

Revealed Śaiva scripture spoken by Śiva/Sadāśiva, the 'higher knowledge' as against the lower knowledge beginning with the Veda; in South Indian usage especially the 28 Siddhānta scriptures and their upāgamas.
The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās as scripture spoken by Bhagavān himself (Bhagavacchāstra).
In Buddhist usage: the transmitted scripture (the sūtra collections — Dīrgha, Madhyama, Saṃyukta, Ekottarika); one of the two aspects of the true Dharma.
Scripture is not a means of knowledge in matters open to inference; a scripture contradicted by valid cognition is not established.
Scripture and unbroken tradition, without which dharma cannot be established by reasoning (VP 1.30).

notes: A widely quoted etymology (ā-gata from Śiva's mouth, gata to Girijā, mata by Vāsudeva) is of uncertain source and not recorded as a definition here.

definitions.definition: The canonical scripture: the words of the Tīrthaṅkara as composed by the gaṇadharas and elders, fixed at Valabhī — forty-five texts for Mūrtipūjakas, thirty-two for Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs.

The Digambaras hold the original āgama (the Aṅgas and Pūrvas) lost; the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa preserve parts of it and are called 'āgama', and the works of later ācāryas in the four anuyogas serve as scripture.

definitions.definition: Bengali songs of Umā's homecoming from Kailāsa to her mother Menakā at the autumn Durgā festival; with the vijayā songs of farewell, composed by Rāmprasād, Kamalākānta and others.
Karma done after knowledge, which does not cling to the knower, as water to a lotus leaf.
Defilements that are not the mind's nature but come to it like dust or clouds, separable from the tathāgatagarbha and removable.
Defilements are adventitious to the luminous mind and therefore removable.
The stains are adventitious; they have no support in the nature of mind and cannot survive the cultivation of their antidote.
An offence, especially against the gods' ordinances, which the worshipper asks Varuṇa to loosen like a rope (RV 2.28.5).
The four biases by which evil is done: desire, hatred, delusion, fear (DN 31).
'Not terrible' (a-ghora): the benign-terrible face of Śiva, name of one of the five Brahma-mantras; the lineage takes it as its name, holding that nothing is to be feared or shunned as impure.

notes: The Aghora Brahma-mantra is in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka's tenth book (chapter-level ref; not checked).

definitions.definition: An ascetic of the Aghora lineage.
Visualising fire rising from the syllable 'arhaṃ' and burning the lotus of the eight karmas and the body (YŚ 7).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the digestive-metabolic fire; no fire in the body exists apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); life, complexion, strength, health, ojas, tejas and the prāṇas depend on it — extinguished one dies, balanced one lives long, disturbed one falls ill; 'agni is the root' (Ca Ci 15.3-4); its states are balanced, irregular (vāta), sharp (pitta) and weak (kapha) (AHS Sū 1.8); later counted as thirteen: the belly-fire, the five element-fires and the seven tissue-fires (Ca Ci 15.13-15).
Fire and the god of fire: household priest and messenger between men and gods, carrier of oblations, present in all fires, guardian of ṛta (RV 1.1).

The year-long building of the great brick fire-altar (often in the shape of a falcon) in five layers, explained in ŚB 6–10 as the rebuilding of Prajāpati who fell apart, so that the sacrificer builds and becomes an immortal self.

The twice-daily milk offering into the sacred fires by one who has set them up; the Brāhmaṇas explain it as healing the junction of day and night (ŚB 1.6.3.36), as an offering of 'truth in faith' when nothing else exists (ŚB 11.3.1.4), and as a cycle through the worlds and the body (ŚB 11.6.2).
Interiorized as the offering into the breaths at meals (ChU 5.19–24) and as the continuous 'inner Agnihotra' of speech and breath (KU 2.5).
Offerings into the consecrated fire in a kuṇḍa, part of daily and occasional worship.
The formless (amūrta) worship of Viṣṇu through fire offerings.
The condition of beings who lack the lineage for liberation — the fifth of the five lineages; the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra distinguishes those temporarily cut off from those lacking the cause altogether.
In the Kārikā 3.26: ungraspable; the reason by which the unborn is shown.

Devotion without any motive of gain, which does not even seek liberation.

definitions.definition: The 'I': the fusion of the first letter 'a' and the last 'ha', the union of Śiva and Śakti that holds the universe (KKV 5).
The supreme 'I', spanning the letters from A (Śiva) to HA (Śakti) joined by the bindu (PTV).
The self as what the word and awareness 'I' refer to; not the ego-evolute of prakṛti but the soul itself, which persists as 'I' in deep sleep and liberation.
'I am Brahman' (BĀU 1.4.10): the realization sentence (anubhava-vākya), mahāvākya of the Yajurveda and of Śṛṅgeri.

The evolute of mahat whose nature is self-assertion (abhimāna); from it proceed the eleven organs (from its vaikṛta, sāttvika form) and the five subtle elements (from its bhūtādi, tāmasa form), both with its taijasa form (SK 24–25). It, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

Ego, one of the eight constituents of the lower nature (BhG 7.4); the deluded by ego think 'I am the doer' (3.27); free of 'mine' and ego one attains peace (2.71); in the Nārāyaṇīya, Aniruddha is called ahaṃkāra (12.327.26).

The I-maker: the 'teaching of I' (ahaṃkārādeśa) precedes the teaching of the self (ChU 7.25.1); listed among the faculties resting in the self (PrU 4.8); the jīva is endowed with intention and ahaṃkāra (ŚU 5.8).

The sense and grasping of 'I'; with 'mine'-making it ceases when self and mine are pacified (MMK 18.2–4); grasping at aggregates brings 'I'-making, action and birth (RĀ 1.35); the aggregates arise from it (RĀ 1.29).
The notion 'I' and 'mine', at whose arising the mind is to go to the supportless (VBT 131); in the Krama it is dissolved in the phases of Kālāgnirudra and Mahākāla (TĀ 4.161-168).

An evolute of prakṛti; distinct from the true 'I' (aham-artha), which is the self; the false identification of body as self is the obstacle.

Violence is prohibited; hence the Śyena rite, whose aim is violence, is harmful (anartha) though the Veda states it as a means for one who wishes to harm (Śabara on MS 1.1.2).
The Tathāgatas describe the Dharma in brief as non-harming, and nirvāṇa as emptiness (CŚ 12.23); non-harming is part of the dharma of higher status (RĀ 1.10).
Tamil kollāmai: the Siddhar poets condemn killing and flesh-eating (Paṭṭiṉattār; Pattirakiriyār 14; Kaṭuveḷi 25, 29).
Strict non-harming, down to the smallest creature, required of the renunciant.

Buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, the threefold internal instrument operating in all three times; the door-keeper, of which the ten external instruments are the doors (SK 33, 35).

The inner organ, one in substance and fourfold in function — mind (manas, doubting), intellect (buddhi, deciding), memory-store (citta) and ego (ahaṅkāra); the adjunct through which consciousness becomes the knower.
Tamil antakkaraṇam: the four inner faculties (maṉam, putti, cittam, akaṅkāram) among the ninety-six principles.
Mind and the rest, which one contemplates as absent in oneself (VBT 94).

The inner fire-offering of Pratardana: offering breath into speech while speaking and speech into breath while breathing, continually, waking or asleep (KauU 2.5).
An existence between death and rebirth — rejected by the Theravāda (Kathāvatthu 8.2), which holds that rebirth-linking follows death immediately.
Intermediate existence between death and birth, having the form of the coming existence, seen by its own kind and the divine eye, feeding on smells.

Denied (Vasumitra).
Denied (Vasumitra).
The intermediate state between death and rebirth, in which the yogin practises deity yoga or rests in reality to block rebirth (Tilopa, from Sukhasiddhi).
bar do, the intermediate state: in the Nāropa system three bardos — of birth-and-death (this life), of dream, and of becoming — in which clear light, illusory body and union are to be recognized.
Concentration, meditation and samādhi, inner relative to the first five limbs (3.7).
The Lord's internal, essential power, of three aspects (sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), which constitutes his form, abode and associates.
The soul that discerns itself as distinct from the body — from right view onward (Samādhitantra 5).
An obstacle on the path of yoga; the ten of LiP 1.9 and ŚiP 7.2.38; the powers themselves are antarāyas (BhP 11.15.33).
The nine obstacles, distractions of the mind (1.30), removed through devotion to Īśvara (1.29) and practice on a single principle (1.32).
The obstructive karma, one of the four whose destruction gives omniscience (TS 10.1); not the antarāya of the Yoga Sūtra.
Obstructive karma: obstructs giving, gain, enjoyment, repeated enjoyment and energy (8.13); inflow at 6.27.
Karma obstructing giving, gain, enjoyment and energy (TS 8.13, 6.27).

definitions.definition: The atmosphere between earth and heaven, the middle of the three worlds.
Any interval less than 48 minutes — the maximum span of one meditation (TS 9.27).
Ratnākaraśānti's view that pervasion is established within the subject itself, without an external example.
Inner worship, in which knower, knowing and known are offerer, fire and oblation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad; PKS 1.26); the Yoginīhṛdaya's inner worship is held sufficient for those firm in it (Setubandha).
Mental worship of the deity in the heart and body before external worship.
Mental worship (mānasayāga) preceding external worship.
In this text: inner controller, one of the names of "this one" (eṣaḥ) in MU 6, together with lord of all, knower of all and source of all; the verse does not name its referent (commentators: prājña).
The inner controller: 'he who dwells in the earth yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who controls it from within' — the self, the immortal (BAU 3.7).
The Lord dwelling within every soul and thing as its self and controller, and, in a special form, in the heart of the meditator.
The Lord dwelling within beings, one of his five modes.
The inner controller: Īśvara as the consciousness governing each being from within (BĀU 3.7), the 'starched canvas' of the Citradīpa.

Remembering the Lord at the moment of death; required of the bhakti-yogin but not of the surrendered, whom the Lord remembers.
The funeral rite — cremation (or burial of infants), bone-collection, water-offerings and the rites of the first year.
Minute, 'smaller than the small': the self in the heart smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3; KU 1.2.20; ŚU 3.20).
The soul is atomic in size, dwelling in the heart and pervading the body by its quality of knowledge.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness (cit-kaṇa).
(Tamil report) Four kinds of beginningless, indestructible atoms — earth, water, fire, air — which with life (uyir) make the five principles.
The four preliminaries of a teaching text: qualified student, subject, relation and purpose.
Bondage of intensity, i.e. fruition (vipāka) = experiencing, according to the name (8.21-8.22).
The strength of the karma's fruition, depending on the intensity of passion (TS 8.21–22).

Direct experience of the Lord, set against book-learning ('I speak of what I have seen with my eyes'); aṇbhai vāṇī is speech from such experience.

In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prāṇaliṅgi stage. More widely, lived experience of Śiva — the authority the śaraṇas appeal to, which gave the Anubhava Maṇṭapa its name.
Consequent: the outward signs by which an emotion is known — glances, gestures, movements (NŚ 6–7).

definitions.definition: The assembly at Kalyāṇa where, in the tradition's account, the śaraṇas of every birth and both sexes discussed their experience of Śiva under Allama's presidency.
Cognition other than memory; every experience is a means of knowledge (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Experience/awareness itself, the self as pure self-established consciousness (Iṣṭasiddhi).
One learned in the Veda, who is 'great among us' regardless of age or wealth (MDh 2.154).
The low accent.
The Lord's fifth power/act — grace — called compassion (kṛpā) and śaktipāta; one of Lakṣmī's five acts.
The Lord's favouring of the effect; also the teacher's right favour to qualified disciples, which preserves the tradition and itself leads to the end of suffering.
Grace, the fifth cosmic act, bestowed as Sadāśiva (LSN 64).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna says his delusion is gone by the word spoken out of favour to him (mad-anugrahāya) (11.1).
The Lord's grace, identical with puṣṭi.

The substitute prescribed in place of a Kaula substance for those not eligible or in the Kali age — e.g. the 'sweet triad' of milk, sugar and honey for wine (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171), one's own wife only for the last tattva (6.14).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa pumpkin, sugarcane and spirits are 'equal to' an animal victim, and coconut water or honey replace wine for the twice-born (67.23; 67.114-115).
A substitute used in place of a prescribed substance, notably for the five 'M's in the right-hand mode.
Compassion, one of the marks of right faith; the elephant's compassion for the hare won Megha human birth.
Distinguished into worldly (laukika) compassion that preserves bodily life and spiritual (lokottara) compassion that leads beings to restraint; only the second is dharma.
An index of seers, deities, metres and hymns of a Veda (e.g. the Sarvānukramaṇī).
Favourableness: devotion is cultivation of Kṛṣṇa in a way pleasing to him (not as enemies 'think' of him).
The resolve to do only what pleases the Lord; first limb of prapatti.
The last mundane insight, conforming to the eight preceding knowledges and to the requisites of awakening.
Faultless reasoning (upapatti) based on invariable concomitance; includes presumption and comparison.
Threefold inference preceded by knowledge of the mark and the marked (SK 5); by inference from general correlation supersensible things (prakṛti, puruṣa) are known (SK 6).

Cognition of an object through a reason with three characteristics; its object is a universal (an exclusion); for oneself it is cognition, for others it is the statement of the reason; testimony of a reliable person is included in it.
Inference: an activity that chiefly ascertains the general through a relation present in like and absent from unlike cases (YBh 1.7); it reaches only the general (1.49, YBh 1.25).
Knowledge preceded by perception, of three kinds (NS 1.1.5); resting on perception and scripture it is anvīkṣā (NBh 1.1.1).
Knowledge from a mark (laiṅgika): effect, cause, connected, co-inherent, opposed (VS 9.18); includes verbal knowledge.
The instrument of inferential cognition, i.e. consideration (parāmarśa); for oneself or for others.
Cognition of an unperceived part from seeing another part whose relation is known; of two kinds, by a relation seen directly or by one seen in general (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
(As reported) Not a means of knowledge, since pervasion cannot be established; or (Purandara) valid only as known in worldly life.
Autonomous inference is required to establish emptiness (Bhāviveka).
Only inference acceptable to the opponent (paraprasiddha) and consequences are used (Candrakīrti).
In Bāul usage: inference, hearsay and scripture — everything not verifiable in the living body — set aside in favour of bartamān.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.23: one of the names of 'the highest puruṣa in this body'.

Another name for the sixth means of knowledge, by which absence is known.
A reason proving absence: the non-perception of something that fulfils the conditions of perceptibility; one of the three valid reasons, not a separate means of knowledge.
Proposed (as 'abhāva') as a separate means of knowledge; not different from inference (NS 2.2.2); later, absence is perceived through the qualifier-relation contact.
Non-cognition: the means by which absence is known (a jar's absence on the ground), accepted as a separate means following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā.
Not finding or grasping any dharma as an object — the way the bodhisattva courses in the perfection of wisdom; rejoicing and dedication are done 'without apprehension'.
The meditative non-apprehension of objects, and then of mind, by which the dharmadhātu is apprehended; understanding (parijñā) of the three natures is non-apprehension.
The vehicle (honey, ghee, juice, decoction) with which a medicine is taken.
The 'means-less': realization by the teacher's word alone for the most intensely graced (TĀ 2).
The means that produce valid knowledge: perception, inference and authoritative word (presumption and comparison fall under inference).

Repeated contemplation of twelve themes — impermanence, no refuge, the round of births, aloneness, otherness, impurity, inflow, stopping, shedding, the universe, rarity of enlightenment, and the well-taught dharma (TS 9.7); also a kind of study (9.25).

definitions.definition: The Vedic ritual means, which are like the seen means because impure, perishable and graded (SK 2).
The ten recollections among the forty subjects.
The metre of four eight-syllable lines (the Puruṣa Sūkta's metre), later the śloka.
A Vedic metre of 32 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).

Things do not arise from self, other, both or without cause (MMK 1.1); dependent origination is 'without arising' (dedication); non-arising taught in the Mahāyāna equals the extinction taught to others (RĀ 4.86).
That dharmas do not truly arise or cease; what is born from conditions is unborn by own-nature; non-arising, like suchness, neither comes nor goes and is the Tathāgata.

The bodhisattva's settled acceptance that dharmas are unborn and selfless, marking irreversibility; in the Daśabhūmika it is attained on the eighth ground; its merit surpasses gifts of jewel-filled worlds.

'Unsurpassed yoga tantra': the Tibetan name (rnal 'byor bla med) for the highest class, comprising the Guhyasamāja, Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Kālacakra and related tantras; Indian sources more often speak of yogottara, yoganiruttara/yoginī and mahāyoga tantras.

definitions.definition: The soul's atomic size: it dwells in the heart and pervades the body by its attributive consciousness.
An arthavāda stating what is already known by another means of knowledge (e.g. that fire is a remedy for cold).
Repetition of what has been enjoined, distinct from mere repetition (NS 2.1.66–68 DCS).
A lesson or section, the recitation unit of the Ṛgveda (within maṇḍalas) and of the Taittirīya texts.
The vow kept in part (7.2).
The five vows kept partially by the householder (TS 7.2, 7.20).

The four classes of Digambara literature: narratives (prathama), cosmology and karma (karaṇa), conduct (caraṇa), and substances (dravya) (Ratnakaraṇḍa 43–46).

the cause in which the effect inheres; Vyāsa says the puruṣa is not this for the mark (YBh 1.45)

Words express their meanings only as already connected with other meanings, ultimately with what is to be done (kārya), as learned from elders' usage.
Bodhidharma's 'pacifying' of Huike's mind by showing it cannot be found; in Xu gaoseng zhuan, wall-gazing is 'pacifying the mind'.
Free from desires other than for Kṛṣṇa's service — the first mark of pure devotion.
Dignāga's formulation: a word expresses its object through the exclusion of other objects.
Wrong knowledge — for Madhva the real sense of 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya: the soul's misapprehension (of its relation to the body and to God), which ceases by God's will when he is known.
The Nyāya theory of error: a thing is cognized as qualified by a property it lacks — the silver seen elsewhere is presented in the mother-of-pearl.
An invariable antecedent that is nevertheless not a cause (e.g. the colour of the potter's staff).
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by identity ('a pot is not cloth').
Substance with cold touch, fluid and viscid; bodies of water in Varuṇa's world.
Conduct permitted when normal dharma cannot be kept, illustrated by Viśvāmitra in famine (MBh 12.139).
The relaxed rules of livelihood and conduct permitted in emergencies (MDh 10.81ff.).
The downward breath at the anus (SS 3.7); turned upward by mūlabandha it meets fire and prāṇa and awakens kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.61–69).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the navel.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu in the lower region (pelvis, bladder, genitals, thighs), governing the release of semen, menses, faeces, urine and the foetus (AHS Sū 12.9).
The complementary breath to prāṇa in the Gītā's breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29) and equalization (5.27).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the two paired breaths: some offer prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa (4.29); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are to be made even (5.27). The chapters do not define the direction of each.
The downward (or out-) breath; in PrU 3.5 it is in the organs of excretion and generation; the navel's function whose deity is death (AU 1.1.4).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Joined with prāṇa and apāna, the Lord as vaiśvānara digests the fourfold food (15.14).
Out-breath, named with prāṇa in the Saṃhitā lists of breaths (TS 4.7; AVŚ 8.1, 15.16).

The eight-ingredient binding compound that fixes the image to its pedestal, periodically renewed with rites.

A song of eight stanzas with refrain, set to a named rāga and tāla — the twenty-four songs of the Gīta Govinda; in Kerala the name of the Gīta Govinda singing tradition itself.
The eight protections of the Liṅgāyata: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra; several appear as sub-sthalas of the bhakta-sthala in the SSM (5.27–30).

definitions.definition: The highest dharma, attained by yoga (YS 1.8).
The eight virtues — compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed — without which the forty sacraments do not lead to Brahman (GDh 8.22–25).
The highest of the means to the supreme good, foremost of all sciences, by which immortality is gained (MDh 12.85).
The significator of the self: the planet with the highest degrees in its sign among seven (or eight) (Jaimini 1.1.11; BPHS 32.3); called the king among the kārakas.

In the Kārikā ch.2: the self, imagined like the rope-snake and ascertained; the deva who imagines himself by his own māyā. | In the Kārikā ch.3: like space; the jīvas are manifested from it as pot-spaces.
In this text: the self, which is brahman and has four quarters; Oṃ is just the self.

The self: in the Upaniṣads the innermost reality of a person — the seer of seeing that cannot be seen (BAU 3.4.2), the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the light of a person (BAU 4.3.6) — which is declared to be brahman (BAU 1.4.10, 2.5.19; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2). The word also means body or oneself in narrative passages (ChU 8.8.4).

Breath and self: Sūrya is the self of what moves and stands (RV 1.115.1); the dead man's breath (ātman) goes to the wind (10.16.3); Vāta is the self of the gods (10.168.4); knowing the wise, ageless, young self one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The embodied self, unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.20); to be raised by the self, being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); the Lord as the self in the heart of all beings (10.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self in which the one of steady wisdom is content — in the self alone, by the self (2.55) — and in which one who has nothing to do delights and is satisfied (3.17); knowing what is beyond the understanding (which 3.42 calls only 'he', saḥ; the commentators take it as the self), one steadies the self by the self (ātmānam ātmanā, 3.43). Also used reflexively and for one's person, nature or mind (vidheyātmā 2.64; vimūḍhātmā 3.6, 3.27; ātmavān 2.45; kāmātmānaḥ 2.43). The embodied one of 2.12–30 is called dehin or śarīrin, not ātman.

An eternal substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition, known by the marks desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition (NS 1.1.10); the knower, the one who remembers (NS 3.2.40).
An all-pervading substance marked by breath, eye-movements, life, mind's movement, desire, effort etc. (VS 3.2.4 C); many (VS 3.2.16 C); perceived by yogins (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition; two kinds: the supreme self (the one omniscient Lord) and the individual self, distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The inner self (pratyag-ātman): pure, self-luminous consciousness, the witness of the three states, not the body, senses, mind or ego; identical with Brahman.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the supreme self is changeless, eternal, the cause of consciousness with mind, elements and senses, the seer (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the knower of the field, all-pervading, witness, known by the marks of life (breath, blinking, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, memory, ego-sense) (Śā 1.59-85); knows only through its instruments (Śā 1.54-55).
Suśruta: the knowers of the field in Āyurveda are eternal but not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Used both reflexively (oneself, one's own mind: 'one should raise the self by the self', the self as its own friend or enemy, 6.5–6) and for the self in which all beings are seen (4.35, 6.29), in which the restrained citta rests (6.18) and the manas is made to abide (6.25) and which is seen by the self (6.20); the yoked yogin's self has become the self of all beings (5.7). In 4.35 and 6.29 the locative ātmani can also be read reflexively ('in oneself').

In ritual contexts the body or trunk (of the altar, of the sacrificer) that the rite constructs; in the teachings of Śāṇḍilya and Aśvapati the inner self 'made of mind, with breath for body' (ŚB 10.6.3).
The self to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), its own witness (MDh 8.84), one in all beings though appearing many like space in pots (YS 3.144).
The one self of the deity of which the many gods are limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The self, distinct from body and cognition, known to itself, shown by desire, memory and recognition; taught by negation ('not this, not this') (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; manifested as the subject in cognitions of objects (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Eternal, the agent and enjoyer who reaps the fruits of rites in another world; known through reasoning and made firm by the Upaniṣads (ŚV ātmavāda 148).

The eternal self, distinct from body, senses and intellect, known through the I-cognition and memory (SSM 5.55–60); dwelling in the heart like the hundredth part of a hair-tip, shining like a lamp (18.5–7).
The sūtras deny the self of persons and dharmas (Vajracchedikā 25); the Mahāparinirvāṇa calls the tathāgatagarbha 'self'; the Laṅkāvatāra says this is not the self of the tīrthikas.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The self: 'I am the self seated in the resting-place (āśaya) of all beings' (10.20). In ch. 10–12 the word is also often simply reflexive — the Lord knows himself by himself (10.15); 'show yourself' (11.4); 'by my own yoga' (11.47); 'self-restrained' (12.11, 12.14) — and in 11.24 antarātman is Arjuna's own inner being.
The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the bound self is the mind (3.1); the self is a dancer (3.9).
Only a figurative designation on the transformation of consciousness; the afflicted mind mistakes the store-consciousness for it.
A permanent self is refuted: nothing permanent can be causally efficacious; seeing a self is the root of attachment and all faults.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Read reflexively in ātma-vinigraha, 'restraint of oneself' (13.8), in 'in themselves, by themselves' (13.25), in 'does not harm oneself by oneself' (13.29), in 'praise of oneself' (14.24) and in 'abiding in themselves' (15.11); as 'the self' in 13.25 (ātmānam) and 13.33, where the self present in the body is unstained like space; the supreme self is paramātman (13.23, 13.32, 15.17).

Devotion as the Āḻvārs sing it (Tamil pattu/patti): love (aṉpu), longing (ārvam) and a melting heart offered to Tirumāl, given by his grace as 'knowledge-and-love', lived as service and refuge.
Supreme love (parama-prema) for the Lord, of the nature of nectar (NBS 2–3); supreme attachment (parānurakti) to Īśvara (ŚBS 2); not desire, not knowledge, not an act — the fruit itself.
Devotion to the Lord, by which he is known, seen and entered (BhG 11.54); supreme devotion is attained by one who has become Brahman (18.54), and by devotion one knows him in truth (18.55).
One-pointed devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, 'the one devoted solely, intent on Nārāyaṇa' (MBh 12.336).
Devotion: the natural, motiveless inclination of the senses and mind toward the Lord, greater than liberation; by it alone the Lord is attained; it purifies even outcastes.
Loving devotion to Rāma, the lamp without which knowledge does not shine and the cause of liberation; open to men, women and even animals.
Devotion to the Goddess, the easiest of the three paths, graded by the guṇas and culminating in supreme devotion.

Devotion to Śiva, ninefold (SSM 9.2–3), outer and inner (9.6–9), arising from grace and giving rise to grace (9.11–12); its presence, not birth, makes one a bhakta (9.4–5); in the six-bhakti scheme it rises from faith to samarasa.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The noun does not occur in chs. 4–6, but the verb bhaj- does: the Lord 'responds to' (bhajāmi) people in the way they approach him (4.11); the yogin established in oneness worships (bhajati) him as abiding in all beings (6.31); the one who worships (bhajate) him with faith and inner self fixed on him is the most yoked (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Devotion: the wise, knowing the Lord as the origin of all, worship (bhajante) him (10.8); to those ever yoked who worship him with love he gives the yoga of understanding (10.10); by undivided devotion alone he can be known, seen and entered in truth (11.54).

Unmotivated, uninterrupted love and service directed to the Lord, the highest dharma (BhP 1.2.6); graded by the guṇas and beyond them (3.29); ninefold in practice (7.5.23-24); the one means that 'wins' the Lord (11.14.20-21).
Meditation that has become love: knowledge in the form of supreme affection (prīti) for the Lord, the means to liberation prescribed by the Upaniṣads.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: four kinds of people of good deeds worship (bhaj) the Lord, the knower of single devotion (eka-bhakti) being foremost (7.16–17); devotion joins yoga-power at departure (8.10); the supreme Person is gained by undivided devotion (8.22); the great-souled bow to him with devotion (9.14); he partakes of a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with devotion (9.26); those who worship him with devotion are in him and he in them (9.29); his devotee does not perish (9.31); be my devotee (9.34).
Devotion: 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Unswerving devotion to the Lord is counted among the items called knowledge (13.11); unswerving bhakti-yoga carries one beyond the guṇas (14.26); whoever knows the Lord as the highest person worships (bhajati) him with his whole being (15.19).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Devotion: the one who has become Brahman attains supreme devotion to the Lord (18.54); by devotion he knows the Lord in truth — how great and who he is — and then enters him (18.55); 'be my devotee' (18.65); whoever, with supreme devotion, declares the secret to the Lord's devotees comes to him (18.68); the teaching is not to be told to one without devotion (18.67).

Devotion as the relish of identity with Śiva; for the one rich in devotion Śiva manifests without meditation or procedure (Śivastotrāvalī 1.1); the intense devotion of the dispassionate is Śaṅkara's power (VBT 121).
Tamil patti: 'devotion is the highest thing on earth' (Kaṭuveḷi 18); the Siddhars' devotion is to the Lord within and to the guru, not to temple images.

cross_language.note: as in 'pattuṭai aṭiyavar', TVM 1.3.1

definitions.definition: The relish of love for Kṛṣṇa, when the permanent emotion of love combines with its excitants, effects, bodily signs and transient emotions; the highest rasa.
The scriptures of devotion, to be reflected upon (NBS 76).
Serving the Lord with unswerving devotion, by which one passes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for Brahman (BhG 14.26); the theme of ch. 12.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva, the highest dharma (Nārāyaṇīya).
The yoga of devotion, fitting one in whom faith in the Lord's stories has arisen, who is neither disgusted with nor too attached to the world.
Bhagavad Gītā 14.26: one who serves Kṛṣṇa with the unswerving yoga of devotion, having gone beyond the guṇas, becomes fit for becoming brahman.
The loving meditation of the Upaniṣads, the direct means to the Lord, prepared by karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga and supported by the seven aids.

definitions.definition: The teachers of devotion named in NBS 83 (Kumāra, Vyāsa, Śuka, Śāṇḍilya, Garga, Viṣṇu, Kauṇḍinya, Śeṣa, Uddhava, Āruṇi, Bali, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa and others), who declare the same without fear.
'Vessel and universe': 'what is in the vessel (body) is in the universe' — the correspondence of body and cosmos.

cross_language.note: cf. 'yat piṇḍe tat brahmāṇḍe' in Nāth and haṭha usage

definitions.definition: The demon born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, slain by Lalitā with her powers (LSN 25-33; Lalitopākhyāna).
Insight seeing only the dissolution of formations, with eight benefits.
The 'whirling cave', the fourth region above Mahāsunn, where the flute is heard.
The staging of an aṅkīyā nāṭ in the nāmghar as an act of worship.
The bearer of the burden (Bhārahāra-sūtra), read as the person distinct from the burden of the aggregates.
The earlier aggregates, which harm the later, are spoken of as the bearer.

Lunar mansion bharaṇī: presiding deity Yama (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Venus (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Apabharaṇī; last in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa list.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: The principal act of prapatti: placing the burden of one's protection and its fruit on the Lord; often performed through a teacher.
The southern region of Jambūdvīpa, our world, subject to the ascending and descending time cycles (TS 3.10, 3.27).
The region south of the Himālaya and north of the ocean, the one land of action (karma-bhūmi), where the gods wish to be born.

literal: the knowledge of Bhṛgu taught by Varuṇa

definitions.definition: The knowledge that brahman is food, then breath, mind, understanding and finally bliss, reached by tapas at each step, established in the highest space (3.6.1).

definitions.definition: The fullness of Bhairava's state (bharitākārā, VBT 15) and of the practitioner (VBT 24, 72, 117).
Dramatic allegorical folk song in which a village character (scorpion-bitten man, Jogī, madwoman) carries a hidden spiritual meaning; perfected by Eknāth.
Ash, so called because it reproaches sins; bathing in ash is the supreme 'fire-bath' (SSM 7.4–5; 7.23–25).
Ash consecrated with the mantras, used for bathing thrice daily, lying on, re-bathing and initiation; the sign of the first stage.
The Atharvaśiras identifies all the elements with ash: 'fire is ash ... all this is ash'.
The ash of a cremation, smeared by a Kāpālika (Sattasaī) and listed by Yāmuna among the six Kāpāla insignia.
Sacred ash worn by Śaivas (often as the tripuṇḍra), praised in the Śiva Purāṇa.

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra / later Āyurveda): the calcined preparation of a metal, mineral or gem used as medicine; the texts insist that only properly purified and processed material is used, the impure being life-destroying (RRS 5.47-48, 5.73). RESTRICTED: no processes recorded.
Sacred ash from the sacred fire, smeared on all the limbs in the Pāśupata yoga.
Ash used in the Virajā initiation (Śiva Gītā).
Tirunīṟu, the sacred ash: mantra, medicine and the mark of Śiva's devotee.

notes: Also: vibhūti
alt_notes: Homonym: sacred ash of the Śaiva ascetics.

definitions.definition: Sacred ash, prepared with mantras; worn in the pāśupata vow and the tripuṇḍra.
Bathing the body in consecrated ash at the three junctures of the day.
The retention preceded by forceful bellows-breathing through the nose; it is said to awaken kuṇḍalinī and pierce the three knots.

A clothed Digambara cleric heading a seat (maṭha), who administers temples, institutions and learning and conducts rites; authority of the Bīsapantha, rejected by the Digambara Terāpantha; seats at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Mūḍabidri, Kolhapur and elsewhere.

The eight dispositions of buddhi — virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power and their opposites (SK 23) — innate, natural or acquired (SK 43), which perfume the subtle body (SK 40) and by seven of which prakṛti binds herself (SK 63).
Sensual, form and formless becoming, conditioned by clinging and conditioning birth (SN 12.2); 'the cessation of becoming is nibbāna' (SN 12.68).
A name of Rudra, paired with Śarva (AVŚ 11.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: State, being: understanding, knowledge, forbearance, pleasure and pain, fear and fearlessness and the rest are the various states (bhāva) of beings arising from the Lord alone (10.4–5); Arjuna asks in which bhāvas the Lord is to be contemplated (10.17); the wise worship him 'endowed with bhāva' (10.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Being/disposition: purity of disposition (bhāva-saṃśuddhi) is mental austerity (17.16); sāttvic knowledge sees one imperishable being (bhāva) in all beings, rājasic knowledge many beings (18.20–21).
A real existent or existence; with its opposite (abhāva) one of the two extremes: whoever sees existence and non-existence does not see the truth (MMK 15.6), and nirvāṇa is neither (25.4–10).
The practitioner's disposition that governs the mode of worship: paśu, vīra or divya; the Kālīvilāsa assigns them to the ages and allows only paśu in the Kali age (4.2-3; 6.10-16).
Emotion: the stage after attachment in Rūpa's sequence, pure sattva that softens the heart; in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi also the name of mahābhāva's threshold.

definitions.definition: (As reported) The third shaping force: each being's own nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā).

Emotional state; so called because, with speech, body and sattva, it 'brings into being' (bhāvayati) the meaning of the poem (NŚ 7.1–3); of three kinds — eight stable, thirty-three transient, eight involuntary; love directed to gods, gurus and kings remains a bhāva (KP 4).

literal: state, feeling; 'that which brings into being'
notes: Disambiguated from trm:bhava (used by other units for Sāṃkhya's bhāvas, Rudra's name 'Bhava' and the Gauḍīya stage 'bhāva').

definitions.definition: Devotion as emotion: the first sprouting of love, a ray of the sun of prema that softens the heart.

One of the twelve houses counted from the ascendant, each governing a domain of life — body, family and speech, siblings, mother and home, children and intellect, enemies and disease, spouse, longevity and death, fortune and dharma, action, gains, loss and liberation (BJ 1.15–18; BPHS 11).

notes: Homonym of bhāva 'emotion/state/being' in other traditions; id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: The state of the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti, which has becoming as its cause (1.19); Vijñānabhikṣu glosses bhava as birth.
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's power of poetic language to 'make present' its content in generalized form (reported by Abhinavagupta).

literal: the liṅga of feeling / of pure being

definitions.definition: The liṅga in which feeling (bhāva) itself dissolves, grasped by devotion and worshipped with flowers of feeling, superior to liṅgas of clay or stone (SSM 15.37–44); in the vacana triad iṣṭa–prāṇa–bhāva the third, beyond form.

notes: SSM 6.49–50 names the third liṅga of the triad tṛptiliṅga.

definitions.definition: Five contemplations for each vow, for its steadiness (7.3-7.8).
Cultivation: of the meaning of the praṇava (1.28), of the four attitudes (1.33), of the opposites of harmful thoughts (2.33); Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (YBh 3.23).

The operation of the one who brings about, expressed by the verbal suffix: verbal (śābdī) bhāvanā — the prompting power of the injunctive — and objective (ārthī) bhāvanā — the person's activity toward the result; each expects what (sādhya), by what (karaṇa) and how (itikartavyatā).
Contemplative identification: the body as Śrīcakra and worship as non-difference (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); its firmness brings the power of command (PKS 1.13); the Goddess is 'reached by bhāvanā' (LSN 41).

The task regarding the fourth truth: the path is to be developed (SN 56.11); the development of mind (cittabhāvanā) possible for one who understands the luminous mind (AN 1.52); development of concentration (AN 4.41) and of the faculties (MN 152).
VP 6.7.48-51: the three contemplations of beings - of Brahman, of action, and of both.
Cultivation that, carried to culmination, yields vivid non-conceptual cognition — yogic perception.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the unyoked lack; without it there is no peace (2.66). Commentators gloss it as steady contemplation, dwelling on the self, or conviction.
The impression produced by experience that causes memory; resides only in the self (Tarkasaṅgraha).

In Jainism (1) the five contemplations supporting each vow (TS 7.3–8); (2) the twelve reflections (anuprekṣā); (3) the four attitudes of friendliness and the rest; (4) in Haribhadra's Yogabindu, the second of five yogas.
sgom pa, meditation: 'without distraction is the king of meditation'; in Mahāmudrā not the fabrication of a state but becoming familiar (goms pa) with the recognized nature.

definitions.definition: The fourth path, through the remaining grounds, cultivating non-conceptual and subsequent wisdom until the diamond-like concentration.
Generating desire and effort so that unarisen wholesome states arise (SN 45.8). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four right efforts.
Undivided contemplation of one who has entered the state of power (20); contemplation again and again of the supreme state is japa (145); the supreme bhāvanā is immersion in Rudra's power (151).

The path of cultivation: mundane or pure, abandoning the defilements abandoned by cultivation grade by grade.
The first order of gods, living in mansions in the upper layer of the first earth: asura, nāga and other 'princes' (TS 4.10).

The resultant consciousness that maintains the continuity of an existence when no active process occurs; the same type as the rebirth-linking and death consciousness; identified by the commentary with the 'luminous mind'.
'The cessation of becoming is nibbāna' — seen clearly by Nārada without yet being touched with the body (SN 12.68).

Ignorance as a positive entity (not a mere absence of knowledge), held by the Vivaraṇa line and later Advaita, proved by the experience 'I am ignorant'; rejected as un-Śaṅkaran by Satchidanandendra (recent).
Second of the three cravings (DN 22:19).
Craving for continued existence, one of the three cravings (SN 56.11); those who hold back delight in becoming (Iti 49).

Knowing the self as distinct from body, karma and passions; the cause of liberation (Samayasāra-kalaśa 131; Iṣṭopadeśa 50).
The central practice of the Adhyātma path: discerning the knower from all that is known.
Difference-and-non-difference: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world (one as cause, many as effect).
Natural difference-and-non-difference of cit and acit from Brahman, like snake and coils.
Held to be inconceivable (acintya) in the relation of the Lord and his powers.
Taking the mendicant's garb: the Bāul initiation into renunciation (with the ālkhāllā robe), after the first initiation (dīkṣā).
The yogī's garb and, by extension, the Nāth order as a body ('the bhekh of the twelve panths').
The sectarian garb and marks of ascetics (ochre, matted locks, earrings, beads, ash), which the Sants reject as display.
A remedy — plants, waters, amulets and spells; Rudra has a thousand (RV 7.46.3); 'the waters are the remedy for all' (10.137.6).

Living by begged food, part of the renunciant discipline Cakradhar enjoined.
Living on alms, the mendicant's life (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22; cf. MuU 1.2.11).
One who lives on alms; four kinds in the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad.
Experience, which buddhi accomplishes for puruṣa (SK 37); with liberation, one of the two purposes for which prakṛti acts (commentaries on SK 21).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Enjoyments born of contact (saṃsparśaja bhoga) are wombs of sorrow, having a beginning and an end; the wise one does not delight in them (5.22).
Enjoyment, which in the Kula dharma 'becomes yoga' (Kulārṇava 2.24).

The regions other than Bhārata, where beings only enjoy the fruits of past deeds.
Regions where wish-fulfilling trees provide all needs, lifespans are long and liberation is not possible (TS 3.28–31).
The soul at the stages of prasādi and prāṇaliṅgi, correlated with the subtle body and the prāṇaliṅga.
The body, as the locus in which the self experiences pleasure and pain.
Limiting things used once (food) and things used repeatedly (clothes, dwellings) (TS 7.21).
the buddhi-side as object of enjoyment (YBh 2.6)

definitions.definition: Puruṣa as experiencer, one proof of its existence (SK 17); experience culminates in consciousness (SS 1.104).
Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The Lord is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices; not recognizing him in truth, worshippers of other deities fall (9.24).

definitions.definition: The pitta in the skin that gives lustre (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.14).
Delusion — above all the sectarian delusions of Hindu and Turk and the belief in outward means; 'bhram bidhauṃsaṇ' is its destruction.
The 'bee's cave' in the head, a place of inner absorption in Hindi Nāth and Sant songs.
The retention with a bee-like humming on inhalation and exhalation (HYP); in the GS a nocturnal practice of listening to the inner sounds with the ears closed, the means to nāda-samādhi.
Erroneous vision: false knowledge (YBh 1.30).
Humility — the attitude of a servant toward Śiva and his devotees (dāsōhaṃ).
The point between the eyebrows where gaze and mind are fixed; the HYP calls it the place of Śiva where the mind dissolves.
The twofold fruit that all four pādas of Śiva's scripture serve.
The double fruit of Kaula practice (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.15; Kulārṇava 3.11).
Plenitude: that in which one sees, hears and understands nothing else; it is happiness and immortal, established in its own greatness (ChU 7.23-24).
A plane of existence (thirty-one) or of consciousness (four).
The ten grounds of the bodhisattva from Joyful to Cloud of Dharma, each with a predominant perfection.

One of the ten grounds of the bodhisattva, the first beginning with the transformation of the basis on the path of seeing; the grounds are the antidotes to ten ignorances regarding the dharmadhātu (Madhyāntavibhāga 2.16).
The ten bodhisattva grounds from the Joyous (pramuditā) to the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), each marked by the predominance of a perfection (MA chs. 1–10).
Ground of the bodhisattva; ten in the Mahāvastu, from Hard to Enter to Consecration.
Plane (of existence or of meditation): the nine planes — desire realm, four dhyānas, four formless — in which defilements are abandoned grade by grade.

Not required as a separate condition of birth in Hōnen's reading of the three grades (a point Myōe attacked).
The other-power aspiration for awakening, crosswise transcending: it is shinjin itself, given by Amida.
The mind wishing for complete awakening for the sake of all beings, generated after love and the sight of beings' suffering; aspiring bodhicitta grows only with the engaging vow.
The second principal aspect: renunciation held by bodhicitta becomes the cause of buddhahood; generated by the seven-point cause-and-effect instruction or by equalizing and exchanging self and other.
Absence of attachment to one's own purpose (Parting 3); relative and ultimate bodhicitta under the experiential vision.

The mind of awakening: conventional (the aspiration) and ultimate (emptiness and compassion inseparable, 'free of all entities … one's own mind unborn', GST 2); in the completion stage also the white drop.
In the mind series, bodhicitta (byang chub kyi sems) is the primordial nature itself, the 'all-creating king': 'byang' purified, 'chub' all-pervading, 'sems' the unceasing all-maker.

byang chub kyi sems: (1) the aspiration for awakening for others' sake, aspiring and engaging, relative and ultimate (Jewel Ornament); (2) mind's nature itself, 'the root of all phenomena' (Tilopa); (3) in the completion stage, the white element of the subtle body.

In the Ṛgveda, the potent sacred formulation or prayer and the power in it (Bṛhaspati/Brahmaṇaspati is its lord); in the Atharvaveda and Yajurveda, the highest principle: 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33).

The one reality without a second: existence–consciousness–bliss, attributeless (nirguṇa) in itself, identical with the inner self; associated with māyā it is Īśvara, the world-cause.

In Dvaita the word applies primarily to Viṣṇu alone, 'full' (pūrṇa) in qualities; defined as that from which come creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release.

Bhagavad Gītā 7.29; 8.1, 8.3, 8.13, 8.24: asked 'what is that brahman?', the Lord answers: the supreme imperishable (akṣaraṃ brahma paramam); those who take refuge in him to be free of age and death know 'that brahman' entirely; Oṃ is the one-syllable brahman; knowers of brahman go to brahman by the bright path.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: every factor of the sacrifice is Brahman and Brahman is to be reached by one absorbed in action as Brahman (4.24); sacrifice is offered into the fire of Brahman (4.25) and the sacrifices are spread 'in the mouth of Brahman' (4.32); eaters of the sacrifice's remainder go to the eternal Brahman (4.31); the yoked sage soon reaches Brahman (5.6); actions are 'placed in Brahman' (5.10); Brahman is flawless and the same, and those whose mind rests in sameness are established in it (5.19–20).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, said to be neither sat nor asat (13.13), described in 13.14–18; one who sees the separate existence of beings as resting in the one and spreading from it attains brahman (13.31); by unswerving devotion one becomes fit for becoming brahman (14.26); Kṛṣṇa is the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) of brahman (14.27). In 14.3–4 'the great brahman' is Kṛṣṇa's womb (see mahad brahma).
In the Brāhmaṇas: the sacred formulation and the Veda; also the first principle — 'in the beginning this was Brahman' (ŚB 11.2.3.1), 'Brahman the self-existent' (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 13.7.1.1; GB 1.1.1).
The supreme reached by self-knowledge and seeing the self in all (MDh 12.125); 'the one syllable is the supreme Brahman' (VDh 10.5).

The imperishable supreme (BhG 8.3), beginningless, neither being nor non-being (13.12), with hands and feet everywhere (13.13); also the Veda from which ritual action arises (3.15) and the prakṛti called 'great Brahman', the Lord's womb (14.3); 'na mama' is the eternal Brahman (MBh 12.13.4).
In the Purāṇas the supreme reality, identified with Viṣṇu (VP), Śiva (ŚiP), or the Goddess (DBhP); one of three names of non-dual knowledge (BhP 1.2.11).
The supreme reality, Nārāyaṇa, great in essence and qualities and making others great; qualified (saviśeṣa) by souls and matter, never an attributeless consciousness.
The liṅga itself, so named for its vastness and expanding (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga of light by whose light all shines (12.38–41).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna calls Kṛṣṇa 'the supreme brahman (paraṃ brahma), the supreme abode, the supreme purifier' (10.12).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: '[Oṃ] tat sat' is the threefold designation of Brahman (17.23); the one who has attained perfection attains Brahman, 'the highest culmination of knowledge' (18.50); the discipline of 18.51–53 makes one fit for becoming Brahman (brahma-bhūya), and the one who has become Brahman attains supreme devotion (18.54).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.72 in the compounds brāhmī sthiti and brahmanirvāṇa (the state and goal of the one of steady wisdom). In 3.15 'brahma' arises from the imperishable and is the source of action, and the 'all-pervading brahman' is established in sacrifice; commentators take brahma in 3.15 as the Veda or as prakṛti.
U04 usage: the one reality realized as 'so'ham'; the soundless beyond nāda; the goal of renunciation; named as Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Rāma or the Goddess in the sectarian Upaniṣads.
Sundardās: the one without a second, known at the end of the path as one's own self.
Brahm is the ruler of Trikuṭī and the universal mind, the highest god of the Vedas but within Kāl's domain; Pārbrahm is the region above it.

The instrument of cognition (the 'power of seeing') whose apparent identity with the seer is I-am-ness (YBh 2.6); neither the same as the puruṣa nor wholly different (YBh 2.20).
The understanding, higher than mind (BhG 3.42); resolute and one in the yogin (2.41); its destruction follows loss of memory (2.63); threefold by the guṇas (18.29–32).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the instruments with which yogins act for self-purification (5.11); the intellect held in firmness (dhṛti) by which the mind is gradually brought to rest (6.25); the boundless happiness is 'grasped by the buddhi' beyond the senses (6.21); the fallen yogin regains the connection with understanding (buddhi-saṃyoga) of his former body (6.43); sama-buddhi = equal regard (6.9).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Understanding: first among the states of beings that come from the Lord (10.4); the worshippers of the imperishable are even in understanding everywhere (samabuddhi, 12.4); 'let your understanding enter into me' (12.8); the dear devotee has manas and buddhi offered to the Lord (12.14). Named distinctly from manas, citta and cetas.
Bhagavad Gītā 13.6: listed among the constituents of the field; 15.20: understanding this teaching one becomes possessed of buddhi (buddhimat).

A purified understanding is the first element of the discipline of 18.51; an untainted understanding marks the one who does not slay though slaying (18.17); an untrained understanding sees the self alone as agent (18.16).

The intellect is conventional; reality is not within its domain (BCA 9.2).

Wonder, the life of rasa (SD 3.3); for Abhinavagupta the self-relishing of consciousness in aesthetic experience; for Viśvanātha's ancestor Nārāyaṇa the reason why the marvellous is the one rasa.

Kālī's name after slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (DM 7).
Inner heat, 'the fierce woman' who blazes at the navel and melts the moon at the head (Hevajra I.1); one of Tilopa's six dharmas; restricted practice.

gtum mo, 'the fierce one', inner heat: the yoga of kindling heat at the navel, melting the drops and bringing winds into the central channel, 'the main trunk of the path' and 'armour' of the six yogas; restricted practice.

equivalents.note: Both are a feminine inner power at the base/navel rising through the central channel; the systems and goals differ (Buddhist: melting bliss joined with emptiness).

definitions.definition: The fierce Goddess of the Devī Māhātmya.
The moon in the head / at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58; SS 2.6–9); the left channel; in the Amṛtasiddhi identified with bindu.
The moon at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58); the left side and left nostril (AmŚ 71).

The Moon among the grahas: the mind (manas) of Kālapuruṣa and a king (BJ 2.1); female, vaiśya, sattva, of vāta–kapha constitution (BJ 2.6–8); rules Cancer, exalted in Taurus 3°; period 10 years; Kṛṣṇa is born from him (BPHS 2.5); the natal Moon is the base for transits (BS 103).
Where the Kubjikā teaching was first given (Kubjikāmata 1, 'Candradvīpāvatāra'; 2.21).
Where the Kaula scripture came down, brought by Matsyendra (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.12).
The penance in which food follows the waning and waxing moon (MDh 11.216) — restricted content.
the body of one whose afflictions are worn away, the only place of the burnt-seed state (YBh 2.4)

definitions.definition: The body in which a soul will attain liberation; its lifespan cannot be cut short (TS 2.53).
Bhagavad Gītā 18.66, read as the Lord's command to surrender to him alone, with the promise of freedom from all sins.
The last cycle of matter-transformation (pudgala-parāvarta) before liberation, in which alone yoga takes hold (Yogabindu, Yogaviṃśikā).
A school of Vedic study and ritual practice, often coextensive with a śākhā and its sūtras.

The 'four moons': coded name for four bodily substances whose secret handling under a guru belongs to Bāul body practice; recorded only as a name (restricted), with the tradition's warnings that it is secret and ruinous without a guru.

notes: RESTRICTED: no method or substance-handling details are recorded.

definitions.definition: The four things of the dharma: the name (nāma), God (deva), the guru and the community of devotees (bhakta).
(Jain report) The 'eight finalities' proclaimed around Gosāla's death: last drink, song, dance, salutation, storm-cloud, sprinkling elephant, battle of stones, and the last tīrthaṅkara.

The six temperaments (greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent, speculative); 'cariyā', 'pakati' and 'ussannatā' are one in meaning; discerned by posture, work, eating, seeing and the arising of states, with the text's caution that this is by the teachers' opinion (Vism III p. 101-107).
The six temperaments — greedy, hating, deluded, faithful, intelligent, speculative — determining suitable meditation subjects.

definitions.definition: Right conduct, of five kinds — equanimity, re-initiation, special purificatory austerity, subtle passion, perfect conduct (TS 9.18).
The twenty-five karmas deluding conduct: sixteen passions and nine quasi-passions (TS 8.9).
The Kaula sacrificial food (caru) of the non-dual rite (caru-advaita), including substances ordinarily forbidden; restricted, summary only (KJN 11).
Name of the materialist school, after its legendary teacher Cārvāka, Bṛhaspati's disciple; explained by Guṇaratna as those who 'chew up' merit, demerit and the unseen.
'Chewing': the relishing through which rasa exists — for Abhinavagupta rasa is not a thing produced but consists in this relishing and lasts as long as it lasts.
The series of acts from ash-bathing to feigned folly; threefold as gift, worship and austerity; twofold as vows and doors; the second means to the gains.
(1) The yogin's conduct or observance (spyod pa), undertaken after realization; (2) the caryā songs (caryāgīti) sung to rāgas at the feast.
spyod pa, conduct: 'without effort is the king of conduct' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā); conduct follows the view — from renunciate discipline to the 'madman's conduct' of the realized.
Conduct: the first of the four pādas (and a section of each Āgama) — rules of life and service.
Cariyai: temple service — cleaning, lamps, garlands, singing — the servant's path (dāsa-mārga), leading to sālokya.
Conduct of the bodhisattva; four — natural, of the vow, conforming, not turning back.
Conduct (or performance) tantra: balancing outer ritual and inner yoga (e.g. the Mahāvairocana, Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka); second of the fourfold classification.

notes: Homonym: 'caryā' also names the siddhas' conduct and their songs (trm:carya).

definitions.definition: Caste (birth-group), which the Siddhars declare baseless — 'is there a difference in flesh, skin and bone?' (Sivavākkiyar); 'the castes called unequal are one' (Kaṭuveḷi 32).

equivalents.note: Tamil form of jāti (in the social sense)

definitions.definition: Taking the four refuges — the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Sādhus and the dharma taught by the omniscient — recited with the 'four auspicious things' and 'four highest things'.

cross_language.note: the liturgical formula

definitions.definition: The sixty-four Bhairava tantras in eight groups of eight (Śrīkaṇṭhīya).
The sixty-four tantras 'of the Mothers' named in the Vāmakeśvara, by which Paśupati 'beguiled the world' before revealing the Goddess's own tantra (Saundaryalaharī 31).
The circle of sixty-four yoginīs worshipped in hypaethral circular temples (Hirapur, Ranipur-Jharial, Bheraghat, Mitaoli); their names differ between lists.
The four verses spoken by the Lord to Brahmā (BhP 2.9.32-35), held to be the seed of the whole Bhāgavata.
The four forms — is, is not, both, neither — in which each of Sañjaya's four questions is put and each refused.

notes: The term catukkoṭi is later than DN 2; the fourfold question form is in the text.

literal: made of the four great elements

definitions.definition: (As reported) 'This person is made of the four great elements', which at death return to their masses.

The four months of the rains during which mendicants stop wandering and stay in one place to avoid harming the many beings that appear, the season of teaching, austerities and Paryuṣaṇa for the laity.

equivalents.note: the Buddhist rains retreat serves the same purpose of not wandering in the rains

definitions.definition: The four seals: action seal, dharma seal, great seal and pledge seal, which Advayavajra orders as stages leading from the action seal to the pledge seal.
Saraha criticizes those who 'set out the four seals by distinguishing the moments' and take the experience for the innate (King Dohā v27).
the one that goes beyond the external and internal spheres (YS 2.51)

definitions.definition: The fourth consecration, 'ultimate' (Sekoddeśa 8), introducing the innate gnosis; in Tibetan often the 'word consecration'.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma, though he is the imperishable non-doer (4.13).
The fourfold order created by the Lord according to the division of guṇas and actions (BhG 4.13).

definitions.definition: The fourfold community founded by each Tīrthaṅkara: monks (sādhu), nuns (sādhvī), laymen (śrāvaka) and laywomen (śrāvikā); itself called the 'ford' (tīrtha).
Praise of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras (the Logassa hymn); one of the six essential duties.
The fourfold scheme of the Yoga śāstra modelled on medicine — saṃsāra, its cause, liberation, the means (YBh 2.15).
The four emanations (vyūha) of the Lord: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha.

notes: Homonym: the same word names a fourfold expository scheme (Yoga, after medicine) and the Pāñcarātra doctrine of four emanations. Recorded so the two are not confused.

definitions.definition: The four alternatives — is, is not, both, neither (or: from self, from other, from both, without cause) — each of which is rejected (MMK 1.1; 22.11; 25.17–18) or, in 18.8, used as a graded teaching.

In 4.83–4.84: the four corners (koṭyaś catasraḥ, 4.84), "it exists", "it does not exist", "it exists and does not exist", "it does not exist, it does not exist", with moving, still, both and non-being, by whose graspings the Lord is covered and by which the childish cover [it]. definitions.definition: The four pillars of treatment — physician, medicine, attendant, patient — each with four qualities (Ca Sū 9.3-9; AHS Sū 1.27).
(Buddhist report) Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's teaching: the Nigaṇṭha is curbed, yoked, cleansed and pervaded by all 'waters' (vāri).
(Jain account) Cāujjāma, the law of four restraints taught by Pārśva, as against Mahāvīra's five vows.
The 'fourfold restraint' taught by Pārśva — from violence, falsehood, theft and possessions — which Mahāvīra expanded into five great vows by making chastity explicit.

cross_language.note: the Pali canon attributes a 'fourfold restraint' to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta

definitions.definition: The square ritual ground and rite (caukā āratī) of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth, performed for initiation and for the dead, with coconut, betel and lamps.
The round of 8.4 million species of birth through which the soul wanders; the human birth, rare within it, is the only chance to be freed.
The true or perfect reality — the Real, Śiva; in the Kuṟaḷ the reality to be seen for birth to end.
A red calcined preparation of a metal or mineral.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: Sentient dependent beings: Lakṣmī (eternally untouched by sorrow) and all souls, divided by their relation to sorrow and their fitness.
Puruṣa is conscious; the manifest and unmanifest are unconscious (acetana) (SK 11); the unconscious liṅga appears conscious through conjunction (SK 20).
'It is intention that I call kamma' (AN 6.63); one of the four nutriments (mental volition) and a component of name (SN 12.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'Of beings I am cetanā' (10.22): the sentience or awareness of living beings, named beside manas as chief of the faculties.
Volition: the factor that organizes its associates in acting on the object; it is kamma (the Buddha: 'volition is kamma').
Bhagavad Gītā 13.7: listed among the constituents of the field (with desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate and steadiness) — i.e. on the side of the field, not of its knower.
Volition, a universal mental factor; mental karma itself, from which bodily and vocal karma arise.
Mental karma includes covetousness, malice and wrong view themselves.
Volition, a universal mental factor; in Vasubandhu's Karmasiddhi, action itself.
The soul as consciousness; in the Samayasāra Nāṭaka the hero of the drama of self and non-self.
Mental action; bodily and verbal action is what is done having intended (MMK 17.2–3).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Awareness (cetas): the hardship is greater for those whose cetas is attached to the unmanifest (12.5); the Lord soon delivers from the ocean of death and saṃsāra those whose cetas is set on him (12.7); seeing the gentle form again, Arjuna is 'sacetāḥ', with his cetas restored (11.51). Named distinctly from manas, buddhi and citta.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Thought: those who have not formed themselves and lack thought (acetas) do not see the one abiding in themselves, even though they strive (15.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Thought: Arjuna is to renounce all actions in the Lord 'in thought' (cetasā, 18.57); Kṛṣṇa asks whether he heard with one-pointed thought (ekāgra cetas, 18.72); those who torment the body with unsanctioned austerity are 'thoughtless' (acetas, 17.6).

definitions.definition: A mental factor that arises and ceases together with consciousness, has the same object and base; fifty-two are enumerated.
Liberation of mind — immeasurable, through nothingness, emptiness, signless, and the unshakeable (MN 43); with liberation by wisdom, the arahant's attainment (AN 3.33).
Countering a statement by supposing an alternative meaning; verbal, generalizing and figurative (NS 1.2.10–17).
Transcription of dhyāna; in the Platform Sūtra 'inwardly seeing the unmoving self-nature'; also the name of the school.

equivalents.note: Chan transcribes dhyāna, but as a school name it means the lineage of the buddha-mind, and the Platform Sūtra redefines it as seeing the self-nature rather than a meditative absorption.

definitions.definition: Wholesome desire to act, the first basis of power (SN 51.20); in 'kāmacchanda' sensual desire.
Wish to act regarding the object; ethically variable; one of the four predominants.
Vedic metre; the metres came from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9).

Metre, the 'feet' of the Veda (PŚ 41); so called because the gods covered (chad) themselves with the metres against death (ChU 1.4.2). In Pāṇini, also the Vedic language as opposed to ordinary speech.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The metres (or the hymns in them): the field and its knower have been sung in them (13.5); they are the leaves of the aśvattha (15.1).

definitions.definition: Concentration due to desire with formations of striving (SN 51.20). One of the thirty-seven qualities conducive to awakening (DN 16.3.50; MN 149): a member of the four bases of power.
Chan's name for itself as against the 'teaching gate' (jiaomen) of the doctrinal schools.
The 'shadow planets' Rāhu and Ketu, without bodies of light, counted with the seven as the nine grahas.

The cutting of the tongue's frenum prescribed, together with 'moving' (cālana) and 'milking' (dohana), in the preparation for khecarī. RESTRICTED: recorded as a term only; the procedure is not reproduced.

A canonical text of monastic law, fixing the atonements for transgressions; named from 'cheda' (cutting of seniority), one of the atonements. Six for Mūrtipūjakas, four for Sthānakavāsīs; traditionally studied only by mature monks.
The fourth stage, ending in the cutting [of bonds], in the cremation ground.
The second of the five kinds of cāritra in the Digambara list (TS 9.18).

The 'great initiation' (baḍī dīkṣā): the second, definitive ordination in which the novice is placed in the vows one by one after learning the Daśavaikālika's fourth chapter; also the name of the second of the five kinds of conduct.

definitions.definition: Meditation that repeatedly investigates its object with discernment — for faith, impermanence, bodhicitta and emptiness — as opposed to placement; necessary, not an obstacle.
Calling (vocally reciting) the Buddha's name; for Shandao the rightly determined act, easy for beings whose minds are too coarse for contemplation.
Shōmyō: saying the name, the great practice (Kyōgyōshinshō, Gyō); for the person of shinjin, gratitude.
An emptiness that is a mere nothing; for the Jonang the error of taking the ultimate to be a non-affirming negation.
The gaps in the mind flowing as discrimination, in which other cognitions arise from earlier saṃskāras (4.27).
