definitions.definition: Ransoming or cheating death: rites (such as saving the lives of animals and offering effigies) performed when signs of untimely death appear.
The sixth Mahāvidyā; her Bhairava is Kabandha, by whose worship one becomes lord of all powers (Toḍala 1.12-13); matched with Nṛsiṃha (10.9).
Buddhadāsa's term for a mind void of 'I' and 'mine', with which one should work and live.
The mind free of self-grasping, the practical form of suññatā.
Signs of death: outer (bodily), inner (breath) and secret (dream) signs that death is approaching.
The practice of cutting ego-clinging, the root of the four māras, by applying the view of the Perfection of Wisdom, especially through the visualized gift of the body in frightening places.
The (often wandering) practitioner of Chöd, known for practice in haunted places and for being called on in epidemics and at deaths.
Impartiality, paired with ris med in the formula phyogs med ris med.
Leaving as it is: the four ways of leaving things as they are (view like a mountain, meditation like an ocean, conduct as appearances, fruit as awareness).

literal: the object to be cut; the 'domain' of cutting

definitions.definition: Both the name of the practice and what it targets: the root of mind, self-clinging.
Examination of urine while warm, cooling and cold, for colour, vapour, odour, bubbles, sediment and film.
Rejuvenation regimens and essences that restore vigour and prolong life (in their retreat forms, which restrict ordinary food, restricted: summary only).

equivalents.note: the rejuvenation branch

definitions.definition: The semblance or reflection of consciousness in the intellect, which makes the inner organ appear conscious; together with the kūṭastha it constitutes the jīva.
The space of consciousness: the knower within and without all beings that reveals existence; mind-space and elemental space arise from it.
'The space of consciousness': Chidambaram (Tillai), where Śiva dances in the 'small hall' (ciṟṟampalam); also the heart-space.
The bliss of consciousness gained by unfolding the centre, which, made firm, is liberation in life (PH 16-17).
The self as consciousness and bliss (YŚ 10.1; Jñānasāra; the pen-name of the poet Cidānanda).
'The play of consciousness': the name later given to Jñāneśvar's teaching in the Amṛtānubhava that the one reality sports as the world without change or second.
The mode of worship of Tārā/Nīlasarasvatī learned in Mahācīna; Vasiṣṭha was sent there by the Goddess and taught the Kula way by the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).
The palace of wish-gems at the centre of Śrīnagara, whose four doors are the four transmissions (PKS 3.10; LSN 22; SL 8).
Sentient reality: the individual souls, eternal, atomic knowers, bound, freed or eternally free; one of the three realities.
Consciousness: self-luminous awareness, the nature of the self and of Brahman, never an object.
The conscious reality: the souls, one of the three realities.
Consciousness-power: the Goddess as the power of the sentient, who is also the power of the insentient (LSN 90).
Śiva's power of consciousness, inseparable from him, identified with Umā and with the supreme ether; the world subsists in it subtly.
Consciousness as free power, the cause of the universe (PH 1); contracted, it is the individual and the mind (PH 4-5); its essence is reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13).
The puruṣa as the power of consciousness: unchanging, not passing over into objects, pure and infinite (YBh 1.2); kaivalya is its establishment in its own form (4.34).

Awareness placed at the end of the visarga (91); supportless awareness which is Śakti shows one's own form (92); the body or world contemplated as made of consciousness (63); dissolution in consciousness (117).

notes: Sense-specific id for the Vijñānabhairava; the bare-word ids in data/ mix other traditions' senses.

definitions.definition: Vācaspati's name for puruṣa as consciousness, to which suffering is disagreeable (on SK 1, 5).

Lunar mansion citrā: presiding deity Tvaṣṭṛ (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mars (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class soft (mṛdu) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). The star Citrā marks the start of Libra in the Citrāpakṣa ayanāṃśa.
Yama's recorder of the deeds of beings, consulted at judgment.
A subtle channel within suṣumnā (within vajrā, per the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa), 'dear to Śiva', in which is the brahmarandhra (SS 2.18).

In this part of the text: the mind is coloured by the seer and the seen and so is 'all-objective' (4.23); it is not self-luminous because it is seen (4.19); though variegated by countless vāsanās it is for another, since it acts in combination (4.24); when discrimination-inclined it slopes towards kaivalya (4.26).

The mind, a product of prakṛti made of the three guṇas, whose activities are to be stilled; it is seen, not self-luminous, and exists for the sake of the puruṣa; one, having many objects, and enduring (YBh 1.32). Commentators gloss it as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

The mind that changes day and night like a monkey (SN 12.61); luminous but defiled by adventitious defilements (AN 1.51–52); to be tamed (Dhp 35); the third establishment of mindfulness; also an iddhipāda (concentration through mind).
Consciousness, the bare knowing of an object and forerunner of the mental factors; the first ultimate reality, classified into 89 (or 121) types; synonymous with viññāṇa and mano.

The heart-mind, 'the one who knows' (Thai: phu ru): the knowing nature which the forest teachers train and purify and which, when released, is described as pure and not subject to death (Ajahn Maha Boowa).
The noting mind, observed arising and passing together with its object.

Explained (Trisvabhāvanirdeśa 7) as twofold: the store, called citta because it is 'accumulated' (cita) with seeds of defilement, and the operative mind, called citta because it arises with 'variegated' (citra) images; in the triad citta–manas–vijñāna it is the ālaya.
Any momentary cognition, which is reflexively aware of itself; mind arises from a previous moment of mind, not from the body alone.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Thought (citta), to be restrained in meditation (6.10, 6.12 — where it is the manas that is made one-pointed); when thoroughly controlled it rests in the self alone (6.18), like a lamp in a windless place (6.19); restrained (niruddha) by the practice of yoga it comes to rest (6.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Thought (citta): the devotees have their citta on the Lord (maccittāḥ, 10.9); if one cannot hold the citta steadily fixed on him, the yoga of practice is prescribed (12.9).

Thought: a rung above intention in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.5); with whatever thought one has one enters breath at death (PrU 3.10); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (cittam eva hi saṃsāraḥ, MaiU 6.34).
The inner organ as remembering and reflecting (in the fourfold Advaita division); in general usage, mind.
Mind, synonymous with manas and vijñāna; it always arises together with mental factors, and they share support, object, aspect, time and substance.
Mind is by nature luminous and pure, defiled only by adventitious defilements (Vasumitra).

definitions.definition: The space of mind: the creator pervading all through its conceiving.
'This triple world is mind only' (Daśabhūmika 6); the world is what is seen of one's own mind (Laṅkāvatāra); buddhas seen in samādhi are mind-made (Pratyutpanna).

Accepted as the account of conventional reality — external objects do not exist — before understanding that mind too lacks self (MAL 92–93).
The sūtra's 'mind only' denies a creator other than mind, not external form; teachings denying external objects are of provisional meaning (MA 6).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one's own deed of a former body (Ca Vi 3.30; Śā 1.116; 2.44); balanced against present effort (Vi 3.29-36).
The divine or fated factor, the fifth cause of action (BhG 18.14); which does not bear fruit without human effort, as a seed without a field (MBh 13.6.7).

In jyotiṣa, fate: karma, good and bad, produced in another birth, which yields birth in a good family and the like, and bears fruit together with human effort, as in farming (Yogayātrā 1.3–4); it is what the horā reveals (BJ 1.3).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The field of the battle is the 'field of dharma' (1.1). In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas and the dharmas of the birth-group perish when a family is destroyed, and adharma prevails (1.40–43); he is bewildered about dharma (2.7). Kṛṣṇa speaks of svadharma: for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (dharmya, 2.31, 2.33); one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's (3.35); even a little of 'this dharma' (the yoga of understanding) protects from great fear (2.40).

The whole of right conduct — ritual, moral, social and legal — rooted in the Veda, smṛti, the practice of the good and self-approval (MDh 2.6); it protects when protected and alone follows one after death (MDh 8.15–17; 4.238–242); its tenfold mark is steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth and absence of anger (MDh 6.92).
The merit that correct usage of words brings, for which grammar restricts usage (first vārttika).

The upholding order and right conduct: its decline occasions the Lord's descent (BhG 4.7); one's own dharma is better than another's (3.35); it is subtle (MBh 8.49) and its truth hidden (vulgate Yakṣapraśna); from it come artha and kāma (18.5.49); non-cruelty is its highest form (3.297.55).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) leading to upward movement (SK 44), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda defines it by compassion, giving and the yamas and niyamas of the Pātañjala. With knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to act as causes (SK 67).

That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); a quality of the self produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); the knowledge of the categories arises from dharma manifested by the Lord's command (Praśastapāda).

The beneficial object (artha) whose defining mark is Vedic injunction (codanā) — concretely the sacrifice and other enjoined acts, which join a person with the highest good; what is enjoined but harmful (e.g. the Śyena, whose aim is violence) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose, made known by the Veda (Arthasaṅgraha): the sacrifice and the like.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.7–8: dharma, whose decline together with the rise of adharma is the occasion of the Lord's coming into being, and whose firm establishment is one of its purposes, age after age.

Dharma: created by brahman as the power of the ruling power, higher than all; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); Naciketas asks for what is other than dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14); one's own dharma rescues the elemental self (MaiU 4.3).
An ultimate constituent that 'holds its own characteristic' (svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇa); seventy-five kinds in five groups, existing as real entities (dravya) in all three times.
A momentary event in a series; only present dharmas exist, and many Vaibhāṣika dharmas are mere designations.
In the Triṃśikā's 'self and dharmas', the factors of existence of Abhidharma, which are only figuratively designated on the transformation of consciousness and lack imagined own-nature.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The Lord is the foundation of everlasting (śāśvata) dharma (14.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna calls the Lord 'the unchanging guardian of the eternal dharma' (11.18); the teaching of the dear devotee's marks is 'this nectar of dharma' (dharmyāmṛta, 12.20).

In Jainism (1) the medium of motion (dharmāstikāya); (2) the tenfold virtue beginning with forbearance (TS 9.6); (3) the three jewels; (4) the nature of a thing and the protection of beings (Kārttikeyānuprekṣā 478).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: 'Abandoning all dharmas, go to me alone for refuge' (18.66 — the verse does not say which dharmas); rājasic understanding knows dharma and adharma incorrectly and tāmasic takes adharma for dharma (18.31–32); rājasic steadiness holds to dharma, desire and wealth (18.34); one's own dharma is better than another's (18.47); the dialogue is 'in accord with dharma' (dharmya, 18.70).

Meditation examining the Jina's command, the harm of wrong ways, the fruition of karma and the structure of the universe (TS 9.36); leads to heaven and toward liberation.

definitions.definition: In prakaraṇa 4: a "dharma" is a thing or state that is known or said to be born or unborn; all dharmas are said to be unborn, sky-like, awakened from the beginning, pure, peaceful and equal.

definitions.definition: The inquiry into dharma through the investigation of Vedic sentences, undertaken after Vedic study and before returning from the teacher's house (MS 1.1.1 with Śabara).
The absence of an imagined own-nature in dharmas themselves, entered through the teaching of cognition-only; knowing it removes the cognitive obscuration.
The change of a property-bearer's manifest property (e.g. emergence giving way to stilling; lump to pot) (3.13).
The capacity-yoga in which the qualities arising from destruction-cum-subsidence are given up (at the second apūrvakaraṇa) (YDS).
One who keeps, recites, explains and copies a sūtra; in the Lotus the Tathāgata's messenger.

Attributive consciousness: the soul's (and the Lord's) consciousness as a quality distinct from the self-luminous substrate; eternal, it contracts in bondage through karma and expands fully in liberation; it goes out to objects as a lamp's light.
The Buddha's teaching as a turning wheel; the Saṃdhinirmocana distinguishes three turnings of differing definitiveness.
The totality and true nature of dharmas; in the Avataṃsaka the boundless realm filled by Vairocana in which all worlds interpenetrate; synonym of suchness.

A synonym of emptiness, so called because it is the cause of the noble dharmas; directly perceived when mind-only is itself abandoned; in its purity it is the buddhas' body operating as the three bodies.
The expanse of reality (chos dbyings), in which all phenomena arise as display — the theme of Longchenpa's Chöying Dzöd.
chos dbyings: the expanse; its stainless wisdom is the fifth wisdom into which the eight consciousnesses resolve (3rd Karmapa).
One of the five gnoses: gnosis of the dharma-sphere (purified consciousness / delusion), tathāgata family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

cross_language.form: chos kyi dbyings kyi ye shes

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: Dharma-knowledge: pure knowledge of the truths regarding the desire realm.
The Buddha as the dharma / suchness, not his physical form: 'the guides have the dharma for body'; not sick, not fed by food; later the first of the three bodies.
The dharmakāya is the tathāgatagarbha freed from defilements; it is permanent, blissful, self and pure and pervades all beings.

The buddhas' body as the purified dharmadhātu; in the three-body scheme the natural body, basis of the other two; at the Triṃśikā's close, the transformed basis 'called the dharma-body of the great sage'.
In Tanluan two dharma-bodies: of dharma-nature and of expedient means, different but inseparable; the Rebirth Treatise's 'uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom'.
The formless dharma-body as suchness from which Dharmākara appeared; Amida is the means to know jinen.
The dharma-body, personified as Samantabhadra; in Dzogchen the ground recognized, empty essence.
The dharma body: 'liberation in an instant is called dharmakāya' (Queen Dohā v8); appearances and sounds are primordially dharmakāya (Tōh 2292 no. 30).
The truth body of the Buddhas, born from the collection of wisdom (RĀ 3.12–13).
chos sku: the emptiness of mind itself, unborn; 'the essence of thought is dharmakāya'; recognized at death as the clear light by those of highest faculties.
The ultimate itself, permanent and the true self (perfection of self), not newly produced at awakening.

equivalents.note: Pali DN 27 'Tathāgata has the dhamma as body' is an epithet; the Mahāyāna makes it a body of the Buddha

definitions.definition: The samādhi that arises for one without desire even in prasaṃkhyāna, from discrimination-vision in every way (4.29); from it the cessation of afflictions and karma (4.30).
The samādhi of one who, detached even from the highest reflection, has complete discriminative discernment and no other cognitions (4.29, YBh 4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30).
The tenth bodhisattva ground, at which the bodhisattva is consecrated by the buddhas and rains the dharma like a cloud.

definitions.definition: The 'dharma seal': the innate nature, the avadhūtī between lalanā and rasanā, cause of the great seal (Advayavajra).
What upholds; an ordinance or foundation; the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16 = 1.164.50); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3).
Follower through dharma: one of sharp faculties on the path of seeing.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: chos skyong, Dharma protector: for the Karma Kagyu above all Mahākāla Bernagchen ('the black-cloaked') and for the Shangpa the six-armed wisdom Mahākāla.

A single, formless, world-pervading substance that assists (without causing) the motion of souls and matter, as water assists fish (TS 5.17); its absence beyond the world stops the liberated soul at the summit (TS 10.8).
The true nature of things, which cannot be cognized by ordinary consciousness; the Buddha is to be seen from it; it abides whether or not buddhas appear.
Suchness without the division of grasped and grasper, which is nirvāṇa, as distinct from dharmas — the appearance of duality and names, which is saṃsāra (Dharmadharmatāvibhāga).
Dharma-nature (faxing), pure and ultimately unborn; 'birth' is said only from the side of those born (Tanluan, Daochuo).
Dharmatā 'not established as anything', one and indivisible; all the teachings flow toward it (Satyadvayāvatāra).
Recollected at waking and rested in, free of elaboration, before sleep (Caryāsaṃgrahapradīpa).
Reality (chos nyid); in the four visions the 'direct perception of dharmatā' and the 'exhaustion of phenomena in dharmatā'; the bardo of dharmatā after death.
The nature of things, unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa, where what is to be named and the domain of mind have ceased (MMK 18.7).
chos nyid: the clear light of dharmatā without arising and ceasing, beyond speech and thought, is the path of Mahāmudrā (Tilopa).
The substrate that conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14).

The seven bodily tissues — rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and semen — called 'the vitiable' (dūṣya) (AHS Sū 1.13); each is formed from the preceding by its own fire, with essence and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16); in Caraka's wider usage every body-constituent whose balance is health (Sū 1.53; 9.4); in Śā 1.16 the six 'dhātus' of the person are the five elements and consciousness.

The four (or six: with space and consciousness) elements of which a person consists (MN 140; MN 62); the eighteen elements of sense, object and consciousness; also 'element' as in nibbāna-element and 'that element stands' (SN 12.20).
A verbal root, listed in the Dhātupāṭha (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1: 'bhū and the rest are roots').
The eighteen elements (six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses); the four great elements; nibbāna as the unconditioned element.
Element, 'lineage' (gotra): eighteen — six faculties, six objects, six consciousnesses; mind (manas) is the consciousness just past, posited to give the sixth consciousness a support.
In Siddha medicine the seven body-constituents (uṭal tātukkaḷ): cāram, ceṉnīr, ūṉ, koḻuppu, eṉpu, mūḷai, cukkilam/curōṇitam; in pharmacy tātu also names the mineral-metal class of drugs.

notes: Other senses (bodily tissue, element) belong to other units.

definitions.definition: In 4.81: "dhātu-svabhāva", the nature of the realm/element by which the unborn dharma is ever once-shone.

definitions.definition: The effect sought and the purpose of the tantra (Ca Sū 1.53); health (Sū 9.4).
Metallurgical alchemy; rasa-śāstra is not merely for this (SDS Raseśvara 23); the 'vāda-khaṇḍa' of the Rasaratnākara is for alchemists (vādin) (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
The seven fires by which each tissue is cooked, yielding essence (the next tissue) and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16).

The first of the six cleansing acts: in the HYP the swallowing and withdrawing of a moistened cloth; in the GS a class of four kinds (inner, of the teeth, of the heart, of the root) with their variants.
The visionary thought or insight of the seer, which is 'yoked' (RV 5.81.1) and which Savitṛ is asked to impel (3.62.10).
The discerning intellect whose lapse — seeing the eternal and non-eternal, wholesome and unwholesome wrongly — is a cause of suffering (Ca Śā 1.99).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast one is not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); the steadfast one, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Steadfast: a mark of the one beyond the guṇas (14.24).
The wise, steadfast one: chooses the good over the pleasant (KU 1.2.2); turns his sight inward (KU 2.1.1).

definitions.definition: Steadfast, wise (as used in Dhp 122, 207, 208, 234, 290).

definitions.definition: The restraining resolve whose lapse leaves the mind unable to turn from the harmful (Ca Śā 1.100); with smṛti and dhī the means of stopping the stream of body and mind (Śā 2.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The firmness in which the intellect is held while the mind is gradually brought to rest (6.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.7: listed among the constituents of the field.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Steadiness: a mark of the divine endowment (16.3) and of the kṣatriya's nature (18.43); threefold — sāttvic steadiness, unwavering through yoga, holds the activities of mind, breath and senses; rājasic holds to dharma, desire and wealth craving their fruit; tāmasic does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency and arrogance (18.33–35); the sāttvic agent has steadiness and zeal (18.26); by steadiness one restrains oneself (18.51).
Steadfastness, threefold by the guṇas; the sāttvic holds mind, breath and senses by unswerving yoga (BhG 18.33–35).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Steadfastness: one of the seven feminine excellences that are the Lord (10.34); before the fierce form Arjuna finds no dhṛti (11.24).

definitions.definition: The immovable principal image standing for Viṣṇu's partless form.

equivalents.note: common temple usage 'mūlabera'

definitions.definition: Unbroken remembrance of the Lord flowing like a stream of oil, the form that liberating meditation takes (from Chāndogya 7.26.2, 'dhruvā smṛtiḥ').
The seventh Mahāvidyā, 'bearing the form of a widow' and so without a Bhairava (Toḍala 1.13); matched with Varāha (10.9).
The sound or melody of the Word heard within; 'Shabd dhun' is the sound current.
The sacred fire kept burning at a Nāth seat or by a wandering yogī; at Gorakhpur an 'unbroken' dhūnī is ascribed to Gorakhnāth; its ash is given as blessing.
The fire of the Aghora ascetic, often kept in or near the cremation ground.

Ascetic practices (twelve or thirteen in the lists): wearing rag-robes, three robes only, alms-round, one meal, living in the forest, at the root of a tree, in the open, in a charnel ground, sitting without lying down, and others.

notes: The same category occurs in every surviving Vinaya (Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṃghika, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Pali); the definition is given once under the Dharmaguptaka code, the living East Asian one.

definitions.definition: The thirteen ascetic practices allowed by the Buddha for effacement and contentment.
The austerities central to forest practice: alms-food only, one meal, forest and charnel-ground dwelling, refuse-rag robes, wandering (tudong).
The audible noise (nāda) produced by effort, which manifests the eternal letters; its loudness increases, not the word (MS 1.1.17).

The audible sound that manifests the sphoṭa; Patañjali calls it a quality of the word (on P 1.1.70); the grammarians distinguish the primary sound that reveals the sphoṭa from the secondary sound responsible for differences of speed and length.

Suggestion: the implied meaning (pratīyamāna) conveyed beyond denotation, and poetry in which it predominates; named after the grammarians' dhvani that manifests the sphoṭa; threefold — suggested fact, figure and rasa (DhĀ 1.1, 1.4, 1.13).

equivalents.note: vyañjanā is the power, dhvani the suggested sense or the poetry

definitions.definition: In Jainism (TS 9.27) the restraining of thought on one point, for one of the best constitution, up to an antarmuhūrta; fourfold: ārta, raudra, dharmya, śukla (9.28), the last two causes of liberation (9.29).
The one-pointedness (ekatānatā) of cognition (pratyaya) in that place (3.2); in the bhāṣya, a like flow untouched by any other cognition.
Sustained meditation on Viṣṇu with his qualities, according to one's fitness, which produces direct knowledge; not a mere subsidiary of hearing.
Meditation: the continuous flow of a single cognition on the place of concentration (3.2); the means of abandoning the afflictions' activities (2.11).
Meditation, which burns away the 'ungodly qualities' and lets one see the course of the inner self (MDh 6.72–73).
VP 6.7.91: one continuous flow of the form's awareness, desiring nothing else; ŚiP 7.2.39: with object and then without.
Meditation is the removal of passion, accomplished through the cessation of mental modifications (SS 3.30–31); meditation is mind without object (SS 6.25).
Meditation: with and without qualities (GŚ 76–77; DYŚ 111–114); gross, of light and subtle (GS 6.1).
Transcribed chan; the Platform Sūtra redefines it as being free of forms outwardly (samādhi being inner non-confusion).

Meditation: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.6); the 'yoga of meditation' by which the sages saw God's power (ŚU 1.3); the friction of meditation (ŚU 1.14); a limb in MaiU 6.18; one sees him 'meditating' (MuU 3.1.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Meditation: those who, laying down all actions in the Lord, worship him meditating (dhyāyantaḥ) with undivided yoga, he soon delivers (12.6–7); in the ranking of 12.12 meditation is superior to knowledge, and relinquishing the fruit of actions is superior to meditation.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Meditation: by it some see the self in themselves by themselves (13.25).

In Jainism the stopping of the mind's wandering by fixing it on one object, for up to a muhūrta (TS 9.27); fourfold — sorrowful, cruel, virtuous, pure (9.28), only the last two leading to liberation; 'a steady mind is dhyāna' (Dhyānaśataka).
The fifth perfection: settling the mind in concentration through solitude, seeking calm first, then insight (BCA 8.1–4).
Meditation with or without qualities; 'so'ham'; one-pointedness on consciousness.
Meditative absorption, four, both as births (heavens) and as attainments; the attainment is good one-pointedness with its accompaniment; each has its factors.

definitions.definition: Meditation as taught in BhG 6.10–32 (a firm seat, erect posture, gaze on the nose-tip, mind fixed on the self or the Lord) and 18.52; in the Mokṣadharma a fourfold dhyāna-yoga (12.188).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Being ever intent on the yoga of meditation is part of the discipline (with solitude, light eating, control of speech, body and mind, and dispassion) that makes one fit for becoming Brahman (18.52; 18.51–53).

definitions.definition: The qualified meditator described in the Jñānārṇava and Yogaśāstra (detached, steady in vows, free of passion).
Seeing beings passing away and reappearing according to their deeds (DN 2; MN 4); the second true knowledge.
Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma; a mundane direct knowledge.
Lifelong limitation of the distance one will travel in each direction (TS 7.21).
'Sky-clad': the naked monk, and the tradition that holds complete nudity necessary for the fully renounced and for liberation.
Called Boṭika (Boḍiya) in Śvetāmbara sources, which trace it to Śivabhūti's schism.

cross_language.note: self-designation
low confidence on form

definitions.definition: One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notion 'this (is) from here' and of directions (VS 2.2.12 C).

That by which supreme knowledge is given (dī) and the bondage of fetters destroyed (kṣī) (SSM 15.7); in Vīraśaiva practice the liṅga-initiation, with bathing, the whispered five-syllable mantra and the giving of the liṅga into the disciple's hand (6.19–25); by it the duality of guru and disciple is removed (19.6–7).

The consecration that makes the sacrificer fit for the soma rite, with restraint, vigil and tapas; with tapas it is among the powers that uphold the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1) and was first undertaken by the seers (AVŚ 19.41.1).
The consecration of the sacrificer before a Soma rite, by which the priests 'make him an embryo again' (AB 1.3); he keeps vows and is reborn at the final bath.
The consecration for sacrifice counted as the twice-born's third birth (MDh 2.169).
Initiation, threefold: śāktī by the entry of power, śāmbhavī by the placing of the foot, māntrī by mantra (PKS 1.32); Bālā is given first, with a name ending in '-ānandanātha' (PKS 1.39-41).
Consecration of a tested brahmin with mantra-sanctified ash before the southern image, with the hearing of the mantra.
Initiation by touch, sight or piercing (sparśa, dṛk, vedha), given only after mutual testing (Kulārṇava 14); there is no initiation higher than the Śākta (12.12).
Initiation in which a qualified guru gives the mantra to a qualified, tested disciple (ŚT 2.141–153).
Initiation into Hari's worship and mantra by the ācārya (with the sipping of the Lord's foot-water and vows); those without it are called 'beasts among men'.

The rite performed on the soul — not on caste or body — by which the guru, empowered by Śiva's mantras, joins the soul to Śiva and destroys its bonds; it is the cause of the other means (ritual, knowledge, conduct).
Initiation into Bhagavān's mantras and worship, in Śrīvaiṣṇava usage centred on the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra).

Initiation, in many forms (TĀ 14-22); for one who knows the Heart, initiation needs no sesame and ghee (Parātrīśikā 25); Spanda calls identification with the meditated 'the initiation of nirvāṇa' (SK 2.7).
Initiation, so called because it gives divine knowledge and destroys sin; the guru gives the mantras (gopāla-mantra, kāma-gāyatrī), which are not published.
Two initiations: the refuge mantra (nāma-nivedana) and the brahmasambandha.

notes: The vacana and manual tradition speak of three modes (by touch, by mantra, by rite: vedhā, mantra, kriyā) — moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: Material (the threefold effect: disciple's and teacher's knowledge, the kalās such as darbha, ash, sandal, thread, flowers, incense, mantras, and the brahmin to be consecrated), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher.
The daily regimen of the healthy: rising at the brāhma muhūrta, cleansing, collyrium, nasal oil, gargling, oil massage, exercise, bathing, conduct and timely sleep (AHS Sū 2; Ca Sū 5; Su Ci 24).
A company of Vārkarī pilgrims walking and singing together behind a flag, with cymbals (ṭāḷ) and drum, as a unit of the vārī.
Samādhi and prajñā as one substance, lamp and light; their equal study.
The content of gradual cultivation: calm yet always knowing, knowing yet always calm (Jinul).
Meditative good: the first thirteen contemplations of the Contemplation Sūtra, practised with a concentrated mind.
'Live as islands to yourselves, with the Dhamma as island' (DN 16; SN 47.13); nibbāna is 'the island' (SN 43.44).
Fourth view: like a lamp; breath-control (inner sense); no agitation; hearing (YDS).
a quality of prāṇāyāma practised thus (YS 2.50)

definitions.definition: (Jain report) Six wandering teachers who drew the Mahānimitta from the Pūrvas and taught Gosāla.
Five grounds for holding supreme nibbāna here and now: sense pleasure, or one of the four absorptions.
A view or theory, especially the speculative views (the sixty-two of DN 1, the ten undeclared of MN 72) that are 'a thicket, a fetter of views'; right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the first path factor.
A speculative view; the sixty-two grounds are views of those who do not know or see, conditioned by contact and craving.
View; as an unwholesome factor, wrong view, especially of self and of the world.

The three constituents of prakṛti — sattva, rajas, tamas — of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, serving illumination, activity and restraint, and functioning by mutual domination, support, production and pairing (SK 12).
What resides in a substance, has no qualities and is not an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.15 C); twenty-four (Praśastapāda).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act helplessly (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas, and the deluded think 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' (3.28); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The states (bhāva) of sattva, rajas and tamas come from the Lord, yet he is not in them (7.12); deluded by these three guṇa-made states the world does not recognize him, who is beyond them (7.13); his māyā is 'made of the guṇas' (7.14).
Strand: the nine-gated lotus is 'covered with three strands' (AVŚ 10.8.43).

The three strands born of prakṛti — sattva, rajas and tamas — which bind the embodied one (BhG 14.5), act upon one another as the true agents (3.27–28), and classify faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 17–18).

The three constituents of the seen — sattva (illumination), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia) (2.18); their conflicting activity makes all suffering for the discerning (2.15); everything is a particular arrangement of them (4.13); at kaivalya they return to their source (4.34).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the twenty qualities in ten opposed pairs — heavy/light, cold/hot, unctuous/dry, slow/sharp, stable/mobile, soft/hard, clear/slimy, smooth/rough, subtle/gross, dense/liquid (Ca Sū 25.36; AHS Sū 1.18); the qualities as a category (Ca Sū 1.49); and the three guṇas of the mind (Śā 4.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The division of guṇas and actions according to which the Lord made the fourfold class-order (4.13); the guṇas are not further explained in chs. 4–6 (rajas is named in 6.27).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: the guṇas arise from prakṛti (13.20, 14.5); puruṣa experiences them and attachment to them causes birth (13.22); the knowable is without guṇas yet their experiencer (13.15). Chapter 14: the three guṇas — sattva, rajas and tamas — bind the embodied one (14.5–9), prevail by overpowering one another (14.10), show their signs (14.11–13), shape what follows death (14.14–15, 14.18) and the fruit of action (14.16–17); one who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains Kṛṣṇa's state (14.19); the embodied one who goes beyond them attains the immortal (14.20). The aśvattha's branches are swollen by the guṇas (15.2).
The three qualities of the self — sattva, rajas, tamas — determining destinies (MDh 12.24–51).

The three qualities belong to the intellect, not to the self; everything is classed by them with a fourth, attributeless class belonging to the Lord; one conquers rajas and tamas by sattva and sattva by desirelessness.
The three qualities of Prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas) by which devotion (BhP 3.29), Purāṇas (Matsya 53.68-69) and the measures of Oṃ (MkP 42.4) are classified.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Faith (17.2), food (17.7–10), sacrifice (17.11–13), austerity (17.17–19), giving (17.20–22), relinquishment (18.7–9), knowledge, action and agent (18.19–28), understanding and steadiness (18.29–35) and happiness (18.36–39) are each threefold by the guṇas; no being on earth or among the gods is free of the three guṇas born of prakṛti (18.40); the actions of the four varṇas are distributed by the guṇas arising from their nature (18.41).

Quality, strand: God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva is bound to the guṇas and has three guṇas (ŚU 5.7); tamas, rajas and sattva as successive states and as Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (MaiU 5.2).

In horā, the planets carry the three qualities: Moon, Sun and Jupiter sattva; Mercury and Venus rajas; Mars and Saturn tamas (BJ 2.7); a sāttvika, rājasa or tāmasa person is recognized by his conduct (BS 68.8–9).
In Jain usage an inherent quality of a substance, present in all its modes and itself without qualities (TS 5.38, 5.41).

Teacher: the self is its own chief teacher; yet ignorance-bound persons need a knower of the principles to give knowledge; the avadhūta takes twenty-four teachers from nature; the guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
In the Guru Gītā: 'gu' is darkness, 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of liberation is his grace.

Īśvara is the teacher (guru) even of the ancients, unlimited by time (1.26); devotion offers all actions to the supreme teacher (paramaguru, YBh 2.1); Vyāsa: in the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).

'Gu' is what is beyond the qualities and 'ru' what is beyond form; the guru gives that (SSM 15.8–9); Śiva stands present as the guru and the two are not to be distinguished (11.19–21); without devotion to the guru no devotion to Śiva arises (11.22–24).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's venerable elders (Bhīṣma, Droṇa), whom he would rather not kill even if it meant living on alms (2.5).
'The teacher is the means' (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); from the teacher comes awakening to the wheel of letters (2.7).
The spiritual teacher relied upon as the root of the path, seen in guru yoga as inseparable from the Buddha (Tsongkhapa as Lobsang Thubwang Dorje Chang).

The good teacher who confers the bodhisattva vow is skilled in the rite, abides in the vow, and has patience and compassion (Lamp 23–24); the tantric master is to be pleased with service and gifts (Lamp 64).
The teacher who is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, through whom alone the knowledge is to be sought (MU 1.2.12); approached with humility, service and questioning.
The one who knows the nine groups and consecrates the disciple; a mere knower of texts without faith is a semblance of a teacher.
'Gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover (Kulārṇava 17.7); the guru is father, mother and Maheśvara (12.49); rare is the guru who removes the disciple's suffering (13.108).
The lama (bla ma), root of blessings and the first of the three roots, to be examined before and followed after accepting; visualized as Padmasambhava in guru yoga.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Arjuna calls the Lord the world's object of worship and its 'weightiest teacher' (guru garīyān) (11.43).
Teacher: 'he should go to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in brahman' (MuU 1.2.12); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).
The 'true guru' (bla ma dam pa), from whose mouth alone the innate is found (Saraha, Tōh 2292 no. 6; People Dohā v19), who points out mind's nature 'as a finger points at the sky'.
The vajra master, to be examined before the bond and then regarded as inseparable from Vajradhara.

The teacher from whose grace the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge; the lineage runs from Nārāyaṇa and Vyāsa through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; devotion to the teacher as to God is enjoined.
Tamil kuru, ācāṉ, āriyaṉ: for the Siddhars the guru comes of his own accord, shows his own form and burns the bonds; guru and Lord are one (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

bla ma: the root of blessing and the one who points out the mind; 'devotion is the head of meditation'; qualified by the three trainings and experience; seeing mind directly 'is the guru's kindness' (Tilopa).
The living guru (also murśid, sāṃi) through whom alone the Man of the Heart is found; Bāuls distinguish the initiating guru (dīkṣā-guru) and the instructing guru (śikṣā-guru).
The Mahāśay, in whom the Kartā is present; 'the guru is truth'.

definitions.definition: In the Kārikā 1.28: the Lord established in the heart of all, whom the praṇava is to be known as.

The Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); the great Lord of beings who comes into being by his own māyā (4.6); in the Mokṣadharma, the Yoga thinkers' argument that without a Lord no one is freed (12.289.3).

Classical Sāṃkhya recognizes no established Īśvara as creator: Gauḍapāda argues the attributeless could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds 'Īśvara is not established' (1.92–99; 5.2–12; 6.64), yet admits emergent lords — the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Theistic Sāṃkhya (Vijñānabhikṣu) salutes the Lord.

A special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27); his lordship has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).

A distinct self free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, possessing merit, knowledge and concentration, who assists human effort and sets karma and the elements in motion; like a father to beings (NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker of the world proved by inference (NK 5.1).
Maheśvara, by whose will the world is dissolved and created through the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort; author of the Veda; whose convention fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The Lord: Brahman associated with māyā (or reflected in it), omniscient ruler, creator, sustainer and dissolver, giver of the fruits of action; his lordship depends on adjuncts of name and form.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness, of which the jīva is the reflection.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is lord of beings though unborn (4.6), and great lord of all the worlds (sarva-loka-maheśvara), enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities and friend of all beings, knowing whom one attains peace (5.29).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord: to be known as 'the great lord of the world' (lokamaheśvara) (10.3); addressed as supreme lord (parameśvara, 11.3), lord of all (viśveśvara, 11.16), lord of gods (deveśa, 11.25) and 'the lord to be praised' (11.44).
Rejected as director of dharma and adharma and as creator: the fruit comes from dharma and adharma with place, time and circumstance (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116); later Bhāṭṭas (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara) teach offering dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
Nārāyaṇa, the third reality: the self of all, cause of the world, opposed to all evil and abode of infinite auspicious qualities, present in five forms.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: seeing the lord equally present everywhere one does not harm oneself (13.29); in 15.8 the living being of 15.7 is called īśvara as it takes up and leaves a body; the highest person is the imperishable lord who enters and sustains the three worlds (15.17).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings, causing them to revolve by his māyā as if mounted on a machine (18.61). The demonic hold the world to be without a Lord (anīśvara, 16.8) and claim 'I am lord' (16.14); lordliness (īśvara-bhāva) is part of the kṣatriya's nature (18.43).

The Lord: all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord (Īśa 1); the two birds, the Lord and the one who grieves (MuU 3.1.2); the great Lord of lords (ŚU 6.7); the māyin (ŚU 4.10); lord of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6).
Rejected: a single permanent cause could not produce successive effects; 'being an effect' does not prove an intelligent world-maker; the Buddha is an authority who has become so, not an eternal one.

The creator posited by others is refuted: if he creates without wishing he depends on another, if by wishing he depends on his wish (BCA 9.119–126); an eternal cause would produce all effects at once or never (Tattvasaṅgraha).

Fourth tattva: knowledge predominant; the outward 'unmeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'this am I' with the 'this' prominent.
Performing dharma with the thought of offering it to Īśvara (Laugākṣi Bhāskara) or Śrī Govinda (Āpadeva), which makes it a cause of the highest good.
Traditional narrative (above all the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa), named with purāṇa as the fifth Veda.
The genre of the Mahābhārata, which calls itself a Veda of Kṛṣṇa (MBh 1.1.205).
The procedure — the subsidiaries (e.g. the prayājas) — that answers the question 'how?' of the bhāvanā; in an ectype it is taken from the archetype (MS 7.4.1).
The Tājika yoga of applying aspect, when a faster planet approaches exact aspect with a slower; the first and chief of the sixteen Tājika yogas.

Debate with the features of vāda in which quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat are also used (NS 1.2.2); permitted to protect the ascertainment of truth (NS 4.2.50).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): each party establishing its own thesis and attacking the other's, e.g. 'rebirth exists' against 'it does not' (Ca Vi 8.28).
Debate aimed at victory, one of the three kinds of debate among the learned.

Rainbow body: the fruit in which the body's gross elements dissolve into their essence of light at death, leaving only hair and nails (or nothing); the 'great transference' ('pho ba chen po) body of Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra departs without death.
The rainbow body attained by masters of the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü and, by Bön tradition, by Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen.
The central island-continent with Meru at its centre, divided into nine varṣas, Bhārata being the southern one.
The central, round continent of the middle world, 100,000 yojanas across, with Meru at its centre (TS 3.9).
Simultaneous disease of many through vitiated air, water, land and season, whose root is adharma arising from prajñāparādha (Ca Vi 3.6-23).

(1) The living, moving devotee or body as Śiva's true temple, against the fixed (Basava's vacana); (2) the wandering Śivayogin teacher whose greatness is taught in the prasādi-sthala — to see him gives accomplishment, to worship him is a means of liberation (SSM 11.37–43); (3) the order of Liṅgāyata priests and monks.
A holy person who, carrying the Lord within, makes even the tīrthas holy.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prāṇaliṅgi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The purification rite for the dead, performed with the deceased's name card (byang bu) and the peaceful and wrathful deities, to purify obscurations and guide the consciousness.

The vacanas reject caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son in the house of the cobbler Mādāra Cennayya and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'.
The birth of beings, their coming to be, the manifestation of the aggregates, the obtaining of the sense bases (SN 12.2); 'birth is ended' marks liberation.

Jāt: caste and creed; Lalon has 'never seen its form' and asks where it is at birth and death.
The universal, which words denote; the true part of things; ultimately Being (sattā) itself (VP 3.1).

DN 22:21 describes four as the content of right concentration: (1) secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, with thought and sustained thought, rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; (2) thought and sustained thought stilled, inner confidence, unification of mind, rapture and pleasure born of concentration; (3) rapture faded, equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending, pleasure felt with the body; (4) pleasure and pain abandoned, neither painful nor pleasant, purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

The four meditative absorptions: the first with applied and sustained thought, rapture and bliss born of seclusion; the second with rapture and bliss born of concentration; the third with bliss and equanimity; the fourth with purity of mindfulness through equanimity (DN 2; SN 45.8); remembered by the bodhisatta as 'the path to awakening' (MN 36); a basis for destroying the effluents (AN 9.36).
Meditative absorption with specific factors; fourfold in the suttas and fivefold in the Abhidhamma method; mundane or supramundane.
Full absorption on a counterpart sign in which the mind is unbroken for long periods; required (or access) before seeing ultimate realities.

definitions.definition: The verse composed by a master just before death, e.g. Huineng's last verse.

The fifth and last ground of monastic judgment: the practice established by accepted teachers, used when no higher authority (supernormal knowledge, scripture, instruction, tradition) is available; the Jītakalpa fixes atonements by it.

In the Kārikā ch.1: the one asleep under beginningless māyā who awakens to the unborn non-dual (1.16). | In the Kārikā ch.3: like the pot-space of the self; not a modification or part of it; no jīva is born. | In 4.68–4.71: made of dream, of māyā or conjured, the jīvas are born and die, "exist and do not exist"; no jīva is born.

The living self: the 'living self' (jīva ātman) with which being enters the elements (ChU 6.3.2); life which does not die when the body dies (ChU 6.11.3); in ŚU 5.9 the jīva is a hundredth part of a hundredth of a hair's tip yet fit for infinity.

The individual self: Brahman appearing as limited, reflected or semblanced through the adjunct of the inner organ (and ignorance); agent, enjoyer and transmigrant only through adjuncts; in truth Brahman.
The reflection of Brahman in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype.
Brahman delimited by the inner organ; the locus of ignorance.

A part of the formless Śiva through connection with beginningless ignorance, in whom Śiva abides as fire in the sunstone (SSM 5.34–36); at the prāṇaliṅgi stage the breath is the jīva and the great liṅga brahman (12.21–24).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the inner self of the embryo, eternal, unaging, deathless, that enters the womb through its connection with mind and 'produces itself' as the embryo (Ca Śā 3.3, 3.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.7: an eternal portion of Kṛṣṇa, become the living being (jīvabhūta) in the world of the living, draws the senses; 15.8–11 describe it taking a body, leaving it, enjoying objects: the deluded do not see it; those with the eye of knowledge, and yogins who strive, see it.

The living being: the Lord's higher nature has become the life-element (BhG 7.5), and an eternal portion of him becomes the jīva (15.7); the living self in the body whose existence Bhṛgu defends (MBh 12.175–185).
The jīva is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).
The individual self: eternal, atomic, a knower by nature and possessing attributive consciousness, agent and enjoyer dependent on the Lord, essentially his servant (śeṣa); countless in number.
Śiva clothed in body and coverings (PKS 1.5).
(As reported) The soul is the seventh of Pakudha's unmade bodies; the Ājīvika texts (as reported) speak of 'all souls' (sabbe jīvā) as powerless.
(As reported) For the materialist the soul is the body itself, bounded by the skin (tajjīva-taccharīra).
A part of Śiva like a spark of fire, covered by ignorance (Kulārṇava 1.8-9); bound it is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva (9.42-43).

The soul: an eternal, formless, conscious substance whose mark is cognitive activity (upayoga), agent and enjoyer of its karma, co-extensive with its body, innumerable in number, each distinct; worldly or liberated (TS 2.8, 2.10, 5.3, 5.16).
An eternal, sentient, dependent self, atomic, distinct from God and from every other soul, a reflection (pratibimba) of God, with an innate fitness that fixes its destiny.
The inner self born with the body that experiences pleasure and pain (MDh 12.13).
The embodied soul, a part of the Lord who dwells in the same body unrecognized, like musk in the deer.
The soul, one of the four eternal realities: countless, bound by ignorance, liberated only by Parameśvara's grace.

definitions.definition: The world of the living to which the widow is bidden to rise (RV 10.18.8).

definitions.definition: The individual-soul portion present in every being alongside the supreme-Self portion; where it predominates the being is a jīva (BPHS 1.22; 2.8).
'Dead while living': the devotee who has let the self, hope and pride die while still alive; death has nothing left to take.
Dying while living: daily withdrawal of the attention from the body to the eye centre as at death.
jyānte marā: the lover who has died to lust and self while alive.

equivalents.note: Both describe freedom in the living body; the Sant term stresses the death of the self rather than the dawning of knowledge.

definitions.definition: Liberation while living: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the seventh stage, in which one acts as custom requires, unimmersed in pleasure and pain, the mind 'dead' (manonāśa).
The liberated one, though in the body, is not in it; his functions are free of intention; the body lives on while its karma lasts.
The destruction of ignorance, the fruit of human birth and the state of liberation while living.

The state of one who, after perfect knowledge, remains embodied through the momentum of impressions like a potter's wheel (SK 67); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the 'one liberated while living' and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers (SS 3.78–84).

Liberation while living, promised by knowledge of the cakra-code (YH 1.86) and of worship (YH 3.1), by three muhūrtas of the Bhāvanā contemplation, and to the steadfast practitioner who may die anywhere (PKS 10.82); the Dīpikā defines it as release from the eight bonds.
A synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the yogin in samādhi is 'liberated' though living (4.107–112); from nirguṇa meditation and samādhi one becomes jīvanmukta (DYŚ 114).

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8); attained through the stable body made by mercury, not after the body falls (Rasārṇava 1.9-13; SDS Raseśvara 1-5).
Firm realization of oneness with consciousness even while body and the rest are experienced (PH 16).
One who sees the whole world as play is liberated in life (SK 2.5).
Though living he is liberated, though acting not stained (VBT 142); liberated though joined to a body (Paramārthasāra 61).
One whose mind is settled that the liṅga is liberation itself is liberated even while embodied (SSM 12.46); the liṅga-sthalas are directed to it (15.1–3).
Liberation while living: the knower remains embodied till prārabdha is exhausted, free of bondage, agency and sorrow.
Liberation while living: the state in which the mind is the seed and the spotless (AmŚ 57–59); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4).
Liberation while the body continues: the cessation of the mind's properties through destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth.
Rejected: while the body lasts karma remains; liberation comes only when the body falls.
Denied by Bhāskara: while the body lasts, real adjuncts remain.
Redefined: one engaged in Hari's service in all conditions is jīvanmukta.
The state of the soul freed by grace while the body, sustained by prārabdha, continues; such a one lives among devotees and acts as Śiva's servant.

notes: The SK itself does not use the word.

definitions.definition: Distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Selves are many because of the distinctness of their states (VS 3.2.16 C).
The life faculty, i.e. lifespan (āyus), the support of heat and consciousness.
The faculty that sustains its co-arising dhammas; mental (a universal factor) and material (in kamma-born matter).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), highest of souls, equal in rank with Brahmā, surpassed only by Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu; paired in the formula 'Hari-sarvottama, Vāyu-jīvottama'.

term: jixin jifo (this very mind is buddha)

definitions.definition: Mazu's teaching that the mind right now is buddha, later complemented by 'neither mind nor buddha'.
Explained in the Platform Sūtra as 'the previous thought not arising is mind, the next thought not ceasing is buddha'.
Dōgen rejects reading it as the Śreṇika view of an eternal knowing mind (Sokushin zebutsu).
The title of Śrīvaiṣṇava renouncers who head maṭhas (Vānamāmalai, Ahobilam, Parakāla and others).
Puruṣa as knower, the third member of 'the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower' whose discriminating knowledge is the better means (SK 2).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Knowledge is covered by desire, the constant enemy of the knower (3.38–40); desire is the destroyer of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna, 3.41); those who carp at Kṛṣṇa's teaching are deluded about all knowledge (3.32).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); through knowledge comes liberation (SK 44); in its highest form the complete, pure, single knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64). Gauḍapāda distinguishes external (scriptural) from internal knowledge (of prakṛti and puruṣa), only the latter liberating.
Synonym of buddhi (NS 1.1.15); a mark and quality of the self (NS 1.1.10), not of the mind (NS 3.2.19).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: the knowledge of the Lord 'entire' (samagra) that Kṛṣṇa declares together with vijñāna; having known it nothing further remains to be known (7.2), and one is freed from the inauspicious (9.1). Its bearer, the jñānin, is foremost of the four kinds of devotees (7.16–18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: (1) the knowledge of the field and its knower is knowledge in Kṛṣṇa's view (13.3); (2) twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to keeping in view the aim of knowledge of reality, are declared knowledge, and what differs from them ignorance (13.8–12); (3) the knowable is itself called knowledge (13.18); (4) the highest knowledge by which the sages reached perfection (14.1–2); (5) sattva binds by attachment to knowledge and knowledge arises from sattva; tamas covers it (14.6, 14.9, 14.11, 14.17); (6) it comes, with memory and removal (apohana), from Kṛṣṇa (15.15).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.33–42 and 5.15–17: knowledge — learned from knowers who have seen the truth through prostration, questioning and service (4.34); by it one is not deluded again and sees all beings in the self and in the Lord (4.35); a raft across all wrong (4.36); a fire that burns all actions (4.37); the supreme purifier, found within oneself in time by one perfected in yoga (4.38); obtained by the faithful, intent and sense-restrained, and followed by supreme peace (4.39); it cuts doubt like a sword (4.42). It is covered by ignorance, which deludes creatures; where ignorance is destroyed, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun (5.15–16). 6.8 pairs it with realized knowledge (vijñāna).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Knowledge: a state of beings that comes from the Lord (10.4); the Lord is 'the knowledge of the knowers' (10.38); his 'lamp of knowledge' destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.11); in 12.12 knowledge is better than practice, and meditation superior to it.
Primordial wisdom (ye shes), distinguished from dualistic consciousness (rnam shes); five wisdoms of the five families; 'self-arising wisdom' in Dzogchen.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Knowledge: threefold — sāttvic knowledge sees one imperishable being in all beings, undivided in the divided; rājasic knowledge sees many distinct beings by separateness; tāmasic clings to a single thing as if it were the whole (18.20–22); knowledge, the known and the knower impel action (18.18); knowledge is part of the brāhmaṇa's work (18.42); Kṛṣṇa calls his teaching 'knowledge more secret than the secret' (18.63).
Knowledge of Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences and gradation, culminating in direct knowledge (aparokṣa); it wins the abundant grace that alone liberates.
Knowledge: as the Lord's power, one of the three; as limited knowing, bondage (Śiva Sūtra 1.2); as right knowledge, the sole cause of liberation (TĀ 1.22).
ye shes, 'primordial knowing': the wisdom that is mind's nature — self-arisen, non-conceptual, clear; distinguished from consciousness (rnam shes), which it becomes when recognized (3rd Karmapa).
Knowledge, of five kinds (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala), the soul's own nature; to be gained before compassion can be rightly exercised.

Karma veiling the five kinds of knowledge (TS 8.4, 8.6).

definitions.definition: The soul as pure knower, neither careless nor careful, beyond all states it knows (Samayasāra 6).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: one of the topics Arjuna asks about (13.1). The knowable is brahman, beginningless and supreme, knowing which one attains the immortal, said to be neither sat nor asat (13.13); it has hands, feet, eyes everywhere, appears through the sense-qualities yet is without senses, is without guṇas yet their experiencer, is inside and outside beings, not to be known because of its subtlety, undivided yet as if divided, sustainer, devourer and generator of beings (13.14–17); light of lights beyond darkness, it is knowledge, the knowable and what is reached by knowledge, set in the heart of all (13.18). Knowing it, the devotee becomes fit for Kṛṣṇa's state (13.19).

The twelve self-manifest liṅgas of Śiva's radiance in sacred sites, told in the Śiva Purāṇa's Koṭirudra Saṃhitā.

definitions.definition: Light — the highest light reached by the worshipper (RV 1.50.10), the light set in the heart (6.9.5–6), the light reached by soma-drinkers (8.48.3), the light of lights that is mind (VS 34.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The knowable is the light even of lights, beyond darkness (13.18).
Light: the light beyond heaven which is the light within a person (ChU 3.13.7); the highest light which the serene one reaches (ChU 8.3.4, 8.12.3); the light of lights (MuU 2.2.9).

The seven transmissions held by Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo: the long oral lineage, earth treasures, rediscovered treasures, mind treasures, recollection, pure vision and the hearing lineage.

The name of Atiśa's tradition: every word of the Buddha (bka') is understood as personal instruction (gdams ngag) for practice, with nothing to be set aside.
Miser, stingy person (as used in Dhp 177, 223).

Dolpopa's designation for his own restatement of the definitive teaching of the age of perfection.

The Eight Pronouncements / Eight Herukas of the Mahāyoga sādhana section: Mañjuśrī-Yamāntaka (body), Hayagrīva (speech), Yangdag (mind), Chemchok / Amṛta (qualities), Vajrakīla (activity), Mamo (sending and calling the mātaraḥ), Jigten Chötö (worldly offering and praise) and Möpa Drakngak (wrathful mantra).

Service to the Lord (and his devotees) that expresses the soul's nature as his śeṣa; the goal both here and in Vaikuṇṭha.

Named at 3.50 (from dispassion even towards the discrimination-born powers, when the seeds of defect are destroyed), 3.55 (sattva and puruṣa equal in purity), 4.26 (the mind slopes towards it) and 4.34 (the return to source of the guṇas empty of puruṣa's purpose, or the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own form).

The aloneness of the seer: the absence of the conjunction (2.25); arising when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity (3.55) or from dispassion even toward the highest power (3.50); defined as the guṇas' return to their source, or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).

(1) Puruṣa's intrinsic isolation (SK 19). (2) The goal: isolation that is certain and final, attained when the body falls and pradhāna, its purpose fulfilled, ceases (SK 68); prakṛti's activity is for its sake (SK 17, 21).
What remains when the mind is dissolved by abandoning the knowable (HYP 4.62).
The Bhāgavata names kaivalya as its sole purpose (BhP 12.13.12).
The state of oneness granted by the Goddess ('giver of the state of kaivalya', LSN 125, 171).
The only true liberation, gained by knowledge alone (Muktikā); also the fruit of yoga in six months (Amṛtanāda).
The enjoyment of one's own pure self apart from the Lord, sought by some seekers; a lesser goal than the Lord's service.
Not permanent: those who attain it eventually go on to the Lord.
A permanent state, in a region at the edge of the eternal realm, from which there is no return.
In the Jaimini system, the liberation indicated by the kārakāṃśa exalted, or by Ketu in the twelfth from it (Jaimini 1.2.13, 1.2.69).

definitions.definition: Inventory or certificate: a guide text indicating the place and content of a treasure.
The 'crow and palm-fruit' coincidence: used for the uncaused, chance-like arising of the world-appearance and of the turn toward inquiry.

literal: like the crow and the palm fruit

definitions.definition: Drinking air slowly through the mouth shaped like a crow's beak (kākacañcu).

The son of the Sat Puruṣ who by austerity won the three worlds, begot Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś, and as Kāl (time/death) devours souls and keeps them from Satlok; the adversary from whom Kabīr frees souls.

Kāl, the 'negative power' (also Brahm, Jot Nirañjan at the lower levels), ruler of the three worlds up to Trikuṭī, the universal mind, who administers karma; contrasted with Dayāl, the merciful supreme.
Kāl as death, who stands over every head and grinds the world.
An eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep.
Time as the first god and lord of all, father of Prajāpati, from whom the waters, brahman, tapas and the Vedas arose (AVŚ 19.53–54).
Time, counted by Kapila as the twenty-fifth principle and identified with the Lord, from whom prakṛti's movement arises.
From the unmanifest arose time, pradhāna and the supreme person (Īśvara Gītā).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notions 'earlier', 'later', 'simultaneous', 'quick' (VS 2.2.6 C).
The insentient part of the effect, dependent on the sentient: ten 'effects' (five elements, five qualities) and thirteen 'instruments' (ten senses, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas); they are the bonds.

Time: 'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (Bali, MBh 12.217.25); time is the sixth with the five eternal elements (12.267); in the Gautamī story, Time points to karma (13.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Time: 'of those that reckon I am time' (10.30); 'I alone am imperishable time' (10.33); answering 'who are you?', the Lord says 'I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds' (11.32); his mouths are 'like the fire of time' (kālānala, 11.25).
Time: a candidate cause (ŚU 1.2) rejected as the cause (6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); two forms of brahman, time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15-16).

In jyotiṣa, time is twofold: the time that ends the worlds, and reckonable time, gross (from the prāṇa) and subtle (from the truṭi) (SS 1.10–11); without beginning or end, it is inferred from the planets and stars (Āryabhaṭīya 3.11).

The substance that makes possible continuity, change, activity and priority (TS 5.22); for the Digambaras a real substance consisting of innumerable time-atoms, one in each space-point; for some Śvetāmbaras only a mode of other substances ('according to some', Śv 5.38). Conventional time is measured by the luminaries.
A subtle stage of the praṇava after nāda and bindu; a light seen in the west.
Time, a form of Viṣṇu that joins and separates pradhāna and puruṣa (VP 1.2); the Lord's form that carries off all beings (BhP 12.4.36-38).
An eternal insentient substance without the guṇas, the Lord's body and instrument; in the eternal realm time exists but does not govern.

definitions.definition: Kañcuka: limited agency ('only a little I do').
The time-power of the Word-Brahman, its independent power (svātantrya) by which sequence and the six modifications of being appear (VP 1.3; 3.9).
Kañcuka: time, limiting to sequence ('only now').

literal: doctrine that time is the cause

definitions.definition: Time as sole cause, one of the five one-sided causal views (with own-nature, destiny, former deeds, effort) that are wrong alone and right together.
'Cheating time (death)': the yoga that overcomes death (GŚ 2; HYP 3.3).
Taught by Bhairava as the most secret practice; placing the mind in the heart until unmanī destroys death (KJN 6.16–28).
The 'wheel of time': name of the tantra and deity; time (kāla) is means/bliss, the wheel (cakra) wisdom/empty form; the outer, inner and other wheels.

The tantra, the deity and the primordial buddha whose teaching of the age of perfection and six-branch yoga is the heart of the Jonang; its 'emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects' names the other-empty ultimate.
The fire of the end of time, visualized rising and burning body and world (VBT 52-53).
Foreknowing the time of death by signs in breath, body and dreams (YŚ 5).

notes: Restricted/summary only.

definitions.definition: Traditional study of the Śrībhāṣya, Gītābhāṣya, the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries and the rahasyas at the feet of a teacher.
The first embryonic stage; the stages beginning with kalala rest on the body, as the dispositions rest on buddhi (SK 43).
Name of the Śaiva order known from Karnataka inscriptions; Yāmuna attributes skull and corpse-ash practices to it; Guṇaratna counts the Kālamukhas as the fourth kind of Śaiva ascetic.
The activity of consciousness named by the root kal: projecting (kṣepa), knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).
The act of devouring (grasana) that gives Mahākāla and Kālī their names (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32 with Hariharānanda's gloss).
The smallest units of matter: groups of inseparable elements (at least eight) arising and ceasing together.
Tiny particles seen with the light of access or jhāna concentration and analysed into their elements as the basis of insight.
The subtle units whose rapid arising and passing is experienced as vibration in the body (U Ba Khin).

The 'Person of Time': the zodiac as a body whose limbs are the twelve signs from the head (Aries) to the feet (Pisces) (BJ 1.4), whose self is the Sun and mind the Moon (BJ 2.1); an ocean no non-seer can cross (BS 2.4).

equivalents.note: the cosmic Person whose limbs are the world (RV 10.90) — an analogy of form, not an identity the jyotiṣa texts assert

definitions.definition: A consecrated water-pot in which the deity is invoked for bathing and installation rites.
Kalaśa rites (e.g. sahasrakalaśa) by which the tantri renews an installed deity's power.
The vase consecration, first of the four; purifies the body and authorizes the generation stage.
The supreme Kālī of the Krama, the last of the goddesses of cognition.
In Abhinavagupta's Trika the fourth goddess above Parā, Parāparā and Aparā.
A pseudo-reason adduced when its time has passed (NS 1.2.9 DCS).

The conquest or postponement of death through yoga: the Siddhas break the staff of time (HYP 1.9); mudrās give 'cheating of time' (3.130); one established in rājayoga cheats time (4.103); a chapter of the Haṭhatattvakaumudī is devoted to it.

She who devours (kalana) Time: because she devours Mahākāla she is the primordial Kālikā (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32); black because all beings enter her as colours enter black (13.5-6); standing on Śiva as a corpse (Toḍala 1.20-25).
The Mother of the Śyāmā-saṅgīt; Dakṣiṇakālī of the Tantrasāra.
The goddess as the power of kalana - projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding - in twelve phases of cognition (TĀ 4.148-173).

literal: the Black One; she of Time

definitions.definition: The fourth and present age, an ocean of faults with one great virtue: that singing the Lord's name gives what meditation, sacrifice and worship gave in the earlier ages; reckoned by tradition from 3102 BCE.

The age in which only the path of the Āgama avails and Vedic mantras are powerless (Mahānirvāṇa 2.7-15); in which only householder and mendicant stages remain (8.8); in which, for the Kālīvilāsa, only the paśu disposition is allowed (4.2-3).

The present, fourth age, whose beginning (3102 BCE by the siddhāntic epoch) is the zero of calendrical computation; Āryabhaṭa was 23 when 3600 of its years had passed (Āryabhaṭīya 3.10); in it the Viṃśottarī is the chief period-system (BPHS 46.14).
The degenerate age in which neither ritual, devotion nor discernment stands on its own and the name is the one support — yet the best of ages for one with faith.
Crossing the Kali age by the sixteen names.

Practices once permitted by the smṛtis but declared forbidden in the Kali age by later authorities (e.g. levirate, the great departure, cow-sacrifice), justified by the principle that dharma differs by age.

literal: to be avoided in the Kali age

definitions.definition: Title of the kings of Śambhala from Mañjuśrīyaśas, who united the castes into one vajra family.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Impurity destroyed by sacrifice (4.30), shaken off by knowledge (5.17), destroyed in the seers who attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25); the yogin who has become Brahman is stainless (akalmaṣa, vigata-kalmaṣa) (6.27–28).

The cosmic period at whose end beings enter the Lord's prakṛti and at whose beginning he sends them forth (BhG 9.7).
A day of Brahmā of a thousand cycles of four yugas with fourteen Manus; his night of equal length is the occasional dissolution; each kalpa bears a name (e.g. the present Śveta-Vārāha).
In the siddhāntas, a day of Brahmā of 1,000 caturyugas with fourteen Manus and their junctions (SS 1.19–20); Āryabhaṭa counts 14 × 72 yugas (Āryabhaṭīya 1.5).
Aeon: of destruction, formation, intermediate (from immeasurable lifespan to ten years and back), and great (eighty intermediate aeons).

definitions.definition: A cognition whose appearance is fit to be joined with verbal expression; for Dignāga, the joining of name, genus and the like.
The defining mark of perception; established by perception itself, since when thought is withdrawn one still sees.
Vaimānika gods above the kalpas — the Graiveyakas and Anuttaras — without ranks, all equal ('ahamindra') (TS 4.17).
In the bhāṣya on 3.43, the outward functioning of a mind that remains established in the body.

definitions.definition: The Lord's infinite, unsurpassed auspicious qualities — knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour and countless others such as compassion, accessibility and motherly love — not born of prakṛti.

One of the five 'auspicious events' in every Tīrthaṅkara's life — descent into the womb (cyavana/garbha), birth (janma), renunciation (dīkṣā), omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and final liberation (nirvāṇa) — celebrated by the gods and re-enacted in temple consecrations and festivals.

The teacher or companion who leads to awakening; the Aṣṭa says the buddhas and the perfections are the bodhisattva's good friends; Sudhana's pilgrimage and Sadāprarudita's search model devotion to them.
The teacher, reliance on whom in thought and deed is the root of the path; qualified by the ten qualities of the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra.
To be relied on while bad friends are abandoned (Jewel Garland 12).
The teacher who guides the bodhisattva; not abandoning the spiritual friend is part of protecting the body for beings' benefit (ŚSK 6).

definitions.definition: Spiritual friendship, 'the whole of the holy life' (SN 45.2); the first condition for maturing the liberation of mind (Ud 4.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire: the ritual-minded are 'desire-souled' (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires that enter the mind (2.55, 2.71) and is entered by desires like the ocean without being moved (2.70); desire is born of attachment and gives rise to anger (2.62); named with anger as the enemy born of rajas that covers knowledge, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, to be slain (3.37–43).
Desire, which arose in the beginning as the first seed of mind (RV 10.129.4; AVŚ 19.52.1).

Desire, born of rajas, the all-devouring enemy that veils knowledge, seated in senses, mind and intellect (BhG 3.37–41); one of the three gates of hell (16.21); yet 'in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma' (7.11); born of intention (saṃkalpa), as Maṅki says (MBh 12.171.25).
The five cords of sensual pleasure (MN 26); like the sores of a leper (MN 75); gratification, danger and escape (MN 13).
The 'spoken word': the long lineage of scriptures and instructions transmitted without interruption from master to disciple since the first diffusion.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire mark the learned (4.19); the unyoked is bound through the drive of desire (5.12); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood before leaving the body (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near those free of desire and anger (5.26); desires born of intention are to be abandoned in meditation (6.24); the yoked one is free of craving for all desires (6.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Desire: with anger and greed the threefold gate of hell, ruinous to the self, to be abandoned (16.21); the demonic resort to insatiable desire (16.10), hold the enjoyment of desires highest (16.11) and say the world is caused by desire (16.8); acting as desire prompts (kāma-kāra) one attains neither perfection, happiness nor the highest course (16.23); letting go of desire is part of the discipline of 18.53. Also one of the aims held by rājasic steadiness (18.34).
Desire: not praiseworthy in itself, yet no action is without it (MDh 2.2–4); never quenched by enjoyment (MDh 2.94).
The aim of love and pleasure, proper to youth, to be pursued without harming dharma and artha (Kāmasūtra 1.2).

Desire: 'a person is made of desire' (BAU 4.4.5); the desiring one returns for action, the one without desire goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); when all desires in the heart are released the mortal becomes immortal (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14). The self's 'real desires' (ChU 8.1.5) are distinguished from ordinary ones.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Those whose desires have turned away (vinivṛtta-kāma) reach the imperishable place (15.5).
Desire for one's own pleasure, which is not destroyed but refined into prema by the Sahajiyā discipline, as gold from ore; the washerwoman's love had no trace of it.
Lust, the downward current that must be mastered before the Man can be held.

Forms, sounds, odours, tastes and tangibles that are desirable, enticing (MN 26).

The 'digit of desire': the white and red points, Śiva and Śakti, and the point of their union (the 'I'); kāma because it is lovely, kalā the two points of fire and moon; knowing this vidyā one becomes Mahātripurasundarī (KKV 6-8); the Goddess 'whose form is the kāmakalā' (LSN 73).
The Goddess of Kāmarūpa, worshipped at the yoni-pīṭha on Nīlācala; she is dharma, artha, kāma and liberation (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.9).

The tenth Mahāvidyā (Kamalātmikā), a tantric Lakṣmī; Sadāśiva in Viṣṇu's form is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.16).
The renouncer's water-pot, among the permitted articles.
The fourth fetter, abandoned by the non-returner (MN 64).
The middle section of the mantra; the Goddess's body from neck to waist (LSN 35).

The land (Assam) where the Kaula scripture is 'in every house of the yoginīs' and the seat Kāmākhyā (KJN 8.20; 22.10–12).
Assam; the seat where Satī's yoni fell at Kāmagiri and Kāmākhyā dwells (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42, 18.49).
Kāmākhya is the 'beyond form' level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).

One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

First of the three cravings (DN 22:19).

The ten unwholesome courses (three bodily, four verbal, three mental) and their opposites (MN 41; AN 10.176).

The skull-cup of the heruka and yogin; Kapālapa's song calls such ornaments adventitious.
The skull, 'best of all vessels' for the Kaula rite (KJN 12.13).
