In the HYP rapid exhalation and inhalation like bellows, drying up phlegm; in the GS a threefold act (vāmakrama with the breath, vyutkrama and śītkrama with water).
The cavity above the palate into which the reversed tongue enters in khecarī.
The tīrtha (at Vārāṇasī in the Purāṇic story) where the skull fell from the Lord's hand and he was freed from brahmin-murder.
The observance of those called kapālavratins, whom the Svacchanda places with the Pāśupatas beyond re-creation.
A Śaiva ascetic keeping the skull vow; named with Kālāmukhas, Pāśupatas and Śaivas as one of four Māheśvara groups (Yāmuna; Vācaspati).
Śiva/Bhairava as bearer of Brahmā's skull; his 'excellent skull-bearer's guise' destroys the sin of those who remember it.
Epithet of Rudra (RV 1.114; VS 16).

Tamil aiyam or kapam: the water-earth humour, third of the three.

The small casket in which the iṣṭaliṅga is worn on a cord at the chest or neck.
A participant in an action as analysed by Pāṇini — agent, object, instrument, recipient, source, locus; 'the independent one is the agent' (1.4.54).

The thirteenfold instrument — buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the ten capacities — which seizes, holds and illuminates (SK 32); it acts only for puruṣa's purpose (SK 31).
Cause (kāraṇa): what invariably precedes an effect (and is not otherwise established); instrument (karaṇa): the special cause (Tarkasaṅgraha).
From the absence of the cause, absence of the effect, not vice versa (VS 1.2.1–2 C).
The Lord, who alone is independent and produces the effect at will, without depending on karma.
Śaṅkara: the Māheśvaras wrongly make Paśupati only the efficient cause; Brahman is both material and efficient cause.
A (divine) technique — used of the mudrās (HYP 1.56, 1.67) and especially of viparītakaraṇī, which cheats the sun of the nectar (3.78).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Instrument: the 'various instruments' are the third of the five factors of action (18.14) and one of the three constituents of action (18.18).

definitions.definition: Action, which no embodied being can abandon (BhG 3.5, 18.11) and which binds only through attachment to its fruit (2.47); also the ritual act (3.14) and the deed that follows its doer 'as a calf finds its mother' (MBh 12.174.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action: one's entitlement is to it, never to its fruits (2.47); mere action is far inferior to buddhiyoga (2.49); no one remains without acting even for a moment (3.5); action is better than inaction (3.8); it binds except when done for sacrifice (3.9); sacrifice arises from action and action from brahman (3.14–15); done unattached it leads to the highest (3.19); Janaka and others reached perfection by it (3.20); all actions are done by the guṇas (3.27) and are to be renounced in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
Ritual action, whose fruit is secured by correct performance and knowledge.
Action of mind, speech and body, bearing good or bad fruit in high, middle or low births (MDh 12.3–9); its residue shapes the next birth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3).
Motion: residing in one substance, without qualities, the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.16 C); five kinds (VS 1.1.6).
Action whose results bind; the body arises from the fruits of past actions (NS 3.2.60); 'activity' (pravṛtti) of speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) action as a category — movement, the cause of conjunction and disjunction (Ca Sū 1.49, 1.52); (2) the deed of a former body, called daiva, whose fruit is this life (Sū 11.31; Vi 3.30); karma-born diseases subside only with its exhaustion (Śā 1.116-117); (3) the five purificatory acts.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Action is the central theme of chs. 4–6: its course is deep and must be understood together with vikarma and inaction (4.16–18); actions do not stain the Lord (4.14); the ancients seeking liberation acted (4.15); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32); all action culminates in knowledge (4.33) and is burned by the fire of knowledge (4.37); for one wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means (6.3); one should do the action that ought to be done without depending on its fruit (6.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: defined as the emission (visarga) that brings beings into existence (8.3); known in its entirety by those striving for release (7.29); the Lord's creative acts do not bind him, seated as if indifferent (9.9); acts done as an offering to him free one from the bonds of action with their good and bad fruits (9.27–28).

Action and its result: 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad action' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, so one becomes' (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and learning' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); action does not cling to one who knows (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2).
Action: volition and what is produced by volition (bodily and vocal action, manifest and unmanifest); the variety of the world is born of it.
Its result comes not from past karma existing now but from the specific transformation of the series it initiated.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Action: those who lay down all actions in the Lord (12.6); doing actions for his sake leads to perfection (12.10); the fruit of all actions is to be given up (12.11–12).
Action is volition, whose imprints in the store-consciousness, with those of the twofold grasping, produce future maturations; mental action is the gravest.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Actions are done in every way by prakṛti alone (13.30); rajas binds by attachment to action (14.7, 14.9); the fruit of well-done action is sāttvika and stainless (14.16); the aśvattha's roots bind through action (15.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Action: the embodied cannot give up actions entirely (18.11); its fruit is threefold — unwanted, wanted, mixed — and accrues after death to non-relinquishers (18.12); every action of body, speech or mind has five causes (18.13–15); knowledge, known and knower impel it, and instrument, act and agent constitute it (18.18); it is sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (18.23–25); the varṇas' actions are distributed by nature-born guṇas (18.41).

Action and its residue; it cannot be exhausted by experience because new karma is always made, so liberation comes by grace through knowledge, while ritual action at best wins the lowest grace (heaven).

Subtle matter drawn into the soul by its activity and bound by its passions, veiling its qualities and producing its states until shed (TS 8.2); 'material karma' (dravya-karma) as distinct from the soul's passional states (bhāva-karma).

Action is intention and what is done having intended (MMK 17.2–3); it neither remains until ripening nor perishes into nothing, because it is without own-nature and unarisen (17.21); agent and action are established only in mutual dependence (8.12), like emanations (17.31–33).
Of three kinds: pralabdh (destiny, lived out in this body), sinchit (stored, burnt by the Master and by practice) and kriyaman (new, avoided by the disciple's vows).

Regions where people live by work, where religious practice and liberation are possible and Tīrthaṅkaras arise (TS 3.37).
The 'action seal': a physical consort in the yoga of the higher consecrations; summary only (restricted).

las kyi phyag rgya, the action seal: practice with a consort, in some lists one of Nāropa's dharmas (the 'method path'); sealed and restricted; the texts warn that the heedless and craving fall to lower realms.
The subtlest body, made of the soul's bound karma, beginninglessly connected with every worldly soul and carrying it between births (TS 2.25, 2.36, 2.40–42).
The supreme workability of mind reached by purifying absorption, the basis for the higher knowledges.
'The one of (buddha-)activity': the title of the head of the Karma Kagyu, regarded as an emanation of Avalokiteśvara, recognized in successive rebirths since Düsum Khyenpa.
The ten courses of action, good and bad, the grossest actions of body, speech and mind.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fruit of action, to which one has no right and which should not be one's motive (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are wretched (2.49); the wise abandon the fruit born of action (2.51); the ritual-minded's speech offers birth as the fruit of action (2.43).
Giving up the fruit of all actions — what the discerning call relinquishment (tyāga) (BhG 18.2, 18.11); the fourth and most accessible step of 12.11, praised above meditation in 12.12.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: expressed as abandoning attachment to the fruit of action (karmaphalāsaṅgaṃ tyaktvā, 4.20), giving up the fruit (karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā, 5.12, which brings lasting peace) and not depending on the fruit (anāśritaḥ karmaphalam, 6.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Giving up the fruit of all actions (sarva-karma-phala-tyāga) is what the discerning call tyāga (18.2); the one who relinquishes the fruit of action (karma-phala-tyāgin) is called the relinquisher, since the embodied cannot give up action entirely (18.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: For one unable even to work for the Lord: resorting to his yoga, self-restrained, relinquish the fruit of all actions (12.11); it is ranked above meditation, and from relinquishment peace follows immediately (12.12).

The residue of meritorious and demeritorious action, rooted in the afflictions, to be experienced in this or a future birth (2.12); ripening as birth, life-span and experience (2.13); normally 'of one life' (YBh 2.13).
Five agents: vaikārika (good acts), taijasa (bad), bhūtādi (deluded), sānumāna (good-deluded), niranumāna (bad-deluded) (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 11).

definitions.definition: The ripening of karma; a genre relating specific afflictions and inauspicious births to specific sins of former lives and prescribing expiations (Karmavipākasaṃhitā; BPHS 83).
Five sources of action — steadfastness, faith, seeking happiness, the wish not to know, the wish to know — of which only the wish to know leads to liberation (Kramadīpikā on Tattvasamāsa 9).
Speech, hands, feet, anus and genitals (SK 26), whose functions are speaking, grasping, walking, excreting and delight (SK 28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Restraining the organs of action while recalling objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6); karmayoga is undertaken with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind (3.7).
Rejuvenating preparations and regimens (kāya kaṟpam) — herbal, mineral-metal, breath and yogic — meant to make the body firm and long-lived; dismissed as needless for the true knower by Kuṭampai (2).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fault (kārpaṇya-doṣa) by which Arjuna says his very nature is struck when he asks for instruction (2.7).
The humble awareness of one's inability to adopt any other means; fifth limb of prapatti.
The fault of pity or faint-heartedness that strikes Arjuna's nature (BhG 2.7).

definitions.definition: A medical image for a remedy that alone cures all illnesses: recognition of mind's nature as by itself sufficient for awakening (Gampopa, Lama Zhang).
In Sakya Paṇḍita's critique: a revival of the Chinese Hashang's teaching, not Mahāmudrā.
The first of the temple-building rites (ploughing the site), opening the series that ends in installation.
The 'Master' or 'Doer': God as the one Lord, present in Āulcānd and in the hereditary head (Kartā) of the sect; the Kartābhajā are 'worshippers of the Kartā'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); Kṛṣṇa says that by not acting he would be the doer (cause) of confusion (3.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord is the maker (kartṛ) of the fourfold class order, yet is to be known as the non-doer (akartṛ), imperishable (4.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.30: one who sees actions done by prakṛti alone and his self as not the doer (akartṛ) sees; 14.19: the seer beholds no agent other than the guṇas.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Agent: the second of the five factors of action (18.14); one of untrained understanding who sees the self alone as agent does not see (18.16); the agent is one of the three constituents of action (18.18) and is sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (18.26–28).

The ascetic's periodic plucking out of the hair of head and face by hand, at initiation and thereafter.

Perfect knowledge of all substances in all their modes, past, present and future, arising when the knowledge-obscuring and other destructive karmas are destroyed (TS 1.29, 10.1).
Spontaneous retention free of inhalation and exhalation; when mastered nothing is unattainable and rājayoga is reached (HYP 2.73–75); no retention equals it (1.43).

Knowledge that accords with its object, of four grades: the Lord's, Lakṣmī's, the yogins' and others'.

The Kaula way itself, in which enjoyment becomes yoga, sin merit, and saṃsāra liberation (Kulārṇava 2.24); those established in it do not return to rebirth (2.30).

The consecrated substances of Kaula worship (the five tattvas); held to manifest the bliss of Brahman in the body when used within the rite, and condemned outside it (Kulārṇava 5.72-80; 5.96-105). Summary only.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The destruction of a family, whose fault Arjuna says the greedy Kauravas do not see but he does (1.38–39); it destroys the family dharmas (1.40).
Trees in which the Kula yoginīs always dwell; one should not eat from their leaves but worship them (Kulārṇava 11.66).
A person born with the dharma of yogins, fit for instruction (YDS).
The rules of conduct of the Kaula, taught in Kulārṇava 11 — honouring women and Kula yogins, keeping the samayas, secrecy.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas perish when a family is destroyed (1.40), are uprooted by the family-destroyers (1.43), and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.44).
One of the patriarchs who, at the end of the age of wish-fulfilling trees, guided people and instituted the first laws; the last was Nābhi, father of Ṛṣabha (lists of seven or fourteen).

definitions.definition: The 'pit of kula' at the base of the spine where the Goddess sleeps coiled (SL 10); she 'dwells in the kula-pit' (LSN 93).
The Goddess as head of the Kula, addressed throughout the Kulārṇava; worshipped with Kuleśvara/Bhairava.
A pill; in the Siddhar legends also the magic pill that gives flight or invisibility.
A young girl worshipped as the Goddess, especially in Navarātri (Devī Bhāgavata 3.26).
Worship of a young girl as the Goddess, prescribed in the eastern tantras (Rudrayāmala and others) and part of Durgā-pūjā in Bengal and of Kāmākhyā worship.

The eleventh sign (Aquarius), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the shanks of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Saturn; fixed; of the air triplicity (later texts); odd, male and cruel (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: hṛdroga (BJ 1.8); dignities: — (BJ 1.13).

Breath-retention: of two kinds, sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) and kevala (alone) (HYP 2.71); eight named varieties in HYP 2.44 and a different eight in GS 5.47. Extreme retention is restricted in this ontology (summary only).
Retention of breath; sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) or kevala (spontaneous). Methods recorded summary-only.
Retention, at whose end, as at the end of exhalation or inhalation, the Peaceful shines (VBT 27).
The prescribed fire-pit, of various shapes, for homa; described in the Kāmika's kuṇḍa chapter.

Called the support of all yoga-tantras (3.1); the text says that when she wakes by the guru's grace all lotuses and knots are pierced (3.2); given seven synonyms (3.104), described as sleeping over the door of Brahman (3.106-107).

The power (śakti) coiled at the base of the central channel, blocking its mouth; the support of all yoga (HYP 3.1); awakened by the guru's grace (3.2) and by breath, locks and mudrās (3.5, 3.66–69), she pierces the lotuses and knots and makes the mind supportless. Synonyms: kuṭilāṅgī, bhujaṅgī, śakti, īśvarī, kuṇḍalī, arundhatī (3.104); coiled eightfold (GŚ 30) or three and a half times (ṢCN). For yogins she is for liberation, for fools for bondage (HYP 3.107).

The Goddess herself as the coiled power: dwelling in the mūlādhāra she pierces the three knots, mounts the thousand-petalled lotus, showers nectar, and returns to sleep in three and a half coils (LSN 38-40; SL 9-10).
The coiled power lying eightfold above the bulb, closing the door of Brahman, awakened by the fire of yoga or by the guru's grace to rise through suṣumṇā (GŚ 30–31; HYP 3.2).
One of the names of Śiva's Will-power (KJN 20.11); in the Akulavīra the kuṇḍalī is the 'made' (kṛtaka) path, the innate abiding in samarasa (B.43).
The world-mother, pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.272–273), coiled three and a half times (6.223).
The Goddess coiled three and a half times around the Svayambhū liṅga at the base, led up through the centres to unite with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 51-53, Pūrṇānanda).
Kubjikā praised as 'coiled like a sleeping serpent' (Kubjikāmata 2.2).
Śabda-brahman in the body: consciousness dwelling coiled in the middle of the body, from which the letters arise (ŚT 1.14).
The power of Brahman in the root centre which, straightened up to the brahmarandhra, bestows nectar (ŚR 1.2.121–122).
The coiled power at the base that blocks the door of Brahman and, awakened, rises to Śiva.
The coiled power in the root centre, meditated upon at dawn as moving up and down the inner path and led through the six centres to union with the supreme.
The power rising from the root through the wheels to the dvādaśānta (VBT 28-29), 'curved in form' as the breath (VBT 154); the Trika distinguishes its forms as power of breath and of consciousness.
Tamil kuṇṭali: the coiled power at the root, roused by the guru's grace to pass the six supports (Vināyakar akaval; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam invocation).
The coiled power whose waking and ascent Jñāneśvar describes in Jñāneśvarī 6 as the Nāths' royal road (summary only).

The base of all: in Bön Dzogchen the ultimate ground, empty and clear, inseparable from awareness; not the saṃsāric storehouse.

definitions.definition: The ultimate aspect of the basis of all: buddha-nature as primordial wisdom, distinguished from the conventional ālaya-consciousness.

A goddess of the Śrīkula; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad 'the mother', deity of the offering; named in LSN 93.
Wholesome: consciousness and factors rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and (often) non-delusion, blameless and producing pleasant results.
Class of mental factors (ten): faith, heedfulness, tranquillity, equanimity, shame, dread of blame, non-greed, non-hatred, non-harming, vigour.
The renunciant with no possessions who gathers merit by offering his own body — the 'kusāli's accumulation' of the preliminaries.

The akiriyavādins' world is 'barren and fixed' (vañjho niyao).
First kind of renouncer: keeps topknot, thread, staff and water-pot; eats in one place.

Taking onto the path: using whatever arises — dreams, thoughts, afflictions, illness, death — as practice; the Shangpa 'three integrations'; the Drukpa 'six equal tastes'.

definitions.definition: Bearing the liṅga, outwardly on the body and inwardly in the mind; the given liṅga is never to be separated from the body (SSM 6.26; 6.30–33; 6.48).
The third level: the great principle (mahat), pure being, from which the unparticularized evolve (YBh 2.19).
The second means of determining subsidiarity: the capacity of a word or mantra to express something, which applies the mantra to it (MS 3.3.14).

The subtle body produced first, unattached, constant, made of the principles from mahat down to the subtle elements, which transmigrates, perfumed by the dispositions, and plays its parts like an actor (SK 40–42); it cannot stand without a support (SK 41).
The subtle body that persists from birth to birth until liberation (Kulārṇava 1.11).

equivalents.note: Within Sāṃkhya the 'subtle' (sūkṣma) bodies of SK 39 are the liṅga of SK 40; Vedānta's sūkṣma-śarīra is composed differently.

definitions.definition: Exclusive worship of Śiva in the liṅga; the SSM forbids worshipping, remembering or praising other gods (9.30–32).
One who bears the Pāśupata sign (ash-bath, lying in ash etc.) that marks his stage, as other āśramas have their marks.
Union with the liṅga — the aikya stage, and in common usage the death of a devotee, who is buried rather than cremated.

literal: equal flavour of liṅga and aṅga

definitions.definition: The goal of the path: the soul (aṅga) and Śiva (liṅga) in a union of equal flavour, 'like water poured into water' in common exposition; in the SSM, contemplation of the self dissolved in the sky of consciousness by the nature of sāmarasya (14.42–44).
The union in equal essence of the liṅga (Śiva) and the aṅga (soul), the goal of Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (Śrīkarabhāṣya).
A member of the community that wears the personal liṅga; the preferred name of the Basava-centred strand, some of whose writers distinguish it from 'Vīraśaiva' while others treat the two as synonyms.

notes: Alternative Kannada form: liṅgavanta.

definitions.definition: The numinous light that shines alone, free of senses and objects (Baizhang's style as proclaimed by Guling).
Designation used in an early-twentieth-century printed series of Sanskrit Vīraśaiva texts (the 'Vīraśaiva-liṅgi-brāhmaṇa-dharma-granthamālā') presenting Vīraśaiva dharma in brāhmaṇical terms.

notes: Evidence: series titles on the Muktabodha e-texts M00602, M00612, M00620; relevant to dsp:lingayata-hindu-identity.

definitions.definition: The bright and pure source whose branches flow in the dark (Cantongqi).
Northern-school key term (from the Awakening of Faith) for the mind free of thoughts as the essence of awakening (Dasheng wusheng fangbian men).

literal: right mindfulness at the end of life

definitions.definition: Right mindfulness at death: dying with an unconfused mind fixed on Amitābha, the aim of deathbed practice.

term: liru and xingru (entry by principle, entry by practice)

definitions.definition: The two entrances of Bodhidharma's treatise.
One of the four passions (8.9); it has four varieties.
The first unwholesome root (MN 9); a source for the origination of kamma (AN 3.34).
Greed, the third gate of hell (BhG 16.21); a sign of increased rajas (14.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The Kauravas' minds are overcome by greed (1.38); Arjuna laments being ready to kill his own people out of greed for the pleasures of kingship (1.45).
Greed, the unwholesome root of attachment to objects; characteristic grasping.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Greed: a sign and a product of rajas (14.12, 14.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Greed, the third gate of hell with desire and anger (16.21); the rājasic agent is greedy (18.27).
Eager longing to attain the emotions of the Vraja residents — the sole qualification for rāgānugā practice.

definitions.definition: The obscurations that are other than the ultimate, separable from it and never of its nature.

equivalents.note: the adventitious defilements of the tathāgatagarbha literature

literal: the four thoughts that turn the mind

definitions.definition: The preliminaries of mind training — the precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of saṃsāra (Seven Points 1.1, as the commentaries explain).
The topics of the impure vision in the Lamdre preliminaries.
The precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of saṃsāra, contemplated to turn the mind from worldly concerns.
The transmutation of metals by mercury, to be tested first before application to the body (SDS Raseśvara 24-25).

The Kadam instruction for transforming the mind through relative and ultimate bodhicitta — especially equalizing and exchanging self and other and sending and taking — and turning adversity into the path, transmitted in terse slogans.
Mind training as integrated into the great scope of the lamrim and the Guru Pūjā.
Mind training as taught in the Parting from the Four Attachments commentaries and by Tokmé Zangpo.

cross_language.note: reconstructions; the genre is Tibetan

definitions.definition: A world or realm: the world of the living, of the fathers, of the well-doers, the immortal world (RV 9.113.7).
A world or plane of beings; the Purāṇas count fourteen within the egg - seven above from Bhūr to Satya and seven below.
The world of the six senses: 'in this fathom-long body with its perception and mind I declare the world, its origin, cessation and the way' (SN 2.26); 'empty of self' (SN 35.85).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: dying when sattva has increased, one reaches the stainless worlds (lokān) of those who know the highest (14.14); there are two puruṣas in the world (loke) (15.16); the highest person enters and sustains the three worlds (loka-traya) (15.17); he is renowned 'in the world and in the Veda' as puruṣottama (15.18).
The finite universe of the six substances within infinite empty space, shaped like a standing man (loka-puruṣa), uncreated and beginningless.
A sphere of existence or post-mortem state; the sacrificer constructs his future world through rites — 'a man is born into the world he has made' (ŚB 6.2.2.27).

definitions.definition: Public shame and family honour (kul-kī-maryādā), which Mīrā casts off for Kṛṣṇa.

literal: inference as known in the world

definitions.definition: (Purandara) The worldly inference the Cārvākas accept, as against inference that transgresses the worldly path to reach the unseen.
The universe pictured as a man standing with arms akimbo: the lower world as legs, the middle world at the waist, the heavens as chest and head, the abode of the liberated at the crown.
The finite portion of space occupied by the other substances — the universe (TS 5.12).
The mountain range beyond the seventh ocean dividing the lit world from the dark regions beyond.
Conformity to the world: the Buddhas wash, eat, drink, take medicine and show age while free of dirt, hunger, thirst, illness and ageing.

literal: what is well known in the world, worldly consensus

definitions.definition: The conventional as accepted by the world without analysis; Candrakīrti admits conventional things on this basis only, not on the basis of own-characteristics.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The holding together of the world, with a view to which one should act (3.20) and the wise act unattached (3.25), since people follow the standard the best person sets (3.21).
The welfare and cohesion of the world, for whose sake the wise act unattached, as Janaka did (BhG 3.20, 3.25).
The skull observance of the Lākulas (and Kāpālikas), 'beyond the world'; the Svacchanda calls the Atimārga knowledge lokātīta.
One who increases the world (as used in Dhp 167).

literal: extended in / directed to the world (of the people)

definitions.definition: The school's name: the view that only this world, as far as the senses reach, exists; the doxographies call it the teaching most people follow.
In the Arthaśāstra, one of the three branches of investigation (ānvīkṣikī), with Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

cross_language.note: Tibetan name of the Lokāyata/Cārvāka school
in the Pali canon a branch of brahmanical learning (disputation/nature-lore), not clearly the school

definitions.definition: Kumārila's description of the state of Mīmāṃsā before him: 'mostly made into Lokāyata' (ŚV pratijñā 10); the Nyāyaratnākara names Bhartṛmitra and others.
(As reported) For the Bārhaspatyas the Veda is a mere cover for one who knows the course of the world.
Supramundane: the Buddha's conduct, roots of merit, postures, body, robes and food are beyond the world.
All Tathāgatas are supramundane and without outflows (Vasumitra).
In the Kośa, 'supramundane' qualifies the pure path (e.g. detachment by the supramundane path), not the Buddha's body.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: 'Supramundane' dharma — acts that stop karmic inflow and foster self-restraint — as against laukika (worldly, social) duty, which may be good conduct but is not spiritual dharma.
In 4.88: beyond the world; without object and without apprehension.

definitions.definition: The mindless, non-apprehending knowledge in which the transformation of the basis takes place.
The noble, taintless path factors, as distinct from the mundane ones affected by the effluents (MN 117).
Transcending the world of the five aggregates: the four paths, four fruits and nibbāna.
The space series: the second series, teaching that everything is self-liberated in the vast expanse (klong), transmitted chiefly through Vairocana.
The visualized offering of one's own body, transformed into nectar, to the four guests (restricted practice: summary only).
The light, rough, cool, subtle, hard and mobile nyepa, arising from desire; seated chiefly in the lower body; the mount of the mind and mover of the others.

equivalents.note: corresponding doṣa; Tibetan qualities and causal derivation differ in detail

definitions.definition: The seven constituents: nutritive essence, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and regenerative fluid.

equivalents.note: the seven dhātus of Āyurveda

definitions.definition: The Goddess addressed as Mother in Bengali devotion; the songs of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta speak to her as her child.
Mother tantra: a later Tibetan category for highest-yoga tantras emphasizing wisdom, bliss and clear light (Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra).

notes: Tibetan classification.

definitions.definition: Uncontrived, unaltered: awareness left as it is, without correction or fabrication; 'let no one alter this' (Kunjed Gyalpo ch.32).
'Mother and son': the base (mother) and awareness (son) recognized as inseparable; the meeting of mother and son clear light at death.
Mother and child luminosity: the ground luminosity at death and the path luminosity recognized in practice, whose meeting is liberation.
A mortal (as used in Dhp 53).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Arrogance/intoxication (of wealth), with hypocrisy and conceit a mark of the demonic (16.10, 16.17); tāmasic steadiness does not let it go (18.35).
Eight kinds of pride obstructing right view — in knowledge, honour, family, caste, power, wealth, austerity and body (Ratnakaraṇḍa).
The exhilaration of soma (RV 9.1.1 'most exhilarating'; 10.119).

definitions.definition: (As reported) The simile for emergent consciousness: as the power to intoxicate arises from kiṇva and other ingredients, none of which has it alone.

Bhagavad Gītā 13.19: Kṛṣṇa's devotee, knowing the field, knowledge and the knowable, becomes fit for his state; 14.19: the seer who sees no agent but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains it.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The state of the Lord, reached by many who were free of passion, fear and anger and purified by the austerity of knowledge (4.10).

definitions.definition: The bee's way of begging: taking a little food from many houses without troubling any.
Alms gathered a little from many houses, after the cooking fires are out.
The bee's way of alms: taking a little from each house as the bee from flowers, harming none (Daśavaikālika 1).
The stage at which the celestials invite the yogin (YBh 3.51); 'the lamp of yoga' from this stage on is part of knowledge born of discrimination (YBh 3.54).
Name of the three powers of 3.48 — swiftness like mind, action without instruments, mastery of pradhāna (YBh 3.48).
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
The amorous or 'brilliant' rasa, love for Kṛṣṇa as beloved, as of the gopīs; the highest of the five, treated in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi.
Milk, sugar and honey, offered as if wine by householders in the Kali age (Mahānirvāṇa 8.170-171).
The central consciousness whose unfolding yields the bliss of consciousness (PH 17).
The middle between two breaths, cognitions or states, where reality shines (VBT 26, 61-62, 103).

equivalents.note: the central channel is one sense of madhya (VBT 35; Śiva Sūtra 3.44)

definitions.definition: The disc of concentric continents and oceans around Jambūdvīpa, where humans and animals live (TS 3.7–9).

The middle level of speech: its material is the intellect alone; it follows sequence and goes beyond the working of breath (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the heart, the level at which the sphoṭa conveys meaning.
The third level of speech, in the heart, where it buds.
The path between the extremes of existence and non-existence, eternalism and annihilationism; identified with emptiness and dependent origination (MMK 24.18).

cross_language.note: in the first sermon the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification

literal: the middle; (the doctrine of) the Middle

definitions.definition: The middle between all extremes; the name of Nāgārjuna's teaching and school, its followers being Mādhyamikas.

cross_language.form: 中觀 zhongguan / 中論 zhonglun

literal: one of the middle, follower of the Madhyamaka

definitions.definition: A follower of the Madhyamaka; 'for one who is a Mādhyamika it is not right to state an autonomous inference' (PsP 1).
Puruṣa's neutrality (SK 19).
(1) Equanimity toward the unruly and incorrigible (TS 7.11); (2) impartiality of mind between doctrines, following reason (Jñānasāra 16; Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 8).
Identified by the commentaries with the Pali of the texts and called the root language of all beings, the language of intrinsic nature.
The fourth noble truth, the way leading to the cessation of suffering: the noble eightfold path (SN 56.11; SN 45.8); in the commentaries also the supramundane path-moment of each of the four stages.
The supramundane path consciousness, occurring once for each of the four stages, which abandons the corresponding fetters.

equivalents.note: same word; in Buddhist usage specifically the noble eightfold path

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion maghā: presiding deity the Fathers (pitṛ) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Ketu (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
Great waking: the notion 'this is I, this is mine' grown firm through past births.
The second mudrā, which stops the upward movement of all channels except the central and brings about the triple confluence (HYP 3.19–24).
Great emotion, the summit of love, found only in the gopīs and fully in Rādhā; divided into rūḍha and adhirūḍha (with modana and mādana, the latter in Rādhā alone).
The supreme love of Rādhā, which the Sahajiyā sees embodied in Caitanya and attainable in the sahaja state of the couple.
The 'great enjoyer' who hates nothing, praises nothing and enjoys all that comes.
Class of mental factors (ten): feeling, volition, perception, desire-to-act, contact, understanding, mindfulness, attention, resolve, concentration.
Space, air, fire, water and earth, produced from the five subtle elements (SK 22; Gauḍapāda on SK 22); specific (viśeṣa), and calm, turbulent or dull (SK 38).
Earth (solidity), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion), internal and external, each seen 'this is not mine' (MN 28; MN 62).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.6: the great elements head the list of the field's constituents.
The four primary elements — earth (hardness), water (cohesion), fire (heat), air (motion/support) — on which all derived matter depends.

The four great elements — earth, water, fire, wind — with the natures of solidity, moisture, heat and motion and the functions of supporting, cohering, maturing and expanding; derived matter depends on them.

definitions.definition: The 'great point' formed when the rays of Paraśiva are reflected in the mirror of vimarśa; it is the 'I' (Kāmakalāvilāsa 4-5).
The 'Buddhist land' beyond the Himalaya to which Vasiṣṭha was sent to learn the Goddess's Kula worship (Rudrayāmala 17.122-125).
The sixteen great gifts described in the Matsya and other Purāṇas.
The perfected yogin endowed with the powers, chief among Mahādeva's troops (Nandin, Mahākāla and the rest).

notes: Distinct from the Gāṇapatya deity Mahāgaṇapati.

definitions.definition: The twelve who know the Lord's dharma: Brahmā, Nārada, Śambhu, Kumāra, Kapila, Manu, Prahlāda, Janaka, Bhīṣma, Bali, Śuka and Yama.
Śiva who devours all beings; Kālī devours him (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31); Dakṣiṇakālī's Bhairava (Toḍala 1.3).
nag po chen po: as Bernagchen, the chief protector of the Karma Kagyu; the six-armed form is the Shangpa protector.
Kālī as primordial Śakti, whose abode is in the thousand-petalled lotus and from whom Brahmā and the gods arise and into whom they dissolve (Nirvāṇa Tantra 10.38-43).

equivalents.note: name of the same goddess

definitions.definition: (As reported) The Ājīvika measure of the fixed round: 8,400,000 great aeons through which every being passes.
The 'great doer' who does whatever comes, without regard to attraction, aversion, merit and demerit, free of ego, like a witness.
The compassion that embraces all beings as an only child and from which the bodhisattva's illness arises; eating meat cuts off its seed.
The root of all the qualities of buddhahood and the cause of the Buddhas' non-abiding nirvāṇa (Bhāvanākrama I).
Great compassion, one of the Buddha's exclusive qualities: a conventional knowledge differing from ordinary compassion in eight ways.
The supreme liṅga identical with supreme brahman (SSM 12.21–24; 12.38–41); in the ṣaṭsthala correspondences the liṅga of the aikya stage.
Human flesh as offering, in hostile literary portraits of Kāpālika and cremation-ground rites.
The 'great mantra' of sixteen names (hare kṛṣṇa … hare rāma …) from the Kalisantaraṇa Upaniṣad, chanted and sung without rules of time or place.
The 'great head-anointing' of the colossal image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, held about every twelve years, pouring water, milk, sugarcane juice, saffron and other substances.

The Goddess as the great power of māyā, who makes the universe whirl yet is the queen of the supreme Brahman (SL 98), who drags even the wise into delusion and when pleased grants liberation (Devī Māhātmya 1).
The Goddess as the power that deludes even the wise and creates the world, and when pleased grants liberation.
The deluding aspect of the root Nature, by which creation proceeds (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.102); in Bengal and Assam a common name of the Goddess.
Another name of bindu, the pure material cause.
The third error, tenfold: attachment to the five objects, divine and human (SK 48; Gauḍapāda).
The first of the ten mudrās; kuṇḍalinī becomes straight like a snake struck with a stick (HYP 3.10–14); first taught in the Amṛtasiddhi. (Not the Buddhist Mahāmudrā realization.)
The result continuum of the Lamdre, reached through the four result-empowerments; for Sakya Paṇḍita, only the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages is the Mahāmudrā the Buddha taught.
Approached through sūtra (emptiness of mind as taught by Nāgārjuna) and through mantra (the clear light of great bliss).
The 'great seal': the innate nature of mind, realized through the guru's instruction, beyond meditation and non-meditation; 'mind without aim is mahāmudrā' (Gaṅgāmā v17).

The third of the four seals: without own-being, like the clear autumn midday sky, the single nature of existence and nirvāṇa, whose body is objectless compassion and whose form is great bliss (Advayavajra); the supreme siddhi reached by the buddhas (Pañcakrama 5.28).

The 'great seal': the nature of one's own mind — empty, luminous, unborn — and its realization, which 'seals' all phenomena; also the path and instructions leading to it. Phyag is non-dual wisdom seizing (it), rgya is the release of saṃsāra's knot, chen po is union, the self-liberated dharmakāya (Karṇatantravajrapada). Distinct from the haṭha-yoga seal of the same name.
Taught as ground, path and fruit: ground — mind itself, clarity-emptiness; path — the vajra yoga of Mahāmudrā; fruit — the stainless dharmakāya (3rd Karmapa).
The Mahāmudrā 'of the amulet box': ground, path and fruit enclosed together; the mind left uncontrived is self-liberated.
In the haṭha sense, the 'great seal', a posture-and-breath practice destroying sins (GŚ 32–33).
In Mahāyoga the third vidyādhara level (the mahāmudrā vidyādhara, body as the deity's form); the 'great seal' of the deity in generation-stage practice.
'Mahāmudrā Chöd': Machig's Chöd understood as resting in the mind's nature once clinging is cut.

notes: Homonym: in haṭha yoga mahāmudrā is a seal-practice (see U28/U29 definitions of the same id).

equivalents.note: Kagyu authors (Karma Chagmé, Tselé) treat Mahāmudrā's mind-nature and Dzogchen's rigpa as one in essence; Nyingma and Kagyu authors also distinguish their methods; not an agreed equivalence.

alt_notes: Homonym of the Buddhist Mahāmudrā (U46); only the haṭha sense is defined here.

definitions.definition: (Jain report) The eightfold prognostication Gosāla learned from the six disācaras, drawn from the Pūrvas.
The eightfold lore (year-lore, dreams, marks, portents, bodily signs, omens and the rest) by which some claim to know the future; the Jain text says it sometimes fails and gives no release.
Head of a Nāth monastery (maṭh), e.g. the mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur.
The active spiritual leader Rāmdās describes: learned, tireless, organising people, teaching and protecting dharma.
The four great references by which a claimed teaching is checked against the discourses and the discipline (DN 16).
The five great sins: killing a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft (of gold), violating the teacher's bed, and associating with such sinners (MDh 11.54).
One of the eighteen principal Purāṇas; the lists differ in naming the Śiva or the Vāyu and in their order (VP 3.6.21-23; BhP 12.7.23-24; KūP 1.1.13-15).
Title of Śaṅkaradeva (and Mādhavadeva) in the tradition, which is therefore also called Mahāpuruṣīyā.
Great passion: passion purified as great bliss and compassion; 'great, great, great passion' is a name of Mañjuśrī (Nāmasaṃgīti 30); non-abiding nirvāṇa is great passion (Sekoddeśa 82).
Saraha: turn the three realms into the one colour of great passion (People Dohā v28).
The fourth upper world, where the wise dwell for a kalpa; passed by the yogin's gradual ascent.
The bodhisattva's resolve to liberate all beings, 'put on' as armor, while knowing that there are no beings to be liberated.
Epithet of the bodhisattva: one armed with the great armor who has set out in the great vehicle to lead countless beings to nirvāṇa.
'Great-souled': a Kartābhajā guru who initiates and collects dues from the disciples (barātī).
A 'great adept' who has attained the supreme siddhi (mahāmudrā) — especially the eighty-four of Abhayadatta's lives.
Great bliss: the bliss joined with emptiness that is the nature of the innate and of the goal; the fourth cakra at the head is 'of great bliss'.
bde ba chen po, great bliss: the taste of mind's nature 'as it is' (Nāropa); the saṃbhogakāya aspect (Karṇatantravajrapada); the object of the method path.
The body of great bliss, a fourth (or fifth) body in the Kālacakra and Hevajra systems, correlated with the fourth consecration.
The 'great empty', third of the four empties.
The 'great void', abode of all powers, reached by the breath in the third stage.
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'Great brahman' (mahad brahma): the Lord's womb, in which he places the germ from which all beings come (14.3-14.4).

The first evolute of prakṛti (SK 22), identical with buddhi; Gauḍapāda lists its synonyms buddhi, āsurī, mati, khyāti, jñāna, prajñā. Vijñānabhikṣu salutes mahat as the self-born Lord, sprout of the world.
The great self: higher than the intellect, below the unmanifest (KU 1.3.10-11); speech is restrained step by step into it (KU 1.3.13).
'Great Brahman', the Lord's womb (BhG 14.3); in the Nārāyaṇīya Aniruddha is called the great self (12.327.26).

definitions.definition: The grace of the great souls — the chief means to devotion, together with a drop of the Lord's grace (NBS 38).
Company of the great: hard to gain, unfathomable, unfailing, itself gained by the Lord's grace (NBS 39–40).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The rare one who at the end of many births takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (7.19); those who have reached the highest perfection and are not reborn (8.15); those of divine nature who worship the Lord with undivided mind (9.13).
In the Mahāparinirvāṇa and Aṅgulimālīya, the Tathāgata's true self, identified with the tathāgatagarbha, in contrast to the imagined self of the aggregates.
The rare one who knows 'Vāsudeva is all' (BhG 7.19); great souls resort to the divine nature and worship with undistracted minds (9.13).

definitions.definition: A text or section glorifying a deity, place, time, vow or scripture and its fruits (e.g. Devī Māhātmya, Kāśī-māhātmya, Bhāgavata-māhātmya).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Greatness: Arjuna has heard in detail of the Lord's imperishable greatness (11.2).

definitions.definition: Understanding of Viṣṇu's supremacy and perfection, which must precede and ground bhakti.
Knowledge of the Lord's greatness, which the gopīs never lacked; love without it is a paramour's love (NBS 22–23).
The 'great renouncer' who has given up all notions of dharma and adharma, desire and thought.
The great saying ('that thou art' and the like) that teaches the identity of the delimited consciousness with the whole; understood by partial implication.

'Great saying': a later (Advaita) name for four Upaniṣadic statements of identity, one from each Veda — prajñānaṃ brahma (AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19). The word does not occur in these texts.

A 'great saying' of the Upaniṣads teaching the identity of self and Brahman: prajñānaṃ brahma (ṚV/Aitareya), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (Yajur/BĀU), tat tvam asi (Sāma/ChU), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharva/Māṇḍūkya); each is assigned to one of the four āmnāya maṭhas.
U04 usage: the four sayings given as secret teaching (Śukarahasya) and at renunciation; read as the Goddess in the Bahvṛca.
The third mudrā, without which mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless (HYP 3.25–29).
An unimagined activity of mind outside the body, which destroys the covering of the light (3.43).
The ten goddesses — Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā — as forms of the one Goddess (Muṇḍamālā in the Tantrasāra; Toḍala 1 and 10).
Satī's ten forms shown to Śiva before Dakṣa's sacrifice (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.125-134).
The consort Śiva worshipped at each Mahāvidyā's right side (Toḍala 1.3-19).
Firm faith that the Lord will certainly protect ('rakṣiṣyati'); third limb of prapatti and, for Deśika, the most essential.
The vow kept wholly (7.2).
The restraints when unlimited by class, place, time or occasion (2.31, YBh 2.31).

The skull-bearer's great vow: living with a skull-bowl and skull-staff in imitation of Bhairava's penance; its keepers are 'mahāvratins'. Yāmuna reports 'by taking the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic'.
The observance of the Lākula division (lokātīta), with skull and khaṭvāṅga.
In Jainism the five vows taken in full by ascetics, to be kept in thought, word and deed, doing, causing and approving (TS 7.2).

notes: Homonym of the Vedic śrauta Mahāvrata rite, which is unrelated.

definitions.definition: Name for skull-observing Śaiva ascetics; Guṇaratna counts the Mahāvratadharas as the third of four kinds of Śaiva ascetics, the Śiva Purāṇa honours them among Śaivas.
The 'great sacrifice': the Goddess is 'worshipped by the sequence of the great sacrifice' (LSN 56).
The five great sacrifices to beings, men, ancestors, gods and Brahman (ŚB 11.5.6.1; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily five sacrifices, expiating the 'five slaughter-places' (MDh 3.68–70).
The vehicle that carries all beings to full awakening; by its own account the Buddha's highest teaching, contrasted with the 'lesser' vehicle (hīnayāna) of those seeking personal nirvāṇa.
Yoga as one, though called fourfold (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja) — a doctrine of the Yogabīja and the Haṭharatnāvalī (recalled).

The seventh vehicle, first of the inner tantras: emphasis on the generation stage and on the view that all phenomena are the great purity and equality of the deities; its tantras divide into a tantra section (the eighteen tantras, chief the Guhyagarbha) and a sādhana section (the Eight Herukas).

notes: Homonym of the haṭha 'mahāyoga' (trm:mahayoga), with a different meaning; kept separate.

definitions.definition: In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā the highest of five yogas: contemplation of Śiva's own nature alone, without adjuncts.
'Great yoga' tantras, an Indian class (Guhyasamāja, Māyājāla) and in the Nyingma nine vehicles the seventh vehicle.
Twelve thousand divine years = 4,320,000 solar years, the unit in which revolutions are counted (SS 1.15; BSS 1.7).
A cycle of the four yugas (catur-yuga) of 12,000 divine years (4,320,000 human years).

notes: Also: caturyuga

definitions.definition: A married woman's mother's home; the saints call Paṇḍharpūr their māher, with Viṭṭhala and Rakhumāī as parents and the saints as kin.
The second sthala: the bhakta in whom devotion rises through dispassion to steady discernment, steadfast in the liṅga even at the loss of life (SSM 10.2–3; 10.21–22).
The Lord whose southern image is worshipped and whose troops the perfected yogin leads; source of the scriptural tradition.
The Lord to be recognized as one's own self: the knower and agent, established from the beginning, full of the undivided awareness 'I am this' (ĪPK 1.1.2, 4.1).
The name under which Praśastapāda's account of dissolution and creation speaks of the Lord.
The third of the eight lordly powers (bhāṣya 3.45): becoming great.

definitions.definition: Cultivated towards all living beings (7.11).
Friendliness cultivated toward the happy, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Friendliness: the devotee dear to the Lord is friendly (maitra) and compassionate (12.13).
In Jainism friendliness toward all beings — 'may no one do evil, may no one suffer, may the world be freed' (TS 7.11; YŚ 4.118).
The friendly mind which, with self-restraint and benefiting others, is dharma, the seed of fruit here and hereafter (MMK 17.1); part of the dharma in brief (RĀ 1.10).
Loving-kindness, the first immeasurable, in substance non-hatred, with the aspect 'may beings be happy'.

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: The sixth tissue: gives affection, unctuousness and strength, nourishes semen and fills the bones (Su Sū 15.5).

The practice that avoids the two extremes of devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification (SN 56.11); also the teaching 'by the middle' that avoids 'all exists' and 'all does not exist' through dependent origination (SN 12.15).

The tenth sign (Capricorn), 30° of the zodiac made of nine asterism-quarters; the knees of Kālapuruṣa (BJ 1.4); ruled by Saturn; movable; of the earth triplicity (later texts); even, female and gentle (BJ 1.11); Varāhamihira's alternative (Greek-derived) name: ākokera (BJ 1.8); dignities: Mars exalted (28°); Jupiter in fall (BJ 1.13).
Hypocrisy, denigrating (as used in Dhp 150, 407).

definitions.definition: Visions, lights, sounds and other unusual experiences arising in zazen, not to be clung to.
Impurity binding the soul; Śiva is so called because he is free of the three impurities (SSM 8.8–11); in union the bond of impurity is shaken off (14.5–7).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the body's wastes — urine, faeces, sweat and the rest (AHS Sū 1.13); each tissue has its waste (Ca Ci 15.18-19); the doṣas when vitiating are also called malas.
Impurity, which is ignorance - the cause of the sprouting of saṃsāra (MVT 1.23; TĀ 1.23); not a substance.
What the practitioner strives to destroy: false knowledge, demerit, the cause of attachment, falling away and the root of the paśu-state.
In the narrow sense āṇava mala; in the wide sense any of the bonds. A real substance (dravya), not ignorance.
Malam: impurity; 'the three malas' (mummalam) are āṇavam, kaṉmam and māyai.
Stain, impurity (as used in Dhp 236, 238, 239, 241, 242, 243, 261, 388).

definitions.definition: The ripening of āṇava mala, whose powers turn away until it is ready to be removed.
Malaparipākam, the ripening that accompanies the balance of deeds and precedes grace.
The alphabet in a scrambled order (beginning NA and ending PHA), with vowels and consonants mixed, uniting Śiva and Śakti; the name of the Mālinīvijayottara's goddess.

definitions.definition: Grasping at things as 'mine'; when 'I' and 'mine' are exhausted, grasping ceases (MMK 18.4).
The sense of 'mine', root of suffering (MkP 38.6), one of the two forms of ignorance (VP 6.7.11).
The sense of 'mine' (as used in Dhp 367).

definitions.definition: The third tissue: gives bulk to the body and nourishes fat (Su Sū 15.5).
One of the four passions (8.9); it has four varieties.
Conceit — 'I am better, equal, worse' (Snp 4.9); the eighth fetter, abandoned only at arahantship.
Conceit: measuring oneself as better, equal or worse; a fetter abandoned only by arahantship.
Love-pique: love so intense it takes the form of feigned anger or sulking, a stage above sneha.
Rādhā's jealous pride that makes her withdraw from Kṛṣṇa; the friend counsels her to give it up, and Kṛṣṇa pleads with her (GG 2, 9, 10).

literal: knowledge of the modes of minds

definitions.definition: Direct knowledge of the thoughts of others, only in restrained ascetics; straight or extensive (TS 1.23–25, 1.28).
Reasoned reflection on what was heard, removing doubts (e.g. with companions); a principal means to knowledge.
In the Śiva Purāṇa the third and greatest of the three means (hearing, singing, reflecting on Śiva).
Reflection: continual consideration of the teaching by reasoning in accord with it, removing doubts about the object.

Mind: the swiftest of flying things (RV 6.9.5); the divine mind that goes far in waking and returns in sleep, the one light of lights, heart-seated charioteer (VS 34.1–6); it can wander to Yama and be called back (RV 10.58); desire was its first seed (10.129.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The turbulent senses carry away the mind (2.60), and the mind following the roving senses carries away wisdom (2.67); recalling objects in the mind while restraining the organs of action is hypocrisy (3.6); the senses are controlled by the mind in karmayoga (3.7); higher than the senses, lower than the understanding (3.42); a seat of desire (3.40).
The mind, declared the supreme cause that turns the wheel of saṃsāra (Bhikṣu Gītā); attached to the guṇas it binds, devoted to the Person it frees (Kapila).
The eleventh organ, partaking of both the sense and action capacities, whose function is constructive thought (saṅkalpa) (SK 27); one of the three internal instruments (SK 33).
One in each body and atomic; its mark is the non-simultaneity of cognitions (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56, 3.2.59).
An eternal atomic substance; its mark is the presence or absence of cognition when self, sense and object are in contact (VS 3.2.1, 7.1.30 C).
The inner sense, instrument of apprehending pleasure etc.; endless in number, atomic, eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): beyond the senses, called sattva or cetas; one in number though it seems many; the senses grasp objects only when led by it (Ca Sū 8.4-7); its marks are the presence or absence of knowledge, its qualities atomicity and oneness, its objects what is thought, considered, reasoned, meditated and resolved, its acts directing the senses and restraining itself (Śā 1.18-21); unconscious though active (Śā 1.75); in Bhela located between head and palate (Ci 8).

Mind as the first existent — 'neither non-being nor being; there was only mind' (ŚB 10.5.3.1); the greater of the pair mind and speech (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the brahman priest's track of the sacrifice (ChU 4.16).
The eleventh sense, of the nature of both the organs of knowledge and of action (MDh 2.92), and the instigator of all action (MDh 12.4).

The mind, higher than the senses (BhG 3.42), restless and hard to restrain like the wind (6.34), the sixth with the senses drawn by the jīva (15.7); in the Nārāyaṇīya the liberated 'become mind' in Pradyumna (12.332.15).
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them (VP 6.7.28).
Used in YS for the mind made fit for concentrations (2.53) and steadied (1.35); YBh 2.19 counts manas as the eleventh sense.

In Yogācāra, specifically the seventh consciousness (kliṣṭa-manas) that thinks of the ālaya as 'I'; in the triad citta–manas–vijñāna, citta is the store, manas the self-grasping mentation, vijñāna the six operative cognitions.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34), but is held by practice and dispassion (6.35); it is to be made one-pointed (6.12), made to abide in the self (6.25) and brought back wherever it wanders (6.26); all actions are renounced 'by the mind' (5.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Mind: of the faculties the Lord is manas (10.22); Arjuna's manas is shaken with fear (11.45), and he is told to look again with a glad manas (11.49); the most yoked worship the Lord fixing their manas on him (12.2); 'place your manas on me alone' (12.8); the dear devotee has manas and buddhi offered to him (12.14). Named distinctly from buddhi, citta and cetas.

Bhagavad Gītā 15.7–9: the senses 'with the mind as the sixth' are drawn by the living being, taken along at death, and presided over in enjoying objects. (The 'one' after the ten senses in 13.6 is taken by the commentators as manas.)

Mind: made of food (ChU 6.5.4); desire, intention, doubt, faith, shame, fear are all mind (BAU 1.5.3); the reins of the chariot (KU 1.3.3); 'the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation' (MaiU 6.34); 'by the mind alone is it to be seen' (BAU 4.4.19).
Mind: the inner organ as doubting and deliberating; for the Bhāmatī, when purified by contemplation, the instrument of direct realization.
The internal sense (the sixth, after the five outer senses), a non-eternal product of prakṛti (with mahat, ahaṃkāra and buddhi); memory arises from mental perception.

In Jain usage the 'quasi-sense' (anindriya/noindriya): the physical mind (dravya-manas) is fine matter, the psychic mind (bhāva-manas) the soul's capacity; its object is scriptural knowledge (TS 1.14, 2.21, 5.19).
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them; bound to prāṇa like a bird on a string.
The mind: restless elephant, thief and bird, the seat of both defeat and victory; it must be tamed by the guru's word and remembrance, for the Name recited while the mind wanders is useless.
The mind is the agent of Kāl, attached to the soul; it is left behind at Trikuṭī/Daswān Dwār.
Man: the mind or heart, addressed in the songs ('o my mind'); also the seat of the Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ).

definitions.definition: In the Kārikā 2.25: mind; those who know mind say "mind". | In the Kārikā ch.3: the mind whose object all duality is; when it is no-mind duality is not perceived (3.31).

definitions.definition: Mental repetition of the series of letters with remembrance of meaning, without movement of head, tongue or lips; a thousand times better.
Perception by mind-consciousness, produced by a sense-cognition as immediately preceding condition together with the next moment of the object; for Dignāga it also includes the awareness of feelings.
The diseases of the mind: delusion the root, lust as wind, greed as phlegm, anger as bile, with jealousy, pride and the rest; cured by Rāma's grace through the guru, faith, restraint and devotion.
Truth, forbearance, sense-control, compassion and the other virtues as tīrthas; purity of mind the highest.
Mental service, the highest form, to which bodily and material service lead.
Attention, a component of name (SN 12.2) and a factor defined in each jhāna (MN 111).
Attention: the turning of the mind to the object; a universal factor.

Attention, a universal mental factor; in the Śrāvakabhūmi also the four attentions of the nine stages (forced, interrupted, uninterrupted, spontaneous) and the seven attentions leading to the absorptions.
One of the ten books of the Ṛgveda.
The maṇḍala (dkyil 'khor) of deities which the Guhyagarbha declares to be the primordial nature of appearances; also the maṇḍala offering of the preliminaries.

The sacred circle — palace and assembly of deities (e.g. the Vajradhātu, Womb, Guhyasamāja and Heruka maṇḍalas) into which the disciple is introduced and as which the world and body are seen; also the offering of the universe.
The coloured diagram on which the deity is worshipped, especially at initiation.
Diagram for worship and initiation, richly described in the Pauṣkara.
The 'Man of the Heart': the divine dwelling in the human body, sought, longed for and met through the guru; also called the unknown bird, the uncatchable man, the neighbour in the mirror-city.

equivalents.note: The Bāul maner mānuṣ and the Sahajiyā sahaja mānuṣa name the same indwelling divine person in the two idioms.

definitions.definition: Mars: strength (sattva) of Kālapuruṣa and the general (BJ 2.1); male, kṣatriya, tamas; lord of fire (BJ 2.6–7); rules Aries and Scorpio, exalted in Capricorn 28°; period 7 years; Narasiṃha is born from him (BPHS 2.5); his Greek-derived name is Āra (BJ 2.2).
Praying for the Lord's own welfare out of love — Periyāḻvār's 'many years' (Tiruppallāṇṭu); the Āḻvārs' singing of each temple is called their maṅgaḷāśāsana of it.
Praying for the Lord's well-being out of love, as the Āḻvārs did, instead of asking anything for oneself.
An amulet (of wood, plant or other material) bound on with Atharvaveda hymns for protection and healing.
The jewel island in the ocean of nectar, the Goddess's highest abode (SL 8; Devī Bhāgavata 12.10-12).
The Goddess's supreme abode beyond the worlds, described in the Devī Bhāgavata.
The sanctum of a sattra or nāmghar in which the guru-āsana with the sacred book is kept.
The Tamil–Sanskrit mixed idiom of the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentaries and rahasya works.

The navel centre, where the Goddess rises (LSN 38); the Saundaryalaharī assigns water to it (SL 9) and there worships the dark rain-cloud with its lightning (SL 40); the Samayins see the Goddess manifest there (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 7; Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
The navel centre, ten-petalled, of fire (RAṂ), where the bulb is strung on suṣumnā like a jewel (GŚ 15).
The navel centre, a twelve-spoked wheel where the jīva wanders.
The inspired wisdom with which the seers searched their hearts (RV 10.129.4).
The mood of Rādhā's young maidservants (mañjarī), who serve the divine couple under Rādhā and seek no union with Kṛṣṇa for themselves; cultivated in rāgānugā practice through an inner identity.
The form of Mañjuśrī at the centre of the Jñānapāda school's Guhyasamāja maṇḍala; the practitioner arises as Mañjuvajra.
Conceiving things as self, in self, from self or as 'mine' (MN 1); 'I am' is a conceiving, a disease, a tumour, a dart (MN 140).
The sixth internal base, cognising mental objects; 'mind is the forerunner of all states' (Dhp 1–2).

equivalents.note: same word; in the suttas the sixth sense, not an evolute of prakṛti

definitions.definition: Destruction of the mind: not the loss of function but the end of the shrinking notions 'this is I, this is not I'; the state of the one liberated while living, in which pure sattva arises.
Mental action, declared by the Buddha the most blameworthy of the three kinds of action — as the sages' anger emptied the Daṇḍaka forest — used to show that mind acts directly on mind.
The power of acting with unsurpassed speed.
The self within the breath-made self and filling it; person-shaped; head yajus, right wing ṛc, left wing sāman, self ādeśa, tail Atharvāṅgiras (2.3.1).
Made of mind: the self within the breath-self (TU 2.3); also the person made of mind in the heart (TU 1.6; BAU 5.6; ChU 3.14.2).

definitions.definition: The sheath of mind: mind with the five organs of knowledge, the seat of doubt and desire.
A body created from this body, complete in its limbs, drawn out like a reed from its sheath (DN 2).
The sixth kind of samādhi in the GS (7.6, 7.16), and in the HYP the effect of mūrcchā retention (2.69).
Dissolution of mind, 'with form' in the jīvanmukta and 'without form' in the videhamukta.
Dissolution of the mind: the mind's ceasing to take on forms, practised by the knower for stable abidance.
The steadiness of mind when the breath moves in the middle (HYP 2.42); the one state (3.54); saluted as a goddess (4.64).
Synonym of unmanī and samādhi (HYP 4.3); also a name of Śakti (KJN 20.11).

In the Kārikā ch.1: the beginning-less māyā under which the jīva sleeps (1.16); duality is mere māyā (1.17); creation imagined as of the nature of dream and māyā (1.7). | In the Kārikā ch.2: the self's own (svamāyā) by which it imagines itself and by which the deva is deluded; the world is seen like dream, magic and the gandharva city. | In the Kārikā ch.3: by māyā alone is the unborn differentiated and born (3.19, 3.24, 3.27); the mind vibrates dual by māyā (3.29). | In ch.4: birth of dharmas is like māyā and that māyā does not exist (4.58); māyā elephant (4.44); māyā seed and sprout (4.59); mind moves dual by māyā (4.61).
The wondrous creative power by which Varuṇa measured out the earth (RV 5.85.5) and Indra goes in many forms (6.47.18); the wise see the bird 'anointed with the asura's māyā' (10.177.1).
The notion of self in the non-self by which saṃsāra is imagined; it has the powers of projection and veiling.
The Goddess's own inseparable power, neither real nor unreal nor both; conventionally called ignorance, in truth not other than her.
The power by which all that is grasped by mind and senses is a perishable mental creation; bondage and liberation are said by reference to its guṇas.
The Lord's beginningless, indescribable power, consisting of the three guṇas, known from its effects, by which the one Brahman appears as the world; neither real nor unreal (VC 108–109).
In Vidyāraṇya's usage, prakṛti with pure sattva, the adjunct of Īśvara, as distinct from avidyā with impure sattva, the adjunct of the jīva.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The Lord's divine (daivī) māyā, made of the guṇas and hard to get beyond; those who take refuge in him alone cross it (7.14). It carries off the knowledge of evil-doers, who do not take refuge in him (7.15).

The Lord's power: by his own māyā he comes into being (BhG 4.6); his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross except by taking refuge in him (7.14); by it he moves beings as if on a machine (18.61).

Śiva's power through which he takes names and forms (SSM 1.9) and by whose concealment difference in Śiva is imagined (14.8–9); the Vīramāheśvara keeps it away (5.17–18). Allama: gold, woman and land are not māyā — the desire before the mind is.
The Lord's power by which what is not real appears (BhP 2.9.33); the gross and subtle forms are fashioned by its guṇas (1.3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: By his māyā the Lord in the heart causes all beings to revolve as if mounted on a machine (18.61).

Power, magic, illusion; deceit: Indra goes about in many forms by his māyās (BAU 2.5.19); know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin (ŚU 4.10); the cessation of all māyā (ŚU 1.10); in PrU 1.16 māyā is deceit.

The illusion of an elephant conjured from a piece of wood by a spell, the simile of the three natures: the elephant is the imagined, its shape the dependent, the elephant's absence the perfected; the spell is the root consciousness, the wood suchness.
In Madhva's usage chiefly God's will (icchā) or wisdom, and also prakṛti; not an indeterminable illusion. The 'māyā' of the Advaitins is identified polemically with the Buddhist saṃvṛti.
A simile, with dream and the city of the gandharvas, for arising, abiding and ceasing (MMK 7.34) and for sense-objects (23.8): things appear though lacking own-nature.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.6 the Lord comes into being 'through his own māyā' (ātmamāyā) while presiding over his own prakṛti; chs. 4–6 do not define the word (commentators divide between a power of appearance and the Lord's will or knowledge).
Not an illusion-producing ignorance but prakṛti, called māyā because it produces manifold wonderful effects, and the Lord's wonderful power; the world it produces is real.
The Goddess's own power by which she becomes and veils the world; she is 'of the form of both knowledge and ignorance' (LSN 87) and 'the substratum of the illusory world' (LSN 142).

Sixth tattva: the Lord's power of concealment - 'the supreme freedom of Maheśa which accomplishes the impossible' (Paramārthasāra 15) - making the knowable appear as separate; real as a power, not an inexplicable illusion.

The great swindler (mahāṭhaginī) with the noose of the three qualities, who takes a different form in every house (Lakṣmī, Bhavānī, idol, pilgrim-water) and binds the world; also 'gold and woman' (kanak-kāminī).
Māyā, the material power ruling the lower regions under Kāl.
One, eternal, insentient, real substance: the material cause of the impure universe (and, as bindu or mahāmāyā, of the pure). Not illusion.
'I and mine, you and yours': the power that holds all beings; a painting without colour on the void, neither simply true nor false.

definitions.definition: The illusory body, of wind and mind, like a reflection or a rainbow; the conventional truth that joins with clear light (Pañcakrama; Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa).

sgyu lus, illusory body: (1) the practice of seeing all appearances and one's body as illusion (mirror image, rainbow, moon in water); (2) the pure illusory body of the deity arising from clear light.

Māyēyam: the products of māyā (bodies, organs, worlds, objects), counted as the fourth of the five malas.
The possessor of māyā, the great Lord who projects the world (ŚU 4.9-10).
A negation that, in negating its object, implies another positive phenomenon; the Gelug denies that emptiness is of this kind.
The impurity of difference: the appearance of the knowable as separate (ĪPK 3.2.5).
The bond of māyā: the body, instruments, worlds and objects given to the soul from māyā, which both bind and help it by awakening its powers partly.

The fourth tissue: gives unctuousness, sweat and firmness and nourishes bone (Su Sū 15.5).
A negation that, having negated its object, implies no other positive phenomenon in its place; emptiness is such a negation of inherent existence.
Wisdom and retentive intelligence, invoked as a goddess by students (AVŚ 6.108; 1.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Retentive intelligence, one of the seven feminine excellences that are the Lord (10.34).

The teacher of the Four Tantras, sitting in Tanaduk and emanating Rigpé Yeshe and Yilé Kyé; object of the physician's devotion.

The central mountain, made of four jewels, rising 80,000 leagues above the water and sunk as deep, ringed by seven golden ranges and the continents; on its summit the Thirty-Three gods.

A boundless mind of love for all beings, as a mother for her only child (Snp 1.8); kept even under the saw (MN 21); its liberation of mind has eleven benefits (AN 11.15) and outshines all merit (Iti 27).
Wishing welfare to beings; developed first towards oneself and then, with the barriers broken down, to all.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits recalling sense objects in the mind is called a hypocrite (3.6).
The first guṇasthāna: wrong view under the rise of view-deluding karma.
The root of the series leading to pain (NS 1.1.2); its forms include 'there is no self', taking the non-self for the self, pain for pleasure, the impermanent for the permanent (NBh 1.1.2).

equivalents.note: Yoga's avidyā (YS 2.5) is likewise taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self; Nyāya's list overlaps but belongs to a different account of self.

definitions.definition: The Advaita claim that the world is false; Dvaita refutes the proposed definitions and the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness.
Wrong view — the first cause of bondage (TS 8.1); five kinds in the Digambara list (one-sided, contrary, indiscriminate reverence, doubtful, ignorant).
Wrong faith; that taught by others falls into the four vāda classes, or five kinds: one-sided, perverse, doubting, vainayika, ajñānika.
Varuṇa's companion, god of alliance; 'may we look on one another with the eye of Mitra (a friend)' (VS 36.18).

definitions.definition: First view: dim, like a straw-fire spark; restraint (yama); no fatigue; non-aversion (YDS).

Mappō: the present age, in which only nominal monks remain and only Amida's vow saves.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast are not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (mohakalila, 2.52); delusion (saṃmoha) arises from anger and leads to loss of memory (2.63); one who attains the brāhmī sthiti is not deluded (2.72); desire deludes the embodied one (3.40).
The second error, eightfold (SK 48): attachment to or self-assertion for the eight powers, through which even gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).
The third unwholesome root (MN 9), one of the three fires (SN 35.28).

Bhagavad Gītā 7.13, 7.27; 8.27; 9.12: the world, deluded by the guṇa-made states, does not know the Lord; the delusion of the pairs; knowing the two paths the yogin is not deluded; the deluding (mohinī) nature of rākṣasas and asuras.
The worst of the faults, since the others arise only in the deluded (NS 4.1.6).
Delusion, the unwholesome root present in all unwholesome consciousness; characteristic blindness to the object's true nature; synonymous with ignorance.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.35: knowing which one does not again fall into delusion; 5.15: creatures are deluded because knowledge is covered by ignorance; 5.20: the knower of Brahman is undeluded.
Delusion born of anger (BhG 2.63) and of the pairs of opposites (7.27); destroyed by the teaching, as Arjuna declares (18.73).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Delusion: whoever knows the Lord as unborn and beginningless is undeluded (asaṃmūḍha) (10.3); Arjuna says his delusion is gone through the teaching (11.1); the Lord tells him not to be bewildered (vimūḍhabhāva) by the terrible form (11.49).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Delusion: tamas deludes all embodied beings (14.8); delusion is a sign and product of tamas (14.13, 14.17); the one beyond the guṇas does not hate it when present (14.22); the undeluded reach the imperishable place and know the Lord as the highest person (15.5, 15.19); the deluded do not see the living being (15.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Delusion: the demonic take up false notions out of delusion (16.10) and are enveloped in its net (16.16); abandoning allotted action out of delusion is tāmasic (18.7), as is action begun from delusion (18.25); Arjuna refuses from delusion what his nature will make him do (18.60); asked whether his confusion born of ignorance is destroyed (18.72), he answers 'delusion is destroyed' (18.73).

definitions.definition: In 4.30: liberation, said to have a beginning, so its endlessness will not be established.

Absolute dissolution of the threefold bond (body, senses, objects), when dharma and adharma are exhausted and no new body arises; not an enjoyment of pleasure (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 105–108; Śāstradīpikā).
The absolute ending of embodiment caused by the complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma; the self remains in mere being, without cognition or bliss (Prakaraṇapañcikā).

The soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss in the Lord's presence, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing; forms: sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya.

In Sāṃkhya, release belongs to prakṛti, not puruṣa (SK 62); it is threefold in the Tattvasamāsa commentaries — by increase of knowledge, calming of passion, and total exhaustion of virtue and non-virtue (Kramadīpikā); it is not the manifestation of bliss (SS 5.74).
When adṛṣṭa is absent, no contact (with a body) and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); quiescence like a fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).
Absolute cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal pleasure (Bhāsarvajña — a minority view).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the complete cessation of all feeling (Śā 1.137); separation from all conjunctions through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma — non-return (Śā 1.142); disengagement (nivṛtti), the supreme, tranquil, imperishable brahman (Śā 5.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The sage intent on liberation (mokṣa-parāyaṇa), with senses, mind and intellect controlled and free of desire, fear and anger, is forever liberated (5.28); cf. the verbal forms 'you will be released' (mokṣyase 4.16, vimokṣyase 4.32).

Release: rare as a noun in the early prose Upaniṣads, which speak of immortality (amṛtatva); 'freed, he is freed' (KU 2.2.1); release (vimokṣa) for one who has a teacher (ChU 6.14.2); the cause of saṃsāra and mokṣa (ŚU 6.16); 'the mark of liberation' (MaiU 6.20); 'desiring liberation (mumukṣu) I go for refuge' (ŚU 6.18).
Liberation, from which there is no return (BS 4.4.22).
Liberation: not produced but the eternal, bodiless nature of the self, realized when ignorance is removed by knowledge; the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow.
Release from karma and saṃsāra after the fall of the body, reaching Vaikuṇṭha and eternally serving the Lord, with individuality kept and knowledge fully expanded.
Liberation, on which one sets the mind after paying the three debts (MDh 6.35–37), reached by renunciation, yoga and self-knowledge (MDh 6.74, 12.85).
Pursued with dharma in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2.4).
Not an abode or a going elsewhere, but the manifestation of one's own power by cutting the knot of ignorance (Paramārthasāra 60); one, whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-166).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Release: those who know the difference of field and knower and the release from the prakṛti of beings (bhūta-prakṛti-mokṣa) go to the highest (13.35).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Release: the divine endowment leads to it (vimokṣa, 16.5); seekers of release act with 'tat' (17.25); the sāttvic understanding knows bondage and release (18.30); 'I will release (mokṣayiṣyāmi) you from all sins' (18.66).

Release from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding; the liberated soul rises to the summit of the universe and abides in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy (TS 10.2–5).
The soul's resting in its own pure nature, known already by the ultimate standpoint; the self conquered by passions is saṃsāra, the self that conquers them is liberation (YŚ 4.5).

Liberation comes from the exhaustion of action and afflictions, which arise from conceptual construction and elaboration, which cease in emptiness (MMK 18.5); definite goodness (naiḥśreyasa) is liberation (RĀ 1.4).

In horā, the liberation whose signs appear in the chart: Jupiter exalted in the 6th, an angle or the 8th, or the 12th rising in a benefic navāṃśa with the other planets weak (BJ 25.15); Ketu in the 12th from the kārakāṃśa gives kaivalya (Jaimini 1.2.69).
Oneness with Brahman after death, when the adjuncts fall away.
Attainment of the Lord's nature and non-separation from him, with difference preserved.
Held lower than loving service; puṣṭi devotees do not seek it.
Made to seem trivial by pure devotion; below prema, the fifth aim.
Equality with Śiva, free of bonds.

Death as a power with its own path (RV 10.18.1) and fetters (AVŚ 8.1); 'may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12).
