literal: one who has come for refuge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge in him and asks to be instructed (2.7).
One who has performed (V) or accepted (T) surrender; he has done what is to be done and lives in service.
Taking refuge in the Lord (prapad-): Arjuna 'has taken refuge' as a disciple (BhG 2.7); those who take refuge in the Lord cross his māyā (7.14); 'I take refuge in that primal person' (15.4).
Surrender to the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa's refuge (6.18.33).
Surrender to the Lord (with Śrī) as one's sole refuge, the path of those who have no other means.
An independent means (upāya) performed once with its limbs, the occasion (vyāja) for the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord as the already-accomplished means, befitting its dependent nature.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: expressed by forms of pra-√pad and vy-apa-√śri: those who take refuge in the Lord alone cross his māyā (7.14); evil-doers do not (7.15); at the end of many births the knower takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' (7.19); people driven by desires take refuge in other deities (7.20); by taking refuge in him even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal (9.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: 'I take refuge (prapadye) in that very primal person from whom the ancient stream of activity flowed forth' — the words with which the place of no return is sought (15.4).
Going for refuge: 'I, desiring liberation, go for refuge (śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye) to that God' (ŚU 6.18); the verb, not the later noun, is used.
Surrender to the Lord, one of the five means; the refuge of Kṛṣṇa's feet (Daśaślokī 8).
Surrender (śaraṇāgati) with six limbs, underlying all devotion.

equivalents.note: the Gītā uses the verb prapad- and 'śaraṇaṃ vraja'; later Śrīvaiṣṇava usage treats prapatti and śaraṇāgati as synonyms

definitions.definition: Possession: a real dissociated force that links a dharma to a particular series (acquisition and endowment); it explains why a defilement 'belongs' to someone even when not manifest.
Not a real entity; 'possession' is the presence of an intact seed in the series.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit; for the knower it moves the body but does not bind; its exhaustion brings bodiless liberation.
Karma that has begun to fruit and keeps the body of the liberated alive until exhausted (BhP 3.28.38: 'the body ... lives on while its karma lasts').
Karma that has begun to bear fruit in the present body and is exhausted by experiencing it; for the surrendered the Lord may end it at once.
The destiny karma that made the present body; not altered by the Master, only borne with detachment.

In jyotiṣa (interpretive gloss): the karma 'earned in a former birth' whose ripening the horā reveals as a lamp reveals objects (BJ 1.3; LJ 1.3). The jyotiṣa texts say 'karma of a former birth'; the Vedāntic word prārabdha is applied by later practitioners.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit and produced the present body; not destroyed by knowledge but exhausted by experience, like the momentum of a potter's wheel.

Viṣṇu's grace, without which there is no liberation; lowest when won by ritual (giving heaven), middling by hearing etc., highest by fullness of knowledge (giving liberation); it reaches lower beings through the higher.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attained by the disciplined one who moves among objects with senses free of passion and aversion (2.64); in it all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.65).

Purity of mind achieved by Śiva's grace; whatever is offered to Śiva is his prasāda, and eating only what has been offered purifies the mind (SSM 11.2; 11.6–11); devotion and grace arise from each other like seed and sprout (9.11–12).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: (1) Grace: by the Lord's grace the one who takes refuge attains the eternal, imperishable state even while acting (18.56), crosses all difficulties (18.58), and attains supreme peace and the eternal abode (18.62); Arjuna regains memory by Kṛṣṇa's grace (18.73); Sañjaya heard the dialogue by Vyāsa's grace (18.75). (2) Clarity: clarity of mind (manaḥ-prasāda) is mental austerity (17.16); sāttvic happiness is born of the clarity of ātma-buddhi, one's own understanding or the understanding of the self (18.37).

Two senses: the serenity of mind of one who moves among objects free of attraction and aversion (BhG 2.64–65, 18.37); and the Lord's grace, by which one attains the eternal abode (18.56, 18.62), sees the universal form (11.47) and regains memory (18.73).
The Lord's grace (īśaprasāda), by which alone the end of suffering is reached; also listed as the fifth means. As 'clarity of mind' (mateḥ prasāda) it is one of the strengths.

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Grace, favour: Arjuna repeatedly asks the Lord to be gracious (prasīda, 11.25, 11.31, 11.45) and seeks his grace (prasādaye, 11.44); the Lord, gracious (prasanna), showed him the supreme form (11.47).

Serenity; grace: 'through the serenity of the constituents' (dhātuprasāda, KU 1.2.20) or 'through the grace of the creator' (dhātuḥ prasāda, ŚU 3.20); by the serenity of knowledge one sees the partless (MuU 3.1.8); by God's grace Śvetāśvatara knew brahman (ŚU 6.21); by serenity of mind one destroys karma (MaiU 6.20, 6.34).
Grace received from the guru met in the unseen.
Parshād: food or grace blessed by the Master.

equivalents.note: Both name divine grace; in Dvaita prasāda is won by knowledge and devotion and graded, so the overlap is partial.

definitions.definition: One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the śaraṇa stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The third sthala: one whose bonds of sin are destroyed through steadfastness in the liṅga and who attains serenity of mind through receiving Śiva's grace (SSM 11.2).
A negation that merely denies without implying any other positive thing; Bhāviveka takes the negations of arising in MMK 1.1 as of this kind.
Emptiness as the mere absence of own-nature is a negation of this kind (Tibetan exegesis of Candrakīrti).

definitions.definition: Named at 4.29 as that in which even the yogin without desire (akusīda) asks nothing; the sūtra and bhāṣya give no further definition of it here.

definitions.definition: Drawing out an unwanted consequence from the opponent's own position (e.g. that self-arising would be pointless and endless: Buddhapālita on MMK 1.1).

The reasoning by which the Prāsaṅgika draws out the unwanted consequences of the opponent's own assertions, since no subject is established as inherently existent for both parties.
A subsidiary performed for one principal also incidentally benefiting another, e.g. the animal's prayājas benefiting the animal-cake (adhyāya 12).

The mind's peaceful flow from the impressions of stilling (3.10, YBh 3.10).
Answering a question from the chart of the moment it is asked, together with the omens then present (Ṣaṭpañcāśikā; Praśna Mārga).

Perception: the identity of the consciousnesses delimited by the knower, the mental mode and the object; affirmative, not grasping difference (Maṇḍana).
In Jain epistemology knowledge by the soul without senses — clairvoyance, mind-reading, omniscience (TS 1.12); later also sense-perception as 'conventionally direct' (Akalaṅka).
The objector holds that perception establishes things (VV 5); Nāgārjuna answers that he apprehends nothing by perception to affirm or deny (VV 30).

definitions.definition: The second path, of the four aids to penetration (heat, peak, patience, supreme mundane quality), in which the yogin realizes that objects are mental speech and mind-only and abandons first the distraction of the grasped, then of the grasper.
The principal injunction, united with the subsidiary injunctions, that conveys the prompt, uninterrupted performance of the whole rite in a fixed sequence.
The aim with regard to which one acts (NS 1.1.24).
Love for Kṛṣṇa: bhāva grown dense, melting the heart completely and marked by intense possessiveness toward him; the supreme goal, desiring only his pleasure (as opposed to kāma).
Love for the Lord, indescribable, 'like a mute's tasting', free of guṇas and desire, ever-increasing, unbroken, subtlest, of the nature of experience (NBS 51–54).
Love of the Lord — 'the two and a half letters of prem' worth more than all books; its lane is too narrow for two.
Selfless divine love, the goal of the siddha stage, refined out of kāma.
Prem: the love-practice (prem-sādhanā) of the one who has died while alive.
The newly dead before being joined with the ancestors; one whose rites are lacking (e.g. no vṛṣotsarga) or who did great wrong remains a preta, hungry and thirsty, troubling kin.
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The departed, worshipped by tāmasic people (17.4).
The newly dead, not yet united with the ancestors, sustained by the first-year offerings until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
Beings who, by shared karma, all see a river of pus where others see water — the Viṃśatikā's example of intersubjective agreement without external objects.

literal: one who has gone forth; the departed

cross_language.note: hungry ghosts in Buddhist cosmology (U36)

definitions.definition: Living unwashed, unshaven and ungroomed like a poor madman (the 'preta' of the sūtra being a living man), so that caste and āśrama marks are cut off.
Arising again (NS 1.1.19); established by the eternity of the self (NS 4.1.10).
The pleasant: chosen by the fool for the sake of getting and keeping (KU 1.2.2).
Happiness; what the word 'svarga' denotes (Śabara on MS 6.1.2); what is for the person is that which gives delight (MS 4.1.2).
Fasting and spending the eighth and fourteenth days of the fortnight in religious practice as a temporary ascetic (TS 7.21); Śvetāmbara pauṣadha.
The pure worldly knowledge obtained after non-conceptual wisdom, which knows dependent things as illusion-like and serves beings.
The unawakened who seize on self and on composites; 'foolish common people' are taught as no people.
The state of an ordinary person: non-possession of the noble dharmas.
The series in which the noble dharmas have not arisen.

equivalents.note: The state of an ordinary person vs the ordinary person.

definitions.definition: Cause of the usage 'separate'; in all substances.
The first pure meditation: scripture-based contemplation shifting among aspects, words and activities of a substance (TS 9.39–44).
Substance possessing smell (with colour, taste, touch); eternal as atoms, non-eternal as products; our bodies are earthy.
The Earth, mother of men (AVŚ 12.1.12), upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice (12.1.1), to whom the dead are returned (RV 10.18.10).

literal: doctrine that all is due to past deeds

definitions.definition: One of the three sectarian tenets; ascribed to the Nigaṇṭhas in MN 101.
Former lives (as used in Dhp 423).

definitions.definition: Recollecting one's many past births with their details (DN 2; MN 4); the first true knowledge.
Direct knowledge recollecting former existences; its range differs among sectarians, disciples, paccekabuddhas and Buddhas.
The last member of each person-shaped self (earth for the breath-made self; brahman for the bliss-made self).

definitions.definition: The person: real, neither the same as the aggregates nor different from them, designated in dependence on the present appropriated aggregates as fire on fuel; the fifth, inexpressible knowable.
A mere designation over the series of aggregates; there is no self (AK 3.18).
Not known as a real and ultimate fact (Kathāvatthu 1.1).

The only substance with form: atoms and aggregates having touch, taste, smell and colour, taking the forms of sound, darkness, light and bodies; karma itself is a subtle kind of matter (TS 5.5, 5.23–28, 8.2).
If the person transmigrated it would be found when sought fivefold among the aggregates, bases and elements; it is not (MMK 16.2).

cross_language.note: Pali puggala means 'person' — a different sense

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: The absence of a self in the person, entered through the teaching of the aggregates, bases and elements; knowing it removes the afflictive obscuration.
The conventional person: 'the bearer of the burden is the person' (SN 22.22); the seven and eight noble persons (MN 70); in the ultimate sense not found (Mil 3.1.1).
A person: a conventional designation (paññatti), not an ultimate reality; the Puggalapaññatti classifies persons, and the Kathāvatthu refutes the view that the person is a real and ultimate fact.
Worship of Śiva with mantras, twofold: for oneself (in the liṅga received at initiation) and for others (in temples, for king and realm), preceded by the five purifications.
Ijyā, worship of Bhagavān, the third of the five daily periods.
Arcana of Viṣṇu in a consecrated image with Vedic mantras; the best of the means.
The daily sequence of temple pūjās performed by the śānti under the tantri's authority.
Not with flowers but the firm mind fixed on the great void (VBT 147); the liberated worships Bhairava with the substances of self-awareness (Paramārthasāra 75).
The first of the five kinds of nirgrantha named in TS 9.46.

definitions.definition: Refusing meat (Kuṟaḷ ch. 26): better than a thousand sacrifices.
Taught in the Tirumantiram's first tantra.
Refusing flesh: Paṭṭiṉattār asks what flesh-eaters will do when Yama seizes them (Tiruvēkampamālai 33).
Established by the argument that each moment of mind arises from a previous moment of the same kind, not from the body alone, including at conception.
Dying again in the other world; the Brāhmaṇas promise its conquest ('apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati') to those who know or perform certain rites — the fire-altar, the Nāciketa fire (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).
Lunar mansion punarvasu: presiding deity Aditi (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Jupiter (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class movable (cara) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The white lotus: one who recollects the Buddha is a puṇḍarīka among people (Contemplation Sūtra).
Those who hear and entrust themselves to the vow are called white lotuses (Shōshinge).
(As reported) Pūraṇa denies it: giving, self-control and truthfulness bring no merit.
Merit, meritorious action (as used in Dhp 16, 18, 39, 108, 116, 118, 122, 196 ...).

definitions.definition: Auspicious karma — pleasant feeling and auspicious lifespan, body-making and status (TS 8.25); in the ultimate view merit too is a fetter, 'a golden chain' (Kundakunda).
Inhalation (HYP 2.71).
Inhalation; inwardly, 'I am Brahman' or scriptural knowledge.
Arthavāda narrating what was done or said in former times.
The 'exterior' genre of Tamil poetry — heroism, kingship, praise; the Āḻvārs turn its praise-forms to the Lord's deeds.
A class of sacred narrative lore, called with itihāsa the 'fifth Veda'; remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas and condensed by Vyāsa in every Dvāpara age into eighteen Purāṇas of four lakh verses.

The preliminary 'going before': a course of a fixed number of repetitions of a mantra (commonly counted by its syllables), with fire offering, libations, sprinkling and feeding brāhmaṇas in fixed proportions, by which the mantra is mastered before use.
The ancient Śaiva saints, above all the Tamil Nāyaṉmārs, whose lives Vīraśaiva hagiography narrates as models for the śaraṇas.
The waste of food: gives support and holds wind and fire (Su Sū 15.5).
(As reported) One of the eight 'stages of a person' in Makkhali's lists; Buddhaghosa glosses them as stages of life from the newborn onward.
Thoroughbred person (as used in Dhp 193).

definitions.definition: (As reported) Denied by Makkhali: there is no doing by self or other, no human effort, strength or vigour.
(Prakrit purisakkāra-parakkama) Affirmed by Mahāvīra against Saddālaputta; one of the five co-causes.
Doing by oneself and by others exists, as the element of initiative shows.
The region into which the mind enters in deep sleep, where, lacking contact with the skin-sense, it produces no cognition (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

Full, complete: 'that is full, this is full; from the full the full arises; taking the full from the full, the full remains' (BAU 5.1.1); the space within the heart is full and unchanging (ChU 3.12.9).
The full Kaula consecration; those consecrated by it are Śaiva avadhūtas (Mahānirvāṇa 14.144).
The 'full consecration' of later Śrīvidyā manuals, conferring the full authority of the tradition after the preliminary initiations.
The 'form' (rūpa) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's shoulders and neck fell; the goddess there is Pūrṇeśvarī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The knowledge 'I am Śiva, I am the guru, I am the whole world' (SSM 14.38–41).
The perfect I-awareness whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20).

notes: Shared vocabulary with Pratyabhijñā (see brw:pratyabhijna-to-virasaiva).

definitions.definition: The reckoning of the lunar month as ending at full moon (usual in the north).

The conscious principle: neither producer nor product (SK 3); the opposite of the manifest and the unmanifest in being without guṇas, discriminating, subject, individual and conscious (SK 11); witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent (SK 19); many (SK 18). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, etc. (SK 17). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

The cosmic Person, thousand-headed, who is all this, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven, and from whose sacrifice the world, Vedas and varṇas came (RV 10.90); the person in whom the gods dwell 'as cows in a stall' (AVŚ 11.8.32).
The seer, pure consciousness, unchanging, not self-luminous objects' owner but always knowing the mind's activities (4.18); utterly unmixed with sattva (3.35); many (2.22).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the conjunction of mind, self and body, subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.47); the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Śā 1.16-17); 'the measure of the world' (Śā 5.3); in Suśruta the union of the five elements and the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 8: the adhidaivata is puruṣa, 'person' (8.4; the verse does not say which); continual contemplation (8.8) and remembrance at departure (8.10) lead to 'the supreme divine Person' (paramaṃ puruṣaṃ divyam); that supreme Person, in whom beings abide and by whom all is pervaded, is gained by undivided devotion (8.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: puruṣa and prakṛti are both beginningless (13.20); puruṣa is the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain (13.21); situated in prakṛti it experiences the guṇas, and attachment to them causes its births (13.22); 'the highest puruṣa in this body' is called onlooker, consenter, supporter, experiencer, great lord and supreme self (13.23); one who knows puruṣa and prakṛti is not born again (13.24). In chapter 15 there are two puruṣas in the world, the perishable and the imperishable (15.16), and the highest puruṣa, another (15.17); Kṛṣṇa is the puruṣottama (15.18); one takes refuge in the primal puruṣa (15.4).

The person: the self-born person at creation (BAU 1.4.1; AU 1.1.3); the inner person in the eye or heart; in KU 1.3.11 the highest principle beyond the unmanifest; in MuU 2.1.2 the divine formless person; in ŚU 3.8-15 the great person of the Puruṣa Sūkta.

The beginningless principle that experiences pleasure and pain, seated in prakṛti and bound by attachment to the guṇas (BhG 13.19–21); the perishable and imperishable puruṣas are surpassed by the highest (15.16–18); in the Mokṣadharma the twenty-fifth principle, many according to the Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers, one in source according to the Nārāyaṇīya's close (12.338).
The cosmic Person with sixteen parts, source of the avatāras (BhP 1.3.1); spirit as one of the four forms of Viṣṇu (VP 1.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Person: Arjuna calls the Lord the eternal divine Person (10.12), the everlasting Person (11.18) and the ancient Person (11.38).
The Person with whom the sacrifice is identical (ŚB 1.3.2.1); Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa who surpassed all beings by the human sacrifice (ŚB 13.6.1.1).
The supreme Person, ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, called by many names (MDh 12.122–123).
The person, beginningless, beyond prakṛti, not touched by its qualities, like the sun reflected in water.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Both name the conscious self; Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is plural, inactive and without properties, whereas Advaita's ātman is one (with Brahman) and Nyāya's ātman bears qualities.

definitions.definition: Īśvara's definition: a puruṣa distinguished from others by never having been touched by bondage (1.24, YBh 1.24).
What is done here in this life, which can overcome a weak daiva (Ca Vi 3.30-33).
Human effort, without which fate does not succeed (MBh 13.6.7); defended by Draupadī (3.28–33).
Śrī's role of intercession: she turns the soul toward the Lord and moves the Lord to forgive and receive it.

In jyotiṣa, human effort: with fate it brings success, as effort and rain together bring a harvest (Yogayātrā 1.3–4); fate is human effort of a former body (YājñSm 1.349); a well-timed undertaking succeeds even with slight effort (BS 103.60).
Mediation of Śrī (and, for the Tiruppāvai's commentators, of Nappiṉṉai): Nammāḻvār surrenders naming 'the lady who says she cannot part from him' (TVM 6.10.10).
Human effort, affirmed by Mahāvīra against Gośāla's fatalism in the argument of the potter's pots.
Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, on all of which the epic claims to contain everything (MBh 1.56.33); for Prahlāda 'puruṣārtha' as human effort is denied as a cause (12.215.15).

The purpose — experience and liberation — for which the instruments act (SK 31, 36), the liṅga plays its parts (SK 42) and prakṛti creates (SK 56); the supreme puruṣārtha is the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1).
The aims of human life — dharma, artha, kāma, and (as the fourth) mokṣa; Manu's settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224).
Of the three, artha is foremost since the others are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three are to be pursued in their proper ages without harming each other; each earlier is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).
Any aim of a person — obtaining what is wanted, avoiding what is not — whose accomplishment depends on right cognition.

literal: for the sake of the person

definitions.definition: That which gives delight to a person, the desire for it being inseparable from it (MS 4.1.2); acts done for it are for the person, not for the rite.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from the 'four aims of life' sense of puruṣārtha.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, beyond both the perishable (souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī).
The Lord, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, who enters and sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).
Nārāyaṇa, reached by the ekāntins; those on the 'fourth path' go to him (MBh 12.336.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 15.18–19: because Kṛṣṇa is beyond the perishable and higher even than the imperishable, he is renowned in the world and in the Veda as the puruṣottama; one who undeluded knows him so knows all and worships him with his whole being. 15.17 calls the highest person (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ) the supreme self and imperishable lord.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Highest Person: Arjuna's address to the Lord (10.15, 11.3).
The Lord as distinct from and higher than both the bound (kṣara) and the freed (akṣara) souls (Gītā 15.16–18).
The highest person, Kṛṣṇa, above Akṣara Brahman; the goal of grace-devotion.

definitions.definition: One of the fourteen 'former' texts, said to have been taught before the Aṅgas and contained in the Dṛṣṭivāda; known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu and then gradually lost.
Portions of the second and fifth Pūrvas survive as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

Lunar mansion pūrva-bhādrapadā: presiding deity Aja Ekapād (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Jupiter (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Proṣṭhapadā.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: The 'prior' Kaula view presented in Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on SL 34, on the Goddess as Śiva's body and the shared relation of principal and subsidiary.
Lunar mansion pūrva-phalgunī: presiding deity Bhaga (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Venus (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The Eastern transmission; in the Kashmir–Nepal scheme usually the Kula/Trika worship of Kuleśvarī and Kuleśvara (moderate confidence).
The first, provisional answer to the doubt, stated in its strongest form before being set aside.
The preliminaries of a performance — songs, instrumental pieces and the benediction (nāndī) — offered to please the gods (NŚ 5).
The unmanifest sign of an impending disease (Mādhava Nidāna 1.5-6).
Lunar mansion pūrvāṣāḍhā: presiding deity the Waters (āpas) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Venus (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fierce (ugra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9).
The preliminaries to yoga: worship of teachers and gods, good conduct, austerity and non-aversion to liberation (Yogabindu).
Inference whose object's class has been seen before (e.g., fire from smoke); with śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa one of the three kinds (commentaries on SK 5).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
The subtle body arising from the subtle elements and consisting of mind, ego and intellect, which confines the individual (SK 3.17).
The guide on the paths who leads the dead to the fathers (RV 10.17.3–6).
Honoring a written sūtra with flowers, incense, garlands and banners, held to exceed the worship of relics.
Grace, the Lord's nourishment (poṣaṇa) of the soul (BhP 2.10.4); the path in which grace alone, independent of means, gives loving service.
Lunar mansion puṣya: presiding deity Bṛhaspati (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Saturn (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class swift (kṣipra) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Tiṣya.

notes: Vedic alternative names from memory where given.

definitions.definition: Calcination in a pit-fire of measured cakes of dung; the basic process of mineral pharmacy.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The uninstructed ordinary person who perceives and conceives (MN 1) and feels two darts (SN 36.6).
An ordinary person who has not reached a path.
An initiate who has received nirvāṇa-dīkṣā and seeks liberation.
Codes regulating Chan monastic life, traditionally from Baizhang; extant from 1103 (Chanyuan qinggui) and 1338 (Chixiu).
Mercury, the central substance of Siddha alchemy and of the mineral medicines; recorded as a term only.

notes: Restricted subject (mercury): no preparations recorded.

definitions.definition: The true name of the supreme being and of the highest region, revealed by Soamiji; glossed in the Agra literature as Rādhā (the soul/current) and Soamī (the Lord).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); set with dveṣa in each sense towards its object, a waylayer (3.34).
The tāmasa opposite of dispassion; from passion of the nature of rajas comes saṃsāra (SK 45); meditation is its removal (SS 3.30); it is not quieted by enjoyment (SS 4.27).
Attachment, which follows on pleasure (2.7).
Lust, one of the three fires (SN 35.28); its destruction is part of nibbāna (SN 38.1).
Attachment to the agreeable, arising from false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2); one of the three groups of faults.
Arises from pleasure, absorption, satisfaction, the unseen and particular birth (VS 6.2.12–16 C).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Passion: the nature of rajas (14.7).
Passion in which even sorrow becomes happiness for the beloved's sake.

definitions.definition: Attachment and aversion, the 'seeds of karma' (Uttarādhyayana 32.7); in the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa, pejja and dosa, under which the four passions are classed.

definitions.definition: Kañcuka: attachment, the sense of lacking something.
A melodic entity: that particular sound adorned with notes and melodic movement which colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281).

notes: Disambiguated from trm:raga (attachment, passion).

definitions.definition: Devotion that follows the rāgātmikā devotion of the Vraja residents, arising from eager longing (lobha); of two kinds, kāmānugā and sambandhānugā.
Devotion consisting of rāga — spontaneous, intense absorption in the beloved — natural to the eternal residents of Vraja.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The ancient yoga now told to Arjuna is 'the highest secret' (4.3).

definitions.definition: The three mantras of the Śrīvaiṣṇava: the tirumantra (aṣṭākṣara), the dvaya and the carama-śloka (Gītā 18.66).
The 'secret sacrifice': the Goddess is worshipped by its sequence and pleased by secret libations (LSN 83). (Interpretations differ; summary only.)

The ascending node counted as a planet: in the epic the asura whose severed head, made immortal by the nectar, swallows sun and moon (MBh 1.17); in the siddhāntas the node (pāta) that deflects the moon (SS 2.6); for Varāhamihira not the cause of eclipses but present at them by Brahmā's boon to receive the offerings (BS 5.13–15); the Boar is born from him (BPHS 2.6); period 18 years.
A daily period of about an eighth of the daytime, falling at a different part of the day for each weekday, avoided for new undertakings (mainly South Indian practice).

notes: Classical textual basis not located; recorded as current practice.

definitions.definition: The welcoming descent: Amitābha with the bodhisattvas and assembly appears to the dying practitioner (19th vow; Smaller Sūtra).
Belongs to birth by various practices; the person of shinjin need not await it.

The aim for which haṭha is taught (1.2); the text lists it as one of the words for samādhi (4.3-4) and says that on the mind becoming one 'this is called rājayoga' (4.77); all means of haṭha and laya are for its accomplishment (4.103).

The goal served by haṭha: samādhi, the mindless, supportless state in which mind and breath are dissolved; HYP 4.3–4 lists it first among the synonyms of samādhi (with unmanī, manonmanī, amanaska, sahaja, turyā…). The DYŚ calls it the best of the four yogas, the Śiva Saṃhitā 'free of duality'; the Jyotsnā identifies it with asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity.
The royal yoga, the goal to which haṭha leads; synonymous with samādhi, unmanī, sahaja and the rest (HYP 4.3–4).
The fourth of the four yogas; in the Yogaśikhā the union of rajas and retas.

equivalents.note: HYP 4.3–4 and GS 7.17 treat rājayoga and samādhi as names of one state

definitions.definition: The front teeth, at whose root the tongue is pressed in some forms of padmāsana and mahābandha (HYP 1.46, 3.22; GŚ 64; ŚS 3.73).
The duties of the king, taught by Bhīṣma in the Śāntiparvan (12.1–128) and by Rāma to Bharata (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
'Sovereign of the king of kings': Lalitā as supreme empress, the form worshipped in South Indian Śrīvidyā temples.

literal: queen of the king of kings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The royal sages who knew the yoga received through succession (4.2).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
A region of space, especially the atmosphere; 'there was no rajas' before creation (RV 10.129.1); the six rajāṃsi propped apart (1.164.6).
The guṇa of passion, arising from thirst and attachment, binding by attachment to action (BhG 14.7); desire and anger are born of it (3.37).
The guṇa that is stimulating and mobile (SK 13), of the nature of pain (SK 12); predominant in the middle world (SK 54); suffering is a modification of rajas (Vācaspati).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): with tamas one of the two doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21); the rājasa mind is faulty, having the part of anger (Śā 4.36); rajas and tamas bind the person to the wheel of births (Śā 1.36, 1.68); their absence is a condition of liberation (Śā 1.142).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has his rajas stilled (śānta-rajas) (6.27).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: rajas is of the nature of passion, bound up with the arising of thirst and attachment; it binds by attachment to action (14.7) and attaches to action (14.9); when it increases, greed, activity, undertaking of actions, restlessness and craving arise (14.12); dying in it one is born among those attached to action (14.15); its fruit is pain (14.16); greed arises from it (14.17); the rājasa remain in the middle (14.18).
The guṇa characterized as attraction and aversion; those in it go to the human state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The guṇa by which faith, food, sacrifice, austerity, giving, relinquishment, knowledge, action, agent, understanding, steadiness and happiness are called rājasic — marked by desire for fruit or return, display, strain, craving, elation and grief (17.9, 17.12, 17.18, 17.21, 18.8, 18.21, 18.24, 18.27, 18.31, 18.34, 18.38).

Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch13-15): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch16-18): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: The later guṇa sense is contributed by other units.

definitions.definition: The female generative fluid, counterpart of bindu, retained by the yoginī in the vajrolī passage (HYP 3.99–102) and identified with Śakti (SS 1.92). Not the guṇa rajas.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: The knowledge Kṛṣṇa declares in ch. 9: royal knowledge, royal secret, the supreme purifier, known by direct apprehension, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, imperishable (9.2).
The royal knowledge and royal secret of ch. 9, supreme purifier, directly perceived and easy to practise (BhG 9.1–2).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch07-09): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A combination making the native a king or like one — by exalted planets (BJ 11), or by the relation of angle- and trine-lords (BPHS 39); distinct from rājayoga as a path of meditation.
In the Kārikā: the rope not ascertained in the dark is imagined as a snake or a line of water; when the rope is ascertained the imagining ceases; so the self is imagined and ascertained.
The rope–snake: stock illustration of superimposition, sublation and substratum.

checks.note: Definition read by J against the cited verses: sense matches the text; linked ids resolve (by code); no modern, health or restricted-practice wording. Level not raised (entities are not promoted by the spot-check).

definitions.definition: The woollen whisk ('dust-remover', ogho) with which Śvetāmbara mendicants gently sweep insects from their path and seat; the chief sign of initiation.
The eight passions among the ninety-six principles — desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, haughtiness and egoism (list recalled at low confidence).
Demonic beings who harm the rite and cause disease, driven off by Agni and the healer (RV 10.97.6).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Rākṣasas, worshipped with yakṣas by the rājasic (17.4).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch16-18): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: The second tissue: gives clarity of complexion, nourishes flesh and sustains life (Su Sū 15.5); counted with the doṣas by Suśruta (Sū 21.3-4).
Bloodletting, counted by the surgical school among the purificatory therapies. Summary only.
Charm, the quality of colouring the mind with delight, lacking in the unstruck nāda and present in music (ŚR 1.2.166); cognate with rāga.
The Sants' most common name for the formless Lord who 'pervades every body' (ghaṭ ghaṭ rām) — explicitly distinguished from Rāma son of Daśaratha.
Rām as the nirguṇa object of remembrance of the 'lovers of Rām'.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit name primarily denotes the avatāra

definitions.definition: The Vārkarī mantra, given to Tukārām in his dream-initiation and chanted by all Vārkarīs.
The name 'Rāma', greater than both the formless and the embodied Brahman, mediating between them, the one support in the Kali age and the ferrying mantra Śiva gives the dying at Kāśī.

equivalents.note: the Rāma name is one of the forms the tāraka mantra takes (Kāśī), not the whole of the tāraka doctrine

definitions.definition: Rāma's reign as the pattern of a righteous order, free of bodily, divine and elemental suffering, where all keep their dharma and love one another.
The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) given at Rāmānandī initiation.

notes: Form of the initiation mantra as commonly reported; verify against Rāmānandī manuals.

definitions.definition: A verse form (caupāī stanzas closed by a sākhī) used for doctrine, especially cosmology, in the Bījak.

Self-liberation: thoughts and appearances liberate by themselves when recognized in awareness, without an antidote; with primordial liberation (ye grol), liberation on arising (shar grol), naked liberation (cer grol) and liberation from extremes (mtha' grol) it forms the modes of liberation.

Self-liberation: thoughts and appearances liberate themselves in their own place when their nature is seen; 'the self-liberated dharmakāya' (Karṇatantravajrapada); in the Shangpa, the 'three self-liberations' of the Amulet Mahāmudrā.

notes: Also central in Dzogchen (U45).

definitions.definition: Self-arising wisdom: the all-creating king's own name for itself in the Kunjed Gyalpo — wisdom without causes and conditions, beyond effort, unobscured.
The thoroughly established nature: self-illuminating wisdom free of subject-object duality, the ultimate.

equivalents.note: Tāranātha's self-aware wisdom is ultimate; Indian svasaṃvedana is a feature of cognition in the pramāṇa tradition

definitions.definition: Emptiness of own-nature; for the Jonang it is true of all conventional phenomena but not of the ultimate.
The Madhyamaka of Nāgārjuna's reasonings, in which every phenomenon including the ultimate is empty of own-nature; in Kongtrul's presentation valid especially for cutting elaborations.
The only correct sense of emptiness: every phenomenon, including the ultimate, is empty of its own inherent existence; the Gelug rejects 'other-emptiness' as a permanent ultimate.

Gorampa holds the self-empty view in the form of freedom from extremes; Shākya Chokden valued it for cutting conceptual elaboration while also affirming the other-empty view for meditative experience.

cross_language.note: Sanskrit phrasing, not a Sanskrit school name

equivalents.note: the rangtong reading of niḥsvabhāvatā applied to all phenomena

definitions.definition: Nature: the second aspect of the ground — luminous, spontaneously present.

term: rang bzhin rdzogs pa chen po

definitions.definition: The natural Great Perfection: the nature of mind as already perfect, the object of Dudjom Lingpa's 'Buddhahood Without Meditation'.
The pitta that colours rasa (into blood): in liver and spleen for Suśruta (Sū 21.10), in the stomach for Vāgbhaṭa (AHS Sū 12.13).

literal: sap; taste; essence; (in Rasa Śāstra) mercury

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) taste, the object of the tongue, sixfold — sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.64-65; 26.9); (2) the first tissue (AHS Sū 1.13).
In Rasa Śāstra, mercury, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.36); rasa as the means of crossing saṃsāra, identified with brahman ('raso vai saḥ', SDS Raseśvara 49).

Aesthetic relish: the stable emotion made relishable by the union of determinants, consequents and transient states, tasted by the sensitive spectator as food is tasted (NŚ 6 rasa-sūtra); eight in drama (NŚ 6.15), nine with śānta; 'twin of tasting Brahman' (SD 3.2).
The emotional flavour that notes, rāgas and dance are to evoke; the music treatises assign notes and rāgas to rasas.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The inner taste for sense-objects that remains when one abstains from them and turns away only on seeing the highest (2.59).
Quality grasped by the tongue; six tastes; in earth and water.
The essence of love tasted in the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, located in the Sahajiyā body; the Sahajiyā reads Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory as a guide to embodied practice.

notes: Homonym: in aesthetics and bhakti the relished sentiment.

definitions.definition: The first tissue, the essence of digested food: gives satisfaction and pleasure and nourishes blood (Su Sū 15.5).
Kṛṣṇa's circle dance with the gopīs on the autumn full-moon night (BhP 10.29-33).

literal: the play of the rāsa dance

definitions.definition: Mercury, which like the mind is by nature unsteady; 'bound' mercury and mind are compared in HYP 4.26–27 (an alchemical analogy; no procedure).
Abstaining from rich or savoury foods (ghee, milk, sweets, salt) (TS 9.19).
The eighteen processings of mercury required before it can be used; named in the SDS (Raseśvara 19-21) and detailed in the rasa texts. RESTRICTED: names and procedures not recorded.

notes: Homonym: saṃskāra as latent impression and as life-cycle rite.

definitions.definition: The seven obstacles to aesthetic relish listed by Abhinavagupta (lack of credibility, particularity of time and place, absorption in one's own feelings, lack of means, lack of clarity, non-predominance, doubt).
Semblance of rasa: an improper or incompatible mixture of rasas, or rasa in an unfit object.
A liṅga made of processed mercury, whose worship is praised above that of all other liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.43; RRS 1.24, 6.19). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.
The right channel (sun, means); the Sekoddeśa equates it with piṅgalā.

equivalents.note: Named together in Sekoddeśa 46.

definitions.definition: The hall for rasa work in a safe, righteous land, spacious and well provided with windows, with a secluded rasa-pavilion beside it (RRS 6.11-14).
The science of processing mercury and minerals for the body's stability, jīvanmukti and medicine; also rasavidyā, rasatantra (Rasārṇava 1.46; SDS Raseśvara 23).
Those who, without abandoning the body, have gained the body born of Hara and Gaurī, whose servants are the mantras (Rasahṛdaya 1.7); twenty-seven are listed in RRS 1.2-5.
Named by commentators for the fault the Kārikā describes at 3.45: not to relish (na āsvādayet) the happiness there; be unattached by discernment.
Relishing: enjoying the bliss of savikalpa samādhi (or of the calm mind), which prevents going further.

definitions.definition: Alchemy — the art (vātam) of transmuting metals and fixing mercury (iracam), in the Siddhar corpus both an outer art and a figure for perfecting the body. Summary only.

notes: 'vātam' also names the wind humour; the homonym is kept apart (see trm:vata). Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the branch and the means by which the healthy gain long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength — 'the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other tissues' (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); taken by the hut-entering or the wind-and-sun mode (Ci 1.1.16); useless in an unpurified body (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4).
In Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (restricted), the fourth section of the Rasaratnākara 'for the aged' (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
A sign: one of the twelve equal divisions of the zodiac beginning with Aries, each of nine asterism-quarters; the limbs of Kālapuruṣa; synonyms kṣetra, gṛha, ṛkṣa, bha, bhavana (BJ 1.4).

In the Jaimini system, aspect by signs: each sign aspects the sign facing it and those at its sides — movable signs the fixed (but the adjacent), fixed the movable (but the adjacent), dual signs one another (Jaimini 1.1.2–3; BPHS 8).
The empirical person, the aggregate of twenty-four, born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma, in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain are established (Ca Śā 1.35-37, 1.53).
A devotee who contemplates the sweet, intimate love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
A connoisseur of the pair's love (rasa) in Vṛndāvana; used of the Rādhāvallabha and Haridāsī poets.
As in the Rādhāvallabha usage: one who tastes the rasa of the nikuñja.
The chariot of the simile: the body (śarīra), 1.3.3.

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

definitions.definition: One of the two principal sāmans of the soma rite, forming part of the Vrātya's seat (AVŚ 15.3).
Love or attraction for Kṛṣṇa; the seed-form of the permanent emotion; in bhāva-bhakti it first appears.
Love-feeling (and, in coded usage, its bodily basis) that the practitioner must stabilize and raise into prema.
Delight (as used in Dhp 214, 310, 373, 418).

notes: Sense-specific id: the existing trm:rati in the ontology carries a different tradition's sense; this entry is the Pali sense as used in the Dhammapada.

definitions.definition: A gem: 'the fate that depends on gems is to be examined by experts', since good gems bring good to kings and bad ones harm (BS 79.1); later texts assign a gem to each planet to be worn as a remedy.
Right view, right knowledge and right conduct, which together are the path to liberation (TS 1.1); in the ultimate sense they are the self itself (YŚ 4.2; Yogaśataka 2).
The Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya saṃhitās, held to issue directly from the Lord's mouth; the Īśvara, Pārameśvara and Pādma are their explanatory expansions.

notes: Not the Buddhist or Jain 'three jewels' (different ids).

definitions.definition: Not eating at night, added as a sixth vow for mendicants and a basic rule for laity, since small beings cannot be seen in the dark.
TS 9.35: dhyāna arising from violence, falsehood, theft and guarding of sense-objects; it belongs to the unrestrained and the partly restrained.
Delighting in violence, falsehood, theft and guarding one's possessions (TS 9.35).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

definitions.definition: The Rudra-gāyatrī ('tatpuruṣāya vidmahe ...') muttered after impurity and as the chosen verse from which yoga proceeds.
Matter (wealth, substance): paired with breath as the first pair produced by Prajāpati; the moon, and all that has form or is formless (PrU 1.4-5); the southern course (1.9).
A metrical verse of praise, the unit of the Ṛgveda; the verses rest on the syllable in the highest heaven (RV 1.164.39); ṛc is speech (VS 36.1).
Magical power: in substance concentration; movement and creation; arising from cultivation, birth, spells, herbs or karma.

equivalents.note: Sanskrit and Pali forms of the same canonical term; school definitions differ (see the per-lineage definitions).

definitions.definition: Hope and fear — for results and against failure — the last grasping to be released: 'without hope and fear the fruit is manifest' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā).
Exhalation, one of the three parts of breath-control (HYP 2.71).
Exhalation; inwardly, negation of the world or renunciation of objects.
A yogin who wears only a single cotton cloth, sustained by inner heat — Milarepa, Rechungpa and their successors.
Seed; desire was 'the first seed of mind' (RV 10.129.4); 'seed-placers' in 10.129.5.

Lunar mansion revatī: presiding deity Pūṣan (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord Mercury (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class soft (mṛdu) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Its junction with Aśvinī is a gaṇḍānta.

Awareness: the knowing, luminous nature of mind recognized as the ground itself — empty, clear, unobstructed and unfabricated. It is distinguished from ordinary mind (sems), which grasps at objects; recognizing rig pa through the master's introduction is the entry to the Great Perfection.
In the Nyingma generally, the awareness that is the fruit of the inner tantras and the object of the introduction; 'awareness-holder' (rig 'dzin, vidyādhara) names those who hold it.
In Bön Dzogchen, awareness inseparable from the base of all (kun gzhi); their union is the natural state.

Awareness: the knowing, clear aspect of mind's nature; in Kagyu Mahāmudrā texts used of self-aware mind (rang rig) that is clear because it is awareness and non-conceptual (Nāropa); 'leave awareness naked' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā).

cross_language.note: translation equivalent; the Sanskrit word has other senses in other traditions

equivalents.note: awareness recognized is the dharmakāya
Mipham identifies buddha-nature as luminosity-emptiness, the nature Dzogchen introduces as rig pa

notes: U45 owns the Dzogchen sense (rigpa vs sems); this is the Kagyu contribution.

definitions.definition: The empowerment of the expressive power of awareness: the Dzogchen empowerment that introduces awareness, beyond the four empowerments of the lower tantras.
The non-sectarian attitude and programme: respecting, receiving and preserving every authentic lineage in its own terms.
Compound pills containing precious substances and processed metals, consecrated and taken under dietary rules (summary only).
A rite on the way to Paṇḍharpūr in which a horse (held to carry the saint unseen) runs in a circle round the assembled pilgrims.
Deathbed rites: placing the dying before an image of Amitābha facing west, the five-coloured cord, recitation and attendants' guidance (Genshin, after Shandao and Daoxuan).
Style, a special arrangement of words (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī); for Vāmana the soul of poetry (KAS 1.2.6).
A separate class of gods fit for the office of Brahmā (Vāyu is among them); only they can reach that office.
The standpoint that attends only to the present mode (TS 1.33); taken absolutely it becomes the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness.
A mantra whose division into feet depends on the sense (MS 2.1.35).
The debts with which one is born — to the seers, gods and ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5), and to men (ŚB 1.7.2.1).
The three debts to be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
The three debts with which, according to scripture, a brāhmaṇa is born; urged as a bar to liberation and answered as figurative (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, hot and astringent, each from a pair of elements.

equivalents.note: rasa in its pharmacological sense

definitions.definition: Heaven and earth as a pair.

Lunar mansion rohiṇī: presiding deity Prajāpati (Brahmā) (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Moon (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class fixed (dhruva) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). The Moon's favourite wife in the Purāṇas.
The red (rising) sun praised as a creative supreme power in Atharvaveda book 13.
Display or play: appearances arising as the ground's self-display, like reflections in a crystal.
Equalizing the taste: the Drukpa practice of meeting adverse circumstances as one taste with the mind's nature (the six cycles of equal taste).
In the Karṇatantravajrapada 'blending and equal taste' are applied to the three pledges; in the bka' dpe phyi ma the 'equal taste of the four elements' is needed for inner heat to progress.
Honorific for a Zen master authorised to teach.
The branch concerned with virility and fertility.

equivalents.note: the same branch of the eight

definitions.definition: A seer of the hymns; 'a ṛṣi is so called from seeing' (Nirukta 2.11); the seers had direct perception of dharma (1.20); Vāc makes whom she loves a ṛṣi (RV 10.125.5).
One who 'saw' the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon them in their austerity (Nirukta 2.11); they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 1.20).
The seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1; AA 2.2.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Seers whose impurities are destroyed, whose dualities are cut, who are self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Seer: the great seers do not know the Lord's origin, for he is their beginning (10.2); the seven great seers, sharing his being (mad-bhāva), were born of mind (10.6); all the seers proclaim him supreme (10.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: The seers have sung of the field and its knower in many ways (13.5).

definitions.definition: A woman seer of Ṛgveda verses (e.g. Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī), recorded in the Anukramaṇīs.
A yantra and hymn centred on 'hrīṃ' with the five supreme beings and twenty-four Jinas, worshipped for protection.

literal: what is fitting; the true course

definitions.definition: The true order that holds together the cosmos (the courses of sun, dawn, seasons and waters), the sacrifice and right conduct; guarded by Varuṇa and Mitra; born with satya from kindled tapas (RV 10.190.1); the twelve-spoked wheel of the year is 'the wheel of ṛta' (1.164.11).
The order of which food, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, calls itself the firstborn (TB 2.8.8.1).
What is right, the order: spoken alongside truth (TU 1.1, 1.9); the right side of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the knower is 'first-born of ṛta' (TU 3.10.6).

equivalents.note: The later tradition speaks of dharma where the Saṃhitās speak of ṛta and dharman (RV 1.164.50 calls the first sacrifices 'the first dharmas'); the scope differs (ṛta is also cosmic order).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan aṣ̌a/arta.

definitions.definition: the insight in nirvicārā samādhi that bears only truth (YS 1.48)

Quality grasped by sight alone; seven colours; in earth, water, fire.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga: being the same in success and failure (2.48); making pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same (2.38); the one who is the same in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality (2.15).
Evenness in success and failure, which is called yoga (BhG 2.48); equality toward friend and foe (6.9, 12.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sameness (sama, sāmya): being the same in success and failure (4.22); the mind established in sameness conquers creation here, because Brahman is flawless and the same (5.19); the yukta sees clod, stone and gold as the same (6.8) and has equal regard for friend and foe (6.9); Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'yoga as sāmya' (6.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Evenness: constant evenness of thought (sama-cittatva) amid the desired and the undesired (13.10); the one beyond the guṇas is the same in pain and pleasure, toward clod, stone and gold, in blame and praise, honour and dishonour (14.24-14.25); the Lord is seen abiding equally (samam) in all beings (13.28-13.29).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Evenness (samatā) is among the states that arise from the Lord (10.5); worshippers of the imperishable are even-minded (samabuddhi) everywhere (12.4); the dear devotee is the same in pain and pleasure (12.13), to enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, and holds blame and praise equal (12.18–19).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Sameness: the sāttvic agent is unchanged in success and failure (18.26); the one become Brahman is the same toward all beings (18.54).

Tilopa warns that guarding vows conceptually falls from the meaning of the pledge (Gaṅgāmā v22–23).

dam tshig, pledge: kept by practising the guru's instruction 'like the flow of a river'; broken by giving the instructions to unfit vessels.
The first Śaiva initiation, making one a samayin, entitled to worship and study under the post-initiatory observances (samaya).
The first initiation, making one a samayin, entitled to the rules (samaya) and to hear the scriptures.

The head of a sattra, who gives initiation (śaraṇ) and guides its disciples.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka a name of the mind, one leg of the tripod of life (Sū 1.46; Vi 8.119); the mind named after the quality that predominates (Sū 8.6); the pure (śuddha) mind as against the rājasa and tāmasa (Śā 4.36); of superior, middling or inferior strength (Vi 8.119).

The luminous, stainless guṇa that binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge (BhG 14.6); its sign is the light of knowledge in all the gates of the body (14.11); in the Mokṣadharma also the intellect as distinct from the knower of the field (12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).
The guṇa that is light and illuminating (SK 13), of the nature of pleasure (SK 12); predominant in the upper worlds (SK 54). Vācaspati also uses 'sattva' for buddhi.
The guṇa of illumination; in YS 3.35, 3.49, 3.55 the buddhi-sattva, whose purity equal to the puruṣa's is kaivalya, and whose difference from the puruṣa is discerned in viveka-khyāti.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: sattva, being stainless, is illuminating and free of affliction; it binds by attachment to happiness and to knowledge (14.6), attaches to happiness (14.9); when illumination-knowledge arises at all the gates of the body it has increased (14.11); dying in it one reaches the stainless worlds of the knowers of the highest (14.14); knowledge arises from it (14.17); those abiding in it go upward (14.18). In 13.27 'sattva' means simply 'a being'.
The guṇa characterized as knowledge; those in it go to the gods' state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: 'I am the sattva of those who have it' (10.36) — goodness or strength; in 10.41 sattva means simply 'a being'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In nityasattvastha, 'ever abiding in sattva' (2.45), one of the qualities of being free of the three guṇas.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: In chs. 16–18: (1) the guṇa by which faith, food, sacrifice, austerity, giving, relinquishment, knowledge, action, agent, understanding, steadiness and happiness are called sāttvic (17–18); the relinquisher is 'pervaded by sattva' (18.10); (2) one's being or inner nature, with which faith accords (17.3), and whose purity (sattva-saṃśuddhi) is a divine mark (16.1); (3) a being, none of which is free of the guṇas (18.40).

equivalents.note: in Caraka's usage sattva, cetas and manas name the mind

notes: Taken as the guṇa sattva or as 'being, the real'; the commentators divide.

literal: discernment of the difference of sattva and puruṣa

definitions.definition: the subtle insight that, once its office is done, is fit for reabsorption (YBh 2.2)

first of the five results of steady purity (YS 2.41)

definitions.definition: Time (kāla), the insentient reality lacking the guṇas, which measures change in the realm of prakṛti.
Neither increases nor decreases; identical with the tathāgatagarbha and the dharmakāya; the element when impure is called a being.
Fourth stage: the mind, from practice of the first three, rests in pure sattva (the state of the Self).
Fourth stage: resting in the Self; the knower of Brahman.
The third kind of therapy: restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects (Ca Sū 11.54); its means are knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Sū 1.58).
The eight involuntary bodily signs of ecstasy: stupor, sweating, horripilation, faltering voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting.
The eight involuntary states arising from sattva (concentrated mind): paralysis, sweat, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting (NŚ 6.22).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Sāttvic relinquishment: doing allotted action simply because it is to be done, giving up attachment and fruit (18.9).
Before every act, relinquishing the sense of being its agent, the sense that it is one's own and desire for its fruit, attributing all to the Lord.

literal: relinquishment in the mode of goodness

definitions.definition: Name for the Pāñcarātra's followers and teaching (the 'Sātvata teaching'); in Manu 10.23 a Sātvata appears among the offspring of degraded twice-born, which opponents used against the Bhāgavatas.

equivalents.note: used together in the Āgamaprāmāṇya

definitions.definition: The ancient great dharma given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and upheld by the Sātvatas (MBh 12.336.27–51).

Truth, the real and the truthful word; upholds the earth (RV 10.85.1; AVŚ 12.1.1); the vow-taker passes 'from untruth to truth' (VS 1.5); Varuṇa's fetters bind the untruthful and release the truth-speaker (AVŚ 4.16.6).
Truth as the nature of the gods, untruth of men; the vow 'I pass from untruth to truth' (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5); truth as the sacrificer (AB 7.10).
One of the common duties; speak truth that is pleasant (MDh 4.138; 10.63).
Speech and mind according to fact, spoken for the good of all beings; truth that harms is a semblance of merit (YBh 2.30); when established, actions and fruits rest on one's word (2.36).

The real, truth: 'the real behind the real' is the hidden name of the self (BAU 2.1.20, 2.3.6); analysed as sa-ti-yam (BAU 5.5.1; ChU 8.3.5); truth-speaking as a virtue (TU 1.11; MuU 3.1.6) and as protection in the axe ordeal (ChU 6.16).
Truth, root of all and higher than any state (Rāmāyaṇa 2.109.13); established in dharma (2.21.40); the highest vow (MBh 3.203.41); part of verbal austerity (BhG 17.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Truthfulness, among the states of beings that arise from the Lord (10.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Truth: a mark of the divine endowment (16.2), not found in the demonic (16.7); true speech is part of the austerity of speech (17.15). The demonic say the world is 'without truth' (asatya, 16.8).
In Jainism abstention from saying what is not good (asat) — false, harsh or harmful (TS 7.14); also a tenfold virtue (9.6).

equivalents.note: Paired in RV 10.190.1 and AVŚ 12.1.1; satya stresses the real and the spoken truth, ṛta the order.

definitions.definition: The understanding 'this is not I, this is not mine' (Ca Śā 1.153), arising in one who sees the world in himself and himself in the world (Śā 5.7).
The 'true religion': the Kartābhajā self-designation for the sahaja teaching revealed by Āulcānd.
actions and fruits rest on him (YS 2.36)

definitions.definition: The True Being, supreme Lord of Satlok, from whom the sixteen sons emanated; Kabīr is his incarnation or messenger.
Sat Purush, the Lord of Sach Khand / Sat Lok, the first manifestation of the Supreme in the purely spiritual region.
The conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate, on which the Buddhas' teaching relies (MMK 24.8–10).
Every thing bears two natures, found by correct and by false seeing (MA 6.23); the intellect is conventional and reality is beyond its domain (BCA 9.2).
The view that cognition's images are real as cognition (rnam bden pa).
The highest world within the egg, Brahmā's world, lasting two parārdhas; the yogin who reaches it passes with Brahmā to liberation.

notes: Also: brahmaloka

literal: brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite

definitions.definition: The characterization of brahman in the verse of Taittirīya 2.1.1.

definitions.definition: Auspicious good fortune and conjugal felicity, the worldly and spiritual blessing the Goddess grants; hence 'Saubhāgya-vidyā' and titles such as Saubhāgyabhāskara.

Outer purity (earth, water, pure food) and inner washing away of the mind's stains (YBh 2.32); yields disgust for one's body and non-contact with others, and purity of sattva up to fitness for seeing the self (2.40–41).
Purity of body, mind and dealings; purity in wealth is the highest; the body is purified by water, the mind by truth (MDh 5.105–109).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Purity: the dear devotee is pure (śuci) (12.16).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Purity, among the items called knowledge (13.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Purity: a mark of the divine endowment (16.3), absent in the demonic (16.7), part of bodily austerity (17.14) and of the brāhmaṇa's work (18.42).
In Jainism the fourth virtue: purity from greed (TS 9.6).

The Lord's easy reach, shown above all in his descents and in the temple image.
second result (YS 2.41)

definitions.definition: The nibbāna-element of the arahant who still has the five faculties and experiences the agreeable and disagreeable (Iti 44).
The Lord's mixing freely with the lowly without regard to his greatness.
One who takes the sūtras, not the treatises, as authority (Yaśomitra).
Śiva without Śakti: 'with Śakti he is Śiva, without Śakti a corpse' (Toḍala 1.25); hence Kālī stands on him.
A vīra rite performed seated on a corpse in the cremation ground to win the Goddess's vision (as in the account of Sarvānanda). Restricted: named only.
Practice seated on a corpse in the cremation ground, attributed to Aghora and Śākta adepts; restricted — summary only.
Disciple (as used in Dhp 59, 195).

definitions.definition: Coalescence with subtle objects delimited by place, time and cause (1.44, YBh 1.44).
Absorption in which the mental mode rests in Brahman while the distinction of knower, knowing and known remains.
Perception with a qualifier, e.g. 'this is Ḍittha, a brāhmaṇa, dark' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The perception that follows the bare awareness and grasps the thing with its universal and other properties; also perception.
Coalescence mixed with the constructions of word, object and cognition (1.42).
The god who impels, to whom the Gāyatrī is addressed (RV 3.62.10) and who first yoked the mind (VS 11.1).
The Gāyatrī verse to Savitṛ (RV 3.62.10) taught at initiation, the 'mother' of the twice-born's Vedic birth (MDh 2.170), recited at the twilights.
A reason that strays from the probandum; common, uncommon, non-conclusive.
Reckoning longitudes from the moving equinox (tropical), used for the seasons and the sun's courses.
The thirteenth guṇasthāna: the living omniscient, teaching and moving until the end of life.
Form of liberation in which the liberated enter the Lord's body and come out again, enjoying with him — without identity.
Liberation as union/oneness (ekatva) with the Lord; reached even by Śiśupāla through enmity (VP 4.15.2).
Union with the Goddess, granted to one who merely says 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22); the highest of the five liberations in Lakṣmīdhara.
Direct conjunction with Rudra, attained by the ascetic dwelling in the cremation ground.
Union with the Lord — the highest of the four kinds of liberation; Śiva-sāyujya by the tripuṇḍra.
Inseparable union with Śiva; fruit of jñāna; the only final release.
Union with the Lord, the only one of the four liberations that does not perish.

notes: Also: ekatva

definitions.definition: A noble disciple in training (stream-enterer to one on the path of arahantship), who should not conceive (MN 1).
A noble person still in training (the first seven noble persons).
Hakuin's kōan 'the sound of one hand'.
The black woollen cord worn by Nāth yogīs, carrying the nād horn; it takes the place of the brahmin's sacred thread.

Ordinary mind: the dualistic, conceptual consciousness that grasps subject and object and arises from not recognizing the ground; to be distinguished from awareness (rig pa). In the Kunjed Gyalpo, however, 'sems' in byang chub sems names the all-creating nature itself.
The moving mind distinguished from the nature of mind (sems nyid) in Bön Dzogchen.

The mind series: the first of the three series of Dzogchen, teaching that all appearances are the display of mind-nature (bodhicitta); root texts the Kunjed Gyalpo and the eighteen mind-series scriptures.
'Holding the mind': a set of Heart-essence exercises (traditionally twenty-one) using postures, sounds, breath and visualization to bring about experiences in which awareness can be recognized.

notes: The number twenty-one and the attribution to the Tegchok Dzöd are from memory.

definitions.definition: Mind itself, the nature of mind, as opposed to the moving, dualistic mind (sems): unborn, empty and luminous; 'the basis of phenomena' (Nāropa); 'mind itself unborn and empty is dharmakāya' (Karṇatantravajrapada).

cross_language.note: Sanskrit forms occur in the dohās; usage differs

definitions.definition: Selection: Dharmākara selected the nenbutsu in the primal vow; Śākyamuni and all buddhas selected it in the sūtras; so the practitioner selects it (Senchakushū).

notes: Read senjaku in Jōdo-shū, senchaku in Shinshū.

definitions.definition: Exclusive nenbutsu: calling the name alone as the practice for birth; the name of Hōnen's movement.
That which exists for the sake of another (MS 3.1.2); for Bādari only substances, qualities and purificatory acts, for Jaimini also acts (MS 3.1.3–4). Its correlate is the principal (śeṣin).
That whose nature is to exist for the purpose of another (the śeṣin) and to enhance him; every soul and thing is śeṣa of the Lord.
The soul's essential nature as belonging to and existing for the Lord; its fulfilment is service (kainkarya).
Inference by exclusion (= avīta) (Vācaspati on SK 5).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
That for whose sake a subsidiary exists.
Periods of intensive sitting, usually of seven days, in Japanese monasteries (e.g. rōhatsu sesshin in early December commemorating the Buddha's awakening).
Service of the wise, the third way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34); the Lord is served with unswerving devotion (14.26).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.34: service, with prostration and questioning, by which knowledge is learned from the knowers of truth. 6.20 uses 'yoga-sevā' for the practice of yoga.
Loving service of the Lord's form: with body (tanujā), wealth (vittajā) and mind (mānasī); the mind flowing to him is sevā itself.
Service in the practitioner's body and in the inner perfected body.
Voluntary service of the Master and the community (physical, financial, mental), a support of meditation.
Sādhu-sevā: feeding and serving the sādhus at melās and ākhṛās.

'Service' or 'approach': the first of the four branches of practice; in GST ch. 18 the ordinary service is the fourfold vajra (emptiness, seed, image, syllables) and the supreme service the six-branch yoga.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

definitions.definition: A body fit for the Lord's service, one of the three fruits of service.

Blending: mixing one practice or state with another — day and night, dream and illusory body, clear light at sleep and at death; 'the five blendings' carried onto the path in the bardo (Karṇatantravajrapada).
The teacher who shows the way to see the nature, needed by those who cannot awaken themselves; Huineng also addresses his audience as 'good friends'.
Liberation upon arising: a thought is freed in the very moment it arises, like a drawing on water.

term: sharen dao, huoren jian (the sword that kills, the sword that gives life)

definitions.definition: The teacher's twofold function of cutting off delusion and restoring life (Yuanwu's pointer).
Priest or practitioner of Bön; also names the ways (theg pa) of the nine (phywa gshen, snang gshen...) and Tönpa Shenrab's clan.
The gate of the holy path: attaining awakening in this world by one's own practice; hard to realise in the last age (Daochuo).
Shōdōmon: to be set aside in favour of the Pure Land gate (Senchakushū 1).

term: shengsi shida (birth and death is the great matter)

definitions.definition: The urgency that motivates practice (Hongren; Yongjia).
For Gorampa, Dolpopa's other-emptiness is the 'eternalist' Madhyamaka; Shākya Chokden accepted an other-empty reading of the Maitreya texts as the view for meditative experience.
Rejected by the Gelug as positing a truly existent ultimate.

In one Karma Kagyu strand (the 8th Situ, Jamgön Kongtrul reading the 3rd Karmapa), the ultimate — buddha-nature — is empty of what is other than it (adventitious stains) but not of its own qualities; contested by others in the school (the 8th Karmapa).

notes: U48 owns the Jonang definition; the id follows the registry's dsp:rangtong-shentong spelling.

definitions.definition: The deep mind, true entrusting, of two kinds: in oneself as an ordinary being without escape, and in Amitābha's vow (Shandao).
Embraced and never abandoned: the Buddha's light embraces beings who recollect him (Contemplation Sūtra 9).
Sesshu fusha: the benefit received at the moment shinjin arises (Tannishō 1).
Sitting wholeheartedly without seeking a further goal or object; taught by Rujing to Dōgen ('only just sit') and by Dōgen as practice-realization.

The 'ten recitations' of the eighteenth vow and of the lowest grade: ten continuous thoughts of recollection without other thoughts, not needing to be counted (Tanluan, Daochuo); ten voicings of the name (Shandao); ten breaths of continuous recitation each morning (Zunshi).

cross_language.note: Sanskrit vow 19: 'ten turnings of the arising of thought'

definitions.definition: True entrusting: the mind free of doubt about the primal vow, given (transferred) by Amida; the true cause of birth, buddha-nature itself, arising in one thought-moment and settling birth.

cross_language.note: in Chinese texts ordinary 'faith'; in Shinran a technical term

equivalents.note: Shinshū insists shinjin is not the practitioner's faith but the Buddha's mind given; general Buddhist śraddhā is a faculty of the practitioner

term: shinjin datsuraku (body and mind dropping off)

definitions.definition: Dōgen's account of Rujing's teaching and of his own awakening; in Genjōkōan, the dropping off of the body and mind of oneself and others when verified by the myriad dharmas.

notes: Rujing's own record has 心塵脫落 (the dust of mind drops off), homophonous in Japanese (tea:rujing-yulu:130c19).

definitions.definition: The dharma-transmission document listing the lineage, discussed in Dōgen's Shisho.
The youthful vase body: the ground's luminosity enclosed within, like a lamp in a vase, not yet radiating outward; when the 'seal' of the vase breaks, the ground-appearances arise.
Deviations from emptiness: from its essence, into sealing, into the antidote, and into the path.
Guarding the original true mind, the root of nirvāṇa (Hongren).
Daoxin's practice of guarding the one without moving (Lengqie shizi ji).
Past karma, by whose conditions one may do what one would not intend (Tannishō 13).

term: shushō ittō (oneness of practice and realization)

definitions.definition: Practice is practice-in-realization, so even a beginner's practice is the whole of original realization (Bendōwa).
A perfected one — master of yoga who has conquered time and roams the cosmos (HYP 1.9); the Nāths count nine Nāths and eighty-four siddhas.
A perfected one: in Tamil, cittar — the yogin-poets, physicians and alchemists who have attained the powers (citti) and the deathless state, and who stand outside caste and temple ritual.
The perfected masters of haṭha — Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the others — who by haṭha broke the staff of time (HYP 1.5–9).
One who has attained siddhi; the tantric adept of the lives and songs, often living in a lay trade or as a wandering yogin.
In Jainism a soul freed of all eight karmas, bodiless, abiding at the summit of the universe in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy (TS 10.4–5).
In the Dāsbodh: The accomplished one who abides in the Self, free of doubt, still acting rightly.
The perfected stage, resting in prema and the sahaja state.

cross_language.note: the Tamil Siddhars; overlapping but distinct lineage

definitions.definition: Arises from particular merits (VS 9.28 C).
The perfected body of the Nāth siddha — deathless, unageing, not cut by weapons — as distinct from the Gauḍīya inner devotional body of the same name.
The inner, perfected spiritual body/identity in which the practitioner serves in Vraja, alongside service in the practitioner's body (sādhaka-rūpa).

The transmission by the guru of the disciple's spiritual identity (name, form, age, dress, service, group, residence and the like) for meditation on the divine play; practised in the Nityānanda and Advaita lineages and among Vraja bābājīs, contested in the 20th c.
The Śvetāmbara yantra of the nine padas (navapada), worshipped especially during the twice-yearly Olī.
A settled position; four kinds: common to all systems, peculiar to one, implied, and provisionally accepted (NS 1.1.26–31).
The final answer of an adhikaraṇa, reached after the prima facie view.
The computational branch: treatises giving time-units, the yugas and kalpa, planetary revolutions, true positions, eclipses and the sphere; also called gaṇita or tantra (BS 1.9; SS).
The scriptures of the upper stream — the 28 Śiva- and Rudra-tantras and their upāgamas.
Each of the four Pāñcarātra divisions (Mantra-, Āgama-, Tantra-, Tantrāntara-siddhānta), so called because those settled in Mīmāṃsā and other śāstras become eligible for it.
The sixth mode, above the Vāma (Kulārṇava 2.8).
The crescent-shaped region (īṣatprāgbhārā) at the summit of the universe, above which the liberated souls abide.
A mantra that needs no preliminary tests; said of the Mahāvidyās by the Muṇḍamālā, a statement Kṛṣṇānanda reads as praise (Tantrasāra).

A power. Powers arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1) and, as the text lists them, from saṃyama on various objects (3.16 onward); for a mind in samādhi they are obstacles (upasarga), for the outgoing mind they are powers (3.37).
Yogic power: eighteen are listed (eight chief, ten from the guṇas) plus lesser ones; they are obstacles and a waste of time for one seeking the Lord.

In the Sāṃkhya Kārikā, the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge: reasoning, words (hearing), study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving (SK 51) — not supernormal powers, which Sāṃkhya calls aiśvarya (SK 23).
Powers arising from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1); those from samādhi are obstacles in samādhi but powers in emergence (3.37).
Success in yoga, and the powers that arise (distant hearing and seeing, speed, invisibility, turning metal to gold, flight — DYŚ 89–90) which the yogin must regard as obstacles and hide (DYŚ 91–94).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Success, as against failure, to which one is to be equal (2.48); perfection, not reached by renunciation alone (3.4) but reached by Janaka and others through action (saṃsiddhi, 3.20).
Powers arising from dhāraṇā - eighteen in the Bhāgavata, eight aiśvaryas in MkP and LiP - which are obstacles to the highest goal.

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: Among thousands hardly one strives for perfection, and of the striving/perfected hardly one knows the Lord in truth (7.3); the great-souled reach the highest perfection (saṃsiddhi) and are not reborn (8.15).
The fifth gain; also the marks of perfection of the yogin (not subject to others, invulnerable, unaging, unobstructed etc.).
Attainment: the common (mundane) attainments — powers such as flight, the sword, the elixir, invisibility, the eight great siddhis — and the supreme attainment, mahāmudrā / buddhahood.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The success of actions sought by those who sacrifice to deities, which comes quickly in the human world (4.12); the unbound one is the same in success and failure (4.22).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Perfection, accomplishment of the goal, attained even by doing actions for the Lord's sake (12.10).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Perfection, attainment: the highest perfection (parā siddhi) to which the sages went by the highest knowledge (14.1) — here the goal, not a yogic power.
