Name of the Lord in the closing prayer 'may Śiva be mine, always Śiva'.
The deity of the Kālāmukha temples (e.g. Kedāreśvara at Balligāve).
Pati, the one Lord, eternally free; the efficient cause; not the material of the world; the guru of all.
In the Śaiva and yoga Upaniṣads the supreme Lord and the jīva's true nature: 'the jīva in the body is Śiva alone'; the jīva freed of the twenty faults is called Śiva.

First tattva: pure consciousness (cit), the 'I'.

Regarding all Śiva's devotees as equal irrespective of birth.
The SSM's name for its own doctrine: the śāstra devoted to Śiva's non-duality agreeing with Veda and Vedānta (3.83–87), taught by gurus devoted to Śiva-non-duality (13.24–27).
Qualified non-dualism of Śiva: Śiva with cit-śakti is one, with souls and world as his body.
Civañāṉam: knowledge of Śiva given by grace through the guru — hearing, reflection, clarity, abiding — the true path (san-mārga), leading to sāyujya.

Direct experience of Śiva; the SSM's author is named Śivayogi from his experience of Śiva in the supreme sky of consciousness-bliss (1.13–24).
The night of Śiva's worship (esp. the great one in Māgha/Phālguna), kept with fast and vigil.

The five aggregates, which Avalokiteśvara saw empty of own-being.
In Jain usage a molecule or compound of atoms, formed by union and division; visible bodies are aggregates (TS 5.25–28).

The five aggregates; the self is neither identical with them nor other than them (MMK 18.1), and the Tathāgata is not found among them in five ways (22.1); grasping at them is grasping at 'I' (RĀ 1.35).

Remembrance: the forgetting of the Lord is supreme anguish (NBS 19); remembrance is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).
Hari-smaraṇa: the Gīta Govinda is offered to those whose minds delight in remembering Hari (GG 1.3).
Remembrance of the Name, inward and constant, with the breath; repetition on beads without the mind is not sumiran.
Simran: mental repetition of the names given at initiation, to gather the attention at the eye centre.

Utpaladeva calls consciousness 'sphurattā', the great being, the Heart of the Supreme (ĪPK 1.5.14).

definitions.definition: Deliberately shaking the limbs as if struck by a wind-disorder.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: External contacts (bāhya-sparśa) to which the self is unattached (5.21) and which are put outside in meditation (5.27); enjoyments born of contact are wombs of sorrow (5.22).
Quality grasped by the skin alone; cold, hot, neither; in earth, water, fire, air.

The grammarians' unitary word-entity distinct from the letters; rejected by Kumārila as superfluous, the letters themselves conveying meaning (ŚV sphoṭavāda); Upavarṣa already identified the word with the letters.

The meaning-bearing word itself, partless and without sequence, distinct from the sounds (dhvani/nāda) that manifest it; it 'bursts forth' as meaning in the intellect when the sounds have planted their seeds (VP 1.44; Mahābhāṣya on P 1.1.70). The later grammarians count eight kinds and hold the sentence-sphoṭa alone real.

definitions.definition: A spontaneous vivid manifestation of the Lord or his play in the devotee's heart, short of full direct vision.
Faith and trust that the offering reaches its end: by faith the fire is kindled and the oblation offered (RV 10.151); 'have faith in him — he is Indra' (2.12.5).
The first of the five means (1.20): serenity of mind which, like a kind mother, protects the yogin (YBh 1.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: Whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that faith unwavering, and through it the devotee obtains desires ordained by the Lord (7.21–22); those without faith in this dharma return to saṃsāra (9.3); devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, not by the rule (9.23).
Faith as the sacrificer's wife, paired with truth (AB 7.10); the Agnihotra of 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4).
The trust by which one may receive good knowledge even from a lower person (MDh 2.238).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who constantly follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping are freed from actions (3.31).

Faith, threefold by the guṇas and according to one's inner being — 'a person is made of faith' (BhG 17.2–3); the one with faith gains knowledge (4.39); what is done without faith is 'asat' (17.28); the Lord makes each devotee's faith steady (7.21).
The rite of offering food and water to the dead and the ancestors (ekoddiṣṭa for one preta, pārvaṇa for the three ancestors), with feeding of brahmins.
Without faith the roots are weak (Gaṇḍavyūha 55); faith in the buddha-element surpasses all other merit (RGV 5); faith in the vow brings birth in Sukhāvatī.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The one with faith, intent on it, with senses restrained, gains knowledge (4.39); the faithless perishes (4.40); Arjuna asks the fate of one endowed with faith who falls from yoga (6.37); the one who worships the Lord with faith is the most yoked (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Faith: the faith of embodied beings is threefold, born of their nature (17.2); each one's faith accords with his sattva, and a person is made of faith — as his faith, so is he (17.3); sacrifice without faith is tāmasic (17.13); austerity with supreme faith is sāttvic (17.17); whatever is offered, given or done without faith is 'asat', of no account here or hereafter (17.28); hearing the Gītā with faith and without cavil brings the worlds of the meritorious (18.71).
Faith: offered by the gods into the fire of yonder world (ChU 5.4; BAU 6.2.9); 'have faith' (ChU 6.12.2); head of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); 'give with faith' (TU 1.11).
Faith: firm trust in the words of scripture and teacher, by which the truth is grasped.
Faith — firm trust that by devotion to Kṛṣṇa all is accomplished; the first stage.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Faith: those who worship the Lord endowed with supreme faith are the most yoked (12.2); those who with faith attend to this nectar of dharma are exceedingly dear to him (12.20).
Faith (xin): 'if one plants good roots but doubts, the lotus does not open; with pure faith it opens'; faith is the source of the way (Wang Rixiu); the first of Ouyi's three provisions.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the bhakta stage. In the SSM's inner worship faith is the incense (12.13–20).
Faith goes first and wisdom is chief (RĀ 1.5); the root to be made firm before setting the mind on awakening (ŚSK 2).

definitions.definition: (As reported) If the śrāddha fed the dead, oil on a quenched lamp would feed its flame; the rites for the dead are a brāhmaṇa livelihood.

definitions.definition: A homeless ascetic outside the Vedic sacrificial order; the rival teachers of DN 2 and the Buddha and Mahāvīra are all śramaṇas; Aśoka pairs 'brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas' as the two orders found everywhere.
A samaṇa is one who has calmed (samita) evils, lives in calm (samacariyā) and harms no one.
One is a samaṇa not by shaving the head but by equanimity (samayā).
In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, a name of the wind-girdled seers who practised austerity and celibacy (TA 2.7.1).

cross_language.note: In Pali and Jain usage the non-Vedic ascetics

definitions.definition: The solemn Vedic sacrifices performed with three fires and priests of the four Vedas.
The Jain householder who hears the teaching and keeps the small vows (TS 7.19–20).
Study of the true scriptures and their correct interpretation from a teacher; the first principal means to knowledge, never to be reduced.
Hearing the Lord's names, qualities and deeds, the first form of devotion and the beginning of the path (BhP 1.2.16-21); for the Śiva Purāṇa the first of the three great means.
Hearing: ascertaining, under a teacher and by the six marks of purport, that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman; for the Vivaraṇa the principal means.
Hearing the Lord's qualities and stories: with singing, a means to devotion even in worldly life (NBS 37); Garga's definition of devotion is attachment to hearing his stories (NBS 17).

notes: Bhakti hearing (of the Lord's names, qualities and deeds), distinct from the Vedāntic śravaṇa of the Upaniṣads recorded by U13/U15.

definitions.definition: Lunar mansion śravaṇa: presiding deity Viṣṇu (VJ r.25–27; BS 97.4–5; MC 2.1); Viṃśottarī period-lord the Moon (BPHS 46.12); muhūrta class movable (cara) (MC 2.2–8; BS 97.6–9). Vedic Śroṇā (moderate confidence).

definitions.definition: A Jain laywoman, fourth member of the fourfold community; the Kalpa Sūtra counts 318,000 in Mahāvīra's time, headed by Sulasā and Revatī.

The good, the better: chosen by the wise over the pleasant (KU 1.2.1-2).

The yantra of Tripurā; the body contemplated as it.
The 'family of Śrī': the Śākta division centred on Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā), contrasted with the Kālīkula.
The Śrīcakra built in raised, three-dimensional form (meru-prastāra), as distinct from the flat form (bhū-prastāra).
Lalitā's city on the central peak of Meru (LSN 22), with its enclosures described in the Lalitopākhyāna and the Āryādviśatī.
Lalitā's city (Śrīnagara) with its enclosures and the Cintāmaṇi palace at the centre.

notes: Also: Śrīnagara

definitions.definition: A member of the community of Rāmānuja's tradition, worshipping Nārāyaṇa with Śrī.

The name of the supreme as never apart from Śrī (Lakṣmī); the Lord is known and approached as her consort.
Making signs of desire toward a young woman from a distance so as to be thought unchaste; the act is feigned and must not violate the restraints.
Stream-enterer: one in the first fruit from the sixteenth moment; 'seven times at most'; for the Sarvāstivāda cannot fall back from the fruit.

Happiness: so called because it makes easy and gulps down or digs out bodily and mental affliction; mark gratification, function enhancing the associated states, manifestation aiding; distinguished from rapture as the gladness at getting a desirable object versus the experiencing of what is got (Vism IV p. 145).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); for one without peace there is no happiness (2.66).
What all experience as agreeable; a quality of the self; bound up with pain and so to be relinquished like food mixed with poison (NBh 1.1.2).
The bliss of the first three jhānas (DN 2); the pleasure the bodhisatta saw no reason to fear (MN 36); nibbāna is the highest happiness (Dhp 203–204).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Happiness, threefold: sāttvic happiness, in which one delights through practice and reaches the end of suffering, is like poison at first and nectar in the end, born of the clarity of ātma-buddhi (one's own understanding, or the understanding of the self); rājasic happiness, from contact of senses and objects, is like nectar at first and poison in the end; tāmasic happiness deludes one's self first and last and arises from sleep, sloth and heedlessness (18.36–39). One who abandons scriptural injunction does not attain it (16.23).

Bhagavad Gītā 5–6: the happiness in the self, found by one unattached to external contacts, imperishable (5.21); enjoyments born of contact are sources of suffering (5.22); happiness, delight and light within (5.24); boundless happiness grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses (6.21); the highest happiness and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Pleasure, paired with pain among the states from the Lord (10.4); the dear devotee is the same in both (12.13, 12.18).
Pleasant feeling; a jhāna factor, distinguished from rapture as the enjoyment is from the thirst for water.

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Happiness, pleasure: listed among the contents of the field (13.7); puruṣa is the cause in experiencing pleasure and pain (13.21); sattva binds by attachment to happiness (14.6, 14.9); the Lord is the foundation of absolute happiness (14.27).

definitions.definition: What a thing would have by itself: unfabricated (akṛtrima) and not dependent on anything else (MMK 15.1–2). Since whatever is produced by causes and conditions would be 'made', nothing has own-nature; the Ābhidharmikas' own-nature of dharmas is the chief target of the critique.
Nothing has own-nature even conventionally; conventional things are accepted only as the world accepts them, without analysis.
One's inherent nature: it is svabhāva that acts (BhG 5.14); the varṇa duties arise from it (18.41); for Prahlāda all states arise and cease by svabhāva (MBh 12.215.15).
What dharmas are empty of: the Heart says the aggregates are empty of own-being.

In Madhyamaka analysis, inherent existence (rang bzhin gyis grub pa) — existence from the object's own side — is the object of negation; 'svabhāva' in the sense of the final nature of things (emptiness) is accepted.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Own nature: the threefold faith of embodied beings is born of it (17.2); the actions of the four varṇas are distributed by the guṇas arising from it, and each varṇa's work is 'born of nature' (18.41–44); doing the action ordained by one's own nature one incurs no fault (18.47); bound by nature-born action, Arjuna will do even unwillingly what he refuses out of delusion (18.60).

definitions.definition: Validity of knowledge belongs to it by itself (and is apprehended by the witness); invalidity comes from extraneous defects.

A principle or level of reality in the ascending scale of 36 from earth to Śiva; the lower 31 (or so) are products of māyā, the pure five of bindu.
Tattuvam: 36 tattvas (24 ātma, 7 vidyā, 5 śiva), elaborated to 96 in the Tamil lists.

definitions.definition: The fifth concentration: seeing oneself as the pure, omniscient self, like a Siddha (YŚ 7).

The repeated contemplation of the principles from which the liberating knowledge arises (SK 64); described by Vācaspati as long, reverent, uninterrupted meditative cultivation after hearing and reasoning, and by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The knowers who see the truth and will teach knowledge to one who approaches with prostration, questioning and service (4.34).

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the true nature of the categories — in the science of the self, of the self and the rest (NBh 1.1.1); it removes false knowledge (NS 1.1.2, 4.2.35) and arises from the practice of samādhi (NS 4.2.38).
Knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the categories, arising from dharma (Praśastapāda).
Bhagavad Gītā 13.12: keeping in view the aim (artha) of the knowledge of reality is the last of the dispositions called knowledge.
Knowledge of reality, which Abhinavagupta makes the stable emotion of śānta: it is the self itself (Abhinavabhāratī).

definitions.definition: The presence of the memory of truth from which all the means of liberation proceed; 'the one path shown by the liberated' (Ca Śā 1.146-150).
The three real categories: cit (souls), acit (insentient matter) and Īśvara (the Lord).
The three realities: cit, acit and Īśvara, established by scripture (Daśaślokī 7).
The adherents' own name for Madhva's system: the doctrine that what is known through valid means is real (tattva = not superimposed), above all the reality of difference.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower of the truth about the division of guṇas and actions, who is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the yoked knower of reality (tattvavit) thinks 'I do nothing at all' (5.8).

definitions.definition: Jayarāśi's thesis that no principle can be established, since no means of knowledge can be defined.
Austerity: bearing pain and not harming others (Kuṟaḷ ch. 27).
The Buddha as proclaiming the path he himself has seen, the four truths.
In the Isibhāsiyāiṃ's chapter of Maṅkhaliputta, the steadfast one who is not moved and does not turn into this or that state, and so saves himself and others from saṃsāra.
Epithet in GK 4.99 of the awakened one whose knowledge does not go out to objects; Śaṅkara explains it as 'pervasive like space' or 'protector'.
A master's formal presentation of a text or kōan.
Substance with hot touch and colour; bodies of fire in Āditya's world; includes gold (mineral fire).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Splendour: the Lord is the splendour of the splendid (10.36); whatever is glorious arises from a portion of his tejas (10.41); the universal form is a mass of tejas (11.17), made of tejas (11.47), heating the universe with its tejas (11.19, 11.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Radiance: the radiance in the sun, the moon and fire is the Lord's (15.12).

Heat, radiance: the first emanation of being, which produced water (ChU 6.2.3); its finest part is speech (6.5.4); in dying breath goes into heat (6.8.6); in deep sleep the mind is overcome by tejas (PrU 4.6).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Vigour, a mark of the divine endowment (16.3) and of the kṣatriya's nature (18.43).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) the fire element, the person's heat (Ca Śā 5.5); (2) 'essence' — ojas is the supreme tejas of the tissues (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); (3) listed with ojas, the fires and the prāṇas among what depends on the body's fire (Ca Ci 15.3).

A supernormal fiery power (labdhi) of ascetics; Mahāvīra's cool power (śītaleśyā) counters it.
The nine vehicles: śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva; kriyā, ubhaya (caryā), yoga; mahāyoga, anuyoga, atiyoga.
The nine ways of Bön: four causal and five fruitional ways.
Interdependent, auspicious connection; the Drukpa 'seven auspicious connections' of Tsangpa Gyare.

definitions.definition: The Śvetāmbara order founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu (1760); the name is explained as 'the path of thirteen' (after the first thirteen monks or laymen) or as 'your path, O Lord' (terā = 'yours').
Also the name of an unconnected 17th-c. Digambara reform (against the bhaṭṭārakas and fresh offerings), contrasted with the Bīsapantha.

Treasure: teachings, objects or substances concealed (chiefly by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal) in the earth, rocks, water, sky or the minds of disciples, to be revealed at the destined time by a treasure revealer — the 'short lineage'.
Bön treasures concealed during the persecutions and recovered from the 10th-11th c. (Shenchen Luga).
Treasure protector: the guardian spirit or deity entrusted with a treasure until its revealer comes.
Treasure revealer: a person prophesied and empowered in a former life (usually as a disciple of Padmasambhava) to reveal treasures; the 'five kings' and many others.

Recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents, attained on the night of awakening (MN 4; MN 36) — the Buddhist re-definition of the brahmin's 'three Vedas' (DN 13; AN 3.58).
'Ordinary knowing' that awakens in the centre of the heart (Koṭali's song, Tōh 2292 no. 44); a key Kagyu term for the nature of mind.

definitions.definition: The path of method: the tantric yogas of the six dharmas (inner heat and the rest, in some usages specifically the consort practice), paired with the path of liberation (Mahāmudrā).

equivalents.note: ordinary mind is the co-emergent mind recognized; 'ordinary' stresses its unfabricated, everyday presence

Impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha) and not-self (anattā): 'all formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self' (AN 3.136; Dhp 277–279); the term tilakkhaṇa itself is commentarial.
The first of Lakṣmī's five acts, the concealing power by which souls are bound.
Śiva's concealing power (rodha-śakti), called a bond by figure because it impels the bonds until the soul is ripe.
Tirōtāyi / tirōtam: fifth of the five malas; 'na' of the five letters.
Concealment, the fourth cosmic act, done as Īśvarī (LSN 64).
A holy place of pilgrimage and bathing; the virtues are inner tīrthas and the purest mind the supreme tīrtha; devotees are living tīrthas.

Pilgrim place; the Sants deny that bathing at tīrthas purifies — the true Gaṅgā is in a pure mind.
The pilgrimage is within: 'the original Mecca is in this human body'.
In TS 9.47 and 10.9, a head under which ascetics and the liberated are set out; the commentators read it as the Jina's dispensation. Not the pilgrimage-place sense of tīrtha.

All Tīrthaṅkaras are male; the Tīrthaṅkara does not eat after omniscience.

'Sacred word/speech': a sequence of hymns, usually in decads, as in Periya Tirumoḻi, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, Nācciyār Tirumoḻi; Tiruvāymoḻi is 'the sacred word of the mouth'.
The Lord's sacred feet — the Āḻvārs' constant object of refuge, service and contemplation ('his radiant feet that end sorrow', TVM 1.1.1).
All beings other than gods, hell-beings and humans — one-sensed beings, insects, animals (TS 4.27).
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, three times (Khp 1); first used as ordination (Vin Mv 1.12).
The 'third eye' or eye centre behind and between the eyebrows, where the scattered attention is gathered by simran and the inner journey begins.

Forbearance, endurance (as used in Dhp 184, 320).

Realization: stable, non-fluctuating recognition of the nature of mind, as opposed to passing experiences; each of the four yogas is marked by its realization.

The practice of taking and giving that completes the exchange of self and other, made the heart of practice in the Guru Pūjā.
Taught in commentaries on the third line of Parting from the Four Attachments and in the Thirty-Seven Practices.

definitions.definition: Forms that appear in the practice of the six-branch yoga, not made of matter, the support for unchanging bliss; the signs of withdrawal are their first appearance.
The ninety-six principles that make up the embodied person in the Siddha tradition (see cpt:ninety-six-tattvas).
Service to Śiva and his devotees; the Nāyaṉmārs are 'toṇṭar', servants.
Ritual cake (bali) offered to deities, protectors and spirits, or used as a support of the deity.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ, 2.45).
The three guṇas taken together, of which prakṛti and the manifest consist (SK 14; Tattvasamāsa 4).
The domain of the three guṇas, which is the Vedas' domain; Arjuna is told to be free of it (BhG 2.45).
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ and Svar - the region dissolved in each occasional dissolution and within which the hells lie.

The central vertical column of the universe, one rajju wide, outside which mobile beings do not live.
Gazing without blinking at a small target until tears fall; one of the six acts, and in the GS a way to śāmbhavī.

The three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman) as the knowledge of the śrauta rite; the Atharvaveda's place beside them was debated.

The second age, in which sacrifice (yajña) is the principal means.
One who has laid down the rods of speech, mind and body (MDh 12.10); outwardly, a renouncer carrying three staves.
Renouncer with the triple staff (Vaiṣṇava mark); inwardly, restraint of speech, body and mind.
The tenth, three-part mudrā of Śrīvidyā worship; the Goddess is 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 180).
The central downward triangle of the Śrīcakra, the eighth enclosure, seat of Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī (in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the unmanifest, mahat and ahaṃkāra).
The 5th and 9th houses (with the 1st), the most auspicious houses; lords of angles and trines together make royal yogas (BPHS 39).
What the yogin sees in the stage of paricaya: the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).
The second inner region ('three prominences'), seat of Brahm/the universal mind and source of the Veda, sounding like thunder or drum; the causal region.
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants, the meeting place between the brows (trikuṭī) where Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī meet.
The 'triple peak' between the brows where the three channels meet (Hindi Nāth and Sant usage).
The three aims (inner, outer, middle) of the yogī's attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The one Lord as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in Śākta Purāṇas the three receive their power from the Goddess.
Naturelessness of characteristic, of arising and ultimate naturelessness — the intent of 'all dharmas lack own-being'.

Latent tendency that sustains mind; pure or impure; its destruction (vāsanā-kṣaya) with dissolution of mind and knowledge gives jīvanmukti.

definitions.definition: The third of the seven standpoints: it divides the general into particulars for practical dealings (TS 1.33); distinct from vyavahāra paired with niścaya.
Empirically real: valid for all practical dealings and sublated only by knowledge of Brahman — the waking world, Īśvara, scripture and the path.
A determinate cognition; 'vyavasāyātmaka' in NS 1.1.4 denotes determinate perception (Vācaspati).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Here it is one, whereas the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless (2.41); it is not established in samādhi for those carried away by enjoyment and power (2.44).
The single, resolute understanding of the yogin, contrasted with the many-branched minds of the irresolute (BhG 2.41, 2.44).
Bodily exertion for steadiness and strength, to be done in measure (to half one's strength); excess causes disease (Ca Sū 7.31-35; AHS Sū 2.10-14).
Space as a place of the subtle body: the 'space-wheel' (vyomacakra) of khecarī between sun and moon (HYP 3.37, 4.45); the five voids (vyomapañcaka) of the Nāth body-map.
The five voids or spaces to be known in the body (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The HYP's name for the place where the reversed tongue meets the junction of the three paths in khecarī, and for the space between sun and moon where the inner khecarī abides.
One of the five spaces seen in the intermediate target (ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa, paramākāśa).
Supreme space (paravyoma) that one becomes at the end of long instrument sounds (41); the thought-free great space (mahāvyoman) in which firm understanding is worship (147).

definitions.definition: The fourfold form (caturmūrti) of the Lord — Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha — each arising from the prior (MBh 12.326.68–69).
The four emanated forms of the Lord — Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha — each manifesting a pair of the six qualities while possessing all six.
The four emanations Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, each manifesting the six qualities or pairs of them, for creation, maintenance, dissolution and for the meditation of seekers.
The fourfold form of the Lord (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) in the Triśikhi's concentrations and the Mudgala.

definitions.definition: The fourth pure meditation, with all activity stopped, just before liberation (TS 9.39–40); also called samucchinna-kriyā.
Giving up external and internal attachments, including the body (TS 9.20, 9.26).
The state of the mind that has come out of samādhi; in it the arisings of 3.36 are powers (3.37).
The mind's outgoing, non-concentrated state, whose impressions are overpowered in stilling (3.9); powers count as powers only in it (3.37); kriyā-yoga is for the emergent (vyutthita) mind (YBh 2.1).

definitions.definition: Going to be born (in the Pure Land) at death — the 'birth of non-birth' from the vow, the condition for completing awakening.
Ōjō: birth in the true land at death, which is at once attaining nirvāṇa; settled at the moment of shinjin.

literal: Pure Land that is only mind

definitions.definition: The Pure Land as mind only, affirmed by Yanshou, Tianru and Zhuhong together with real birth in the West: the mind-only land is born only when the mind is understood; to purify the mind there is no method apart from Pure Land practice.
Rejected as a reading of the Pure Land: Shandao's 'pointing to a direction and establishing form' holds the Western land to be real for ordinary beings.
'As the mind is pure the buddha-land is pure': the Western Land is found in the purified mind (Platform Sūtra).
Zhaozhou's answer to 'does a dog have buddha-nature?', used as the first barrier; not to be taken as nothingness or as the 'no' of being and non-being.
The five gates of mindfulness of the Rebirth Treatise: worship, praise, aspiration, contemplation, transfer.
'Take awakening as the standard' (Dahui), against teachers who deny awakening.
Satori: awakening, used interchangeably with kenshō or for deeper realizations.
The five right practices directed to Amitābha: reciting the sūtras, contemplating, worshipping, calling the name, praising and offering (Shandao).
The blank state of sitting with an empty mind thinking nothing, which the Platform Sūtra rejects.
The tenet of the Platform Sūtra: being amid thoughts yet not thinking, the mind not stained by objects; not a blank absence of thought.
The tenet of Shenhui's teaching.
Musang's 'no thinking' = samādhi.
For Wuzhu, no-thought includes precepts, samādhi and wisdom and replaces all ritual.

equivalents.note: Both mean the absence of conceptual thought, but the Platform Sūtra insists no-thought is thought of suchness, not a cessation of thought; Advaita and Yogācāra uses of nirvikalpa have different bases.

term: wuqing shuofa (the insentient preach the Dharma)

definitions.definition: Nanyang Huizhong's teaching, taken up by Dongshan; heard only when one is free of the feelings of consciousness.
The 'birth of non-birth': birth in the Pure Land arises from the pure vow and is not the deluded birth of the three existences (Tanluan, quoted by Daochuo).
The state of the one who has stopped seeking: ordinary, with nothing to do — 'the noble person is the one with nothing to do' (Linji).
The five ranks of the real and the apparent (lord and minister) of Dongshan and Caoshan.

term: wuwei zhenren (true person of no rank)

definitions.definition: The true person without rank going in and out of the gates of the face; not to be reified ('a dried shit-stick') (Linji).
The substance of the teaching: being amid forms yet free of forms; also the 'formless' precepts, repentance and verse.
The state free of all mind of seeking and discriminating; 'only be without mind and that is the ultimate' (Huangbo).
Practised through ten methods of stopping deluded mind (Jinsim jikseol).

term: wuyi daoren (person of the Way who depends on nothing)

definitions.definition: The one listening to the Dharma who relies on nothing, the mother of all buddhas (Linji).
The root of the teaching and the original nature of people: moment after moment not abiding in any dharma; from the Diamond Sūtra's 'produce a mind that abides nowhere'.
Takuan's mind that does not stop anywhere.

equivalents.note: The Diamond Sūtra's apratiṣṭhitaṃ cittam, which Huineng's awakening line renders.

definitions.definition: The age of the semblance Dharma, when teaching and practice remain without realization.
The land (realm) of sloth and pride west of here, where those of mixed practice stop (Huaigan, citing the Pusa chutai jing).
Kemangai: one of the names of the transformed land.
In Chan the word for the ultimate itself — 'this very mind is buddha' — as well as for deluded mind; which is meant depends on context.
The formless mind-dharma pervading the ten directions, functioning as seeing, hearing and acting (Linji).
Balance of alertness and calm: calm without alertness is dullness, alertness without calm is scattered thought (Yongjia).
Jinul's seongjeok deungji; sequential use is the gradual method of inferior faculties.
Faith, vow and practice — the three provisions for birth (Ouyi).
Beginningless habitual tendencies that remain after sudden awakening and are removed gradually.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The wise one is content with what comes by chance (yadṛcchā-lābha) and is not bound though acting (4.22).
Chance: listed among the candidate causes in ŚU 1.2.

definitions.definition: The patron of the sacrifice who bears its cost and receives its fruit.

The sacrifice: offering into fire to the gods with mantra, the rite that sustains gods and world; the gods first sacrificed the Puruṣa, 'sacrificing to the sacrifice with the sacrifice' (RV 10.90.16).

The Vedic offering-rite performed with fire, mantras and priests; in the Brāhmaṇas it is identified with the cosmic Person, with Prajāpati, with the year and with Viṣṇu ('puruṣo vai yajñaḥ', ŚB 1.3.2.1; 'yajño vai viṣṇuḥ').
Any of the prescribed offerings of the householder — the daily great sacrifices, the cooked-food, oblation and Soma sacrifices counted among the forty sacraments (GDh 8.14–21).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds (3.9); Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, by which gods and humans nourish one another (3.10–12); rain arises from sacrifice and sacrifice from action (3.14); the all-pervading brahman is ever established in it (3.15).

Sacrifice, action done for whose sake does not bind (BhG 3.9); the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16); widened to many kinds — of material things, austerity, yoga, study, knowledge, breath (4.25–30) — the sacrifice of knowledge being highest (4.33); inwardly, the seven priests of the senses offering into the fire within (Anugītā 14.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sacrifice is extended in ch. 4: acting for the sake of sacrifice dissolves action (4.23); every factor of the rite is Brahman (4.24); many kinds are listed — to the gods, into Brahman, senses into restraint, objects into senses, actions of senses and breath into self-restraint, material goods, austerity, yoga, recitation and knowledge, breath-regulation, regulated food (4.25–30); all are born of action and destroy impurity (4.30, 4.32); the sacrifice of knowledge is best (4.33); the non-sacrificer has neither this world nor the next (4.31); the Lord is the enjoyer of sacrifices (5.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Sacrifice: of sacrifices the Lord is the japa-yajña (10.25); not by sacrifices can he be seen in the form Arjuna saw (11.48, 11.53).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Sacrifice, threefold: sāttvic when offered according to injunction by those not desiring fruit, the mind set on 'it simply ought to be offered'; rājasic when offered for fruit or display; tāmasic when without injunction, distributed food, mantras, fee or faith (17.11–13). The demonic sacrifice 'in name only', with hypocrisy and not by injunction (16.17). Sacrifice, giving and austerity purify the wise and are not to be abandoned (18.5); the rites of the expounders of Brahman begin with oṃ (17.24).

Consumption or disease generally, driven out by Atharvavedic hymns (AVŚ 3.7).
Yama son of Vivasvant, first mortal to die, who found the path for many and is king of the dead in the highest heaven (RV 10.14).
The five restraints: non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness (2.30); universal, the great vow (2.31).
The first limb: in the VP and ŚiP non-harming, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession; in MkP 41.16 the ascetic's five vows (non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, non-greed, non-harming).
Non-harming, celibacy, truthfulness, non-dealing and non-stealing (with the five niyamas also counted as yamas).
Ten restraints (non-injury … purity), each with an outer and an inner meaning; moderate diet is chief.
The means of dharma common to all life-stages (NBh 4.2.46).
Without restraint, pure food does not bring prosperity (VS 6.2.9 C).
In Haribhadra's correlation the limb matching the mitrā view (YDS 16); in Jain terms the vows.

definitions.definition: The Diamond Sūtra line at which Huineng awoke.
'One thought': hearing the name and rejoicing even for one thought gains the great benefit (Larger Sūtra); one calling removes eighty koṭis of kalpas of sin (Daochuo).
Ichinen: the one thought-moment of shinjin, 'the ultimate brevity of time', and the one calling that follows.
The doubt aroused by the huatou which must be broken for awakening; 'great doubt, great awakening'.
Doubt involving the whole body — 'with your 360 bones and 84,000 pores raise a mass of doubt' (Wumen).
The one mind that buddhas and beings are; there is no other dharma (Huangbo).
The source (zong) taken by Yongming Yanshou to harmonise Chan and the teachings.
In the Awakening of Faith, the single reality with two aspects — suchness and arising-ceasing — identical with the tathāgatagarbha.
The 'single mind' of Vasubandhu's opening verse ('with single mind I take refuge'); in Tanluan the undivided faith that accords with reality.
Isshin: the one mind into which the three minds of the eighteenth vow are gathered, i.e. true shinjin.
The undistracted single mind in holding the name (Smaller Sūtra); in Zhuhong of phenomenal and principled kinds.

term: yi xin chuan xin (transmission from mind to mind)

definitions.definition: The Dharma transmitted mind to mind, making each awaken for himself, while the robe was only a token (Hongren in the Platform Sūtra).
The easy practice: reaching non-retrogression by faith and calling the buddhas' names (Nāgārjuna), by riding the Buddha's vow (Tanluan).
Always practising a straight mind in all activities, not sitting motionless (Platform Sūtra).
Daoxin's samādhi of one practice drawn from the Wenshu shuo bore jing (Lengqie shizi ji).
The 'gate of restraint': Shandao's reading of the eighteenth vow's exclusion as a deterrent, not a rejection.
In the Tattvārtha Sūtra, activity (karma) of body, speech and mind (6.1); it is inflow (6.2).
The stilling of the activities of the mind (YS 1.2); Vyāsa: 'yoga is samādhi', a property of the mind at all its levels, counting as yoga only in the one-pointed and stilled mind.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga (2.48); yoga is skill in actions (2.50); the understanding 'according to yoga' (2.39); one attains yoga when the understanding stands immovable in samādhi (2.53); karmayoga is the commitment of the yogins (3.3).

In the Gītā: evenness of mind in success and failure (2.48), skill in action (2.50), and the disconnection from union with sorrow (6.23); also the discipline of action as distinct from sāṃkhya (3.3). In the Mokṣadharma, the path relying on direct perception and a Lord, as against Sāṃkhya (12.289.3–7).
The conjunction of the self with the Lord (through the mind); twofold - in action (muttering, meditation) and in the cessation of action.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the state in which, the mind being steady and established in the self, pleasure and pain cease and mastery arises in the embodied — it leads to liberation (Śā 1.137-139); its eight powers (Śā 1.140-141); also 'yoga' = right combination/application of drugs (Sū 1.123).

The discipline by which the self is seen (YS 1.8) and by which the faults that burn beings are removed (ĀpDh 1.8.23); the renouncer's practice of breath-control, fixation, withdrawal and meditation (MDh 6.70–74).
The union of the jīva and the Self (Devī Gītā).
Not union with wealth, kin, powers, heavens or divine ranks, but the undivided understanding regarding Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, the Sun and Gaṇeśa (Gaṇeśa Gītā).
One-pointedness of mind on the Lord by stopping other modifications, with eight means (Īśvara Gītā).

VP 6.7.31: the joining with Brahman of the special, effort-dependent movement of the mind; LiP 1.8: restraint of citta's activities, and the word means nirvāṇa, Maheśa's state; ŚiP 7.2.37.6: the mind's steady activity fixed on Śiva.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the imperishable yoga taught to Vivasvat and handed down to the royal sages (4.1–3); the yoga of action set beside renunciation and Sāṃkhya, which the wise see as one (5.1–6); what is called renunciation is yoga (6.2); the meditative yoking of the self in solitude (6.10–15); the state in which the restrained mind (citta) rests and the self is seen by the self (6.20–22), defined as 'the unyoking from union with sorrow' (6.23); called 'sāmya' (sameness) by Arjuna (6.33); the yogin is greater than ascetics, knowers and ritualists (6.46).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: The Lord's own yoga, to be known together with his vibhūti (10.7, 10.18); his sovereign yoga (yogam aiśvaram), seen with the divine eye (11.8); by his own yoga (ātmayoga) he showed the supreme form (11.47). Of the practitioner: 'unwavering yoga' (10.7), 'undivided yoga' (12.6), 'the yoga of practice' (12.9).

Yoga: 'the firm holding of the senses' (KU 2.3.11); the method taught by Death (KU 2.3.18); the trunk of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the chapter on posture, breath and signs (ŚU 2); the six-limbed yoga (MaiU 6.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: unswerving devotion to the Lord is 'through a yoga that has no other' (ananya-yoga) (13.11); some see the self by the yoga of sāṃkhya, others by the yoga of action (karma-yoga) (13.25); compare bhakti-yoga (14.26).

(1) In Jain karma theory the vibration or activity of body, speech and mind which is the channel of inflow (TS 6.1–2); (2) in Jain yoga texts, whatever joins the soul to liberation — the three jewels (YŚ 1.15; Yogaviṃśikā 1).
The state in which, the mind abiding in the self, the embodied one has no pleasure or pain (VS 5.2.17 C).
A means to liberation, practised in forests, caves and sandbanks, with the method of the inner self learned from the Yoga śāstra (NS 4.2.42, 4.2.46; NBh).
Tamil yōkam: the Siddhars teach the eight-limbed yoga of the Tirumantiram and vāci yoga, yet Kuṭampai asks what need of yoga the realized has.

definitions.definition: The final capacity-yoga in which all activity (yoga) is abandoned, at the end of the omniscient's life (YDS).
Bhagavad Gītā 8.10: at departure the yogin, yoked with devotion and 'by the power of yoga', makes the breath enter fully between the brows.
The power gained by yoga, by which the yogin checks sense-objects as an elephant stems a current and enters other beings at will (MBh 12.289.23–24).

The one who falls away from yoga before perfection; he is not lost but reborn among the pure or in a family of yogins and continues (BhG 6.37–45).

definitions.definition: The five faults to be cut off in yoga: desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep (MBh 12.232.4; 12.266.14).
A planet that rules both an angle and a trine for a given ascendant (e.g. Saturn for Taurus and Libra), producing royal yoga by itself (BPHS 34; Laghupārāśarī).
The unsurpassed security from the yokes, nibbāna, sought in the noble search (MN 26).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of concern for acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema) (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: What the Lord himself carries (vahāmi) for those who, with nothing else, think of him and worship him, ever devoted (9.22).
Gain and security, whose burden the Lord bears for those who worship him with undivided minds (BhG 9.22); Arjuna is told to be free of acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema, 2.45).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: That by which the Lord is veiled, so that he is not manifest to all; through it the deluded world does not recognize him, the unborn and imperishable (7.25).
The Lord's yoga-māyā by which he is veiled and not manifest to all (BhG 7.25).
The Lord's internal power that arranges his play, e.g. making the gopīs appear married to others and veiling his majesty.

definitions.definition: The soul at the stages of śaraṇa and aikya, correlated with the causal body and the bhāvaliṅga.
In the HYP the state to be practised for through khecarī: for one who attains yogic sleep 'there is never time' (4.49).
The Lord's sleep on the waters between creations; in the Devī Māhātmya the Goddess as Viṣṇu's sleep who leaves him so he can wake.

literal: one who has ascended to yoga

definitions.definition: One who has ascended to yoga, for whom quiescence is the means; attached neither to objects nor actions, having renounced all intentions (BhG 6.3–4).
Bhagavad Gītā 6.3–4: one who has ascended to yoga — when one is attached neither to sense objects nor to actions and has renounced all intentions; for him calm (śama) is said to be the means.

definitions.definition: Yoga tantra: emphasis on inner yoga of identity with the deity in the five-family maṇḍala (Tattvasaṃgraha, Sarvadurgatipariśodhana); third class.
Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Lord of yoga: Arjuna's address when asking to be shown the Lord's imperishable self (11.4); Sañjaya calls Hari 'the great lord of yoga' (11.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Lord of yoga: Sañjaya heard the yoga directly from Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yoga (18.75); where the lord of yoga and Pārtha are, there are fortune and victory (18.78).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: Yogins who strive see the one abiding in themselves (15.11).

definitions.definition: Female practitioner or goddess of the maṇḍala; the Yoginī tantras are 'their' tantras.

In Śrīvidyā the classes of attendant goddesses of the nine enclosures — Prakaṭa, Gupta, Guptatara, Sampradāya, Kulottīrṇa, Nigarbha, Rahasya, Atirahasya and Parāparātirahasya yoginīs; the Tripurā Upaniṣad (2) names nine yoginīs.

The goddesses of the Kula — sky-going, mother and earth-going — through whom Kaula knowledge descended; in Kāmarūpa the Kaula scripture is 'in every yoginī's house' (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15; 22.10).
Goddesses of the six centres of the Kubjikā system (Kubjikāmata 15).
The Kaula of the yoginīs, the name the Kaulajñānanirṇaya gives itself in its colophons, brought down by Macchaghnapāda from Candradvīpa.
The meeting with the yoginīs — a sign and power of Kaula practice (KJN 7.22; 16.8).
One born from a Kaula union, by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra (TĀ 29.162-163).

Tantras of the yoginīs (also 'yoganiruttara', 'the unexcelled yoga'): the Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra, Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and related cycles, with female deities, cremation-ground imagery and the yoga of bliss (later Tibetan 'mother tantras').

Perception born of the culmination of meditative cultivation of a real object — vivid, free of the net of construction; the foulness and earth-kasiṇa meditations show that cultivation yields vividness even of the unreal, but only cultivation of the real (the four truths) is a means of knowledge.
Perception of the self and other substances from a special conjunction of self and mind (VS 9.13–14); of yogins in concentration (yukta) and out of it (viyukta) (Praśastapāda).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).
Yogaja, one of the three extraordinary contacts.

equivalents.note: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika also admit yogic perception (yogaja, a kind of extraordinary perception); the Buddhists ground it in cultivation of a real object, not in a special contact.

definitions.definition: 'Higher yoga' tantras, an Indian class name for the Guhyasamāja group (later Tibetan 'father tantras').
Non-contradiction of the meaning ('sprinkle with fire' lacks it).
Fitness: the natural capacity of a word to express its meaning, the eternal relation between them (VP 3.3).
The Goddess's yoni fallen at Kāmagiri, worshipped at Kāmākhyā; Kāmākhyā is 'the great vidyā in the form of the yoni' (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4).
The supreme primal yoni of the supreme, fourfold (Kubjikāmata 11.6).

Bhagavad Gītā 13–15: attachment to the guṇas causes births in good and bad wombs (13.22); the great brahman is Kṛṣṇa's womb and the womb of all forms (14.3–4); dying in tamas one is born in deluded wombs (14.15).
The triangle as womb of the universe: the triangles of the Śrīcakra are yonis; the yoni-mudrā is the ninth mudrā; the Tripurā Upaniṣad calls the Goddess's Śakti the womb of all.

definitions.definition: In the GS, closing the senses, joining prāṇa and apāna and raising the goddess through the centres to union with Śiva; in the ŚS the contraction of the 'yoni' between anus and genitals with meditation on the flame in the brahma-yoni; also the name of a hand-gesture in Śākta worship.
Thoroughly, by right method (as used in Dhp 326).

definitions.definition: Attention that goes to the source: by it effluents do not arise and are abandoned (MN 2); one of the two conditions for right view (MN 43) and a factor of stream-entry (SN 55.5); the bodhisatta's means of penetrating dependent origination (DN 14).
The attention whose single lamp-like act dispels karma and defilements gathered for aeons.

equivalents.note: Pali form (U36)

definitions.definition: In the Śūraṅgama, complete penetration of reality through one entrance — a sense-object, faculty, consciousness or element; twenty-five are told.
Circles and figures used as teaching devices, said to derive from Nanyang Huizhong through Danyuan to Yangshan.
Bhagavad Gītā 7–9: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand yugas and his night ends after a thousand yugas; those who know this 'know day and night' (8.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The Lord comes into being 'age after age' (yuge yuge) to establish dharma (4.8).
The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, presided over by Prajāpati (Ṛk 1).

The four world-ages Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with twilights, in which dharma declines foot by foot (MDh 1.68–86); named already as states of a man in AB 7.15.

An age: the Lord comes into being age after age (BhG 4.8); Brahmā's day and night last a thousand ages each (8.17); the four ages and their decline taught by Hanumān (MBh 3.148) and Nārada (Rāmāyaṇa 7.74).

In the siddhāntas, the caturyuga of 4,320,000 solar years divided 4:3:2:1 into Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali following the feet of dharma (SS 1.15–17; BSS 1.7–9) — or, for Āryabhaṭa, into four equal quarters.
An age or generation; 'in the earliest age of the gods being was born from non-being' (RV 10.72.2).

An age of the world: Kṛta (Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with junctions (sandhyā) of a tenth of that length before and after, so 4,800 + 3,600 + 2,400 + 1,200 divine years; dharma declines through them.

definitions.definition: The divine couple Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, worshipped together (yugala-upāsanā).
Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa as the object of service in mañjarī-bhāva.
The divine couple (Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa) and the human couple in which they are realized.
Union: where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two truths, generation and completion, wisdom and compassion become one (Pañcakrama 5); the goal of the path.

zung 'jug, union: of emptiness and clarity, appearance and emptiness, bliss and emptiness; in the six yogas the 'body of union' that arises from clear light, first as the learner's then as the non-learner's union.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); the undisciplined (ayukta) have no understanding or cultivation (2.66); the knowing one acts disciplined (3.26); one joined with understanding (buddhiyukta) casts off good and evil deeds (2.50).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Used as a defining title: the one who sees inaction in action is yukta (4.18); the yukta knower thinks 'I do nothing' (5.8); gives up fruit and attains peace (5.12); withstands the surge of desire and anger (5.23); is satisfied with knowledge and sees clod and gold alike (6.8); his well-restrained mind (citta) rests in the self (6.18); 'measured' in food, rest, sleep and effort (6.17); the one who worships the Lord with faith is 'most yoked' (yukta-tama) (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 10–12: Yoked: those ever yoked who worship the Lord with love (10.10); Arjuna asks about the devotees ever yoked (12.1); those who fix the mind on him are 'the most yoked' (yuktatama) (12.2).

definitions.definition: Fitting detachment: using things without attachment in Kṛṣṇa's service, as opposed to 'futile' renunciation (phalgu-vairāgya) of what relates to him.

Caraka's fourth means of knowledge: the understanding that sees things produced by the conjunction of many causes, valid for the three times, by which the three aims are achieved (Ca Sū 11.25); also the right application of medicine to place, time and person (Sū 1.123-127).
The four reasonings by which the reality of things is established: of dependence, of efficacy (cause and effect), of valid proof, and of the nature of things (dharmatā).
The planned use of diet and medicines (Ca Sū 11.54): purification and pacification (Vi 8.87).
Prajñāpāramitā personified as the mother of all buddhas; Machig is her emanation.

equivalents.note: the perfection of wisdom as teaching and as the personified mother

definitions.definition: The swastika (left-turning in Bön), emblem of the eternal and indestructible; 'Yungdrung Bön' is 'eternal Bön'.
Containing heaven and earth; cutting off the myriad streams; following the waves.
The post to which the victim is tied in the animal sacrifice.
The interfusing nenbutsu: each person's recitation interpenetrates all others' (one is all, all is one).
Unobstructed, transparent, all-penetrating: a quality of awareness and the name of Rigdzin Gödem's treasure (Gongpa Zangthal).
Miscellaneous practices: all good practices not directed exclusively to Amitābha.
Zōgyō: to be cast aside (Senchakushū 2).
The illness Hakuin contracted from excessive striving — rising heat, cold legs, fear, exhaustion — cured by naikan.
The hall where monks sit, eat and sleep by seniority (Chanmen guishi).
The four relations of illumination and function.

term: zheng and pian (the real and the apparent)

definitions.definition: The real (principle, emptiness, lord) and the apparent (phenomena, form, minister), whose interplay is the five ranks.

The rightly established group (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi): those assured of awakening; those born in Sukhāvatī dwell in it (11th vow); Nāgārjuna's 'stage of certainty' (biding) entered by recollecting Amitābha.
Shōjōju: entered in this life at the moment of shinjin, not first in the Pure Land.

cross_language.note: Nāgārjuna's 'certainty'

definitions.definition: The rightly determined act: calling Amitābha's name single-heartedly at all times, because it accords with his vow (Shandao).
Shōjōgō: the calling of the name, to be chosen over the auxiliary acts (Senchakushū 16).
The name of the primal vow is the act of right assurance; shinjin is its cause (Shōshinge).
The age of the true Dharma after the Buddha's passing, when teaching, practice and realization are present.

term: zhengfayanzang (treasury of the true Dharma eye)

definitions.definition: What the Buddha entrusted to Mahākāśyapa in the flower sermon; also a title (Dahui; Dōgen).
Revulsion from, or turning away from, attachment to saṃsāra — 'the feet of meditation' (Dorje Chang Thungma).

The four-line instruction of Mañjuśrī to Sachen: freedom from attachment to this life, to saṃsāra, to one's own purpose, and from grasping — equivalent to dharma practice, renunciation, bodhicitta and the view.
The ultimate — dharmatā, buddha-nature, the dharmakāya — is empty of everything other than itself (all adventitious conventional phenomena) but not empty of its own nature and qualities.

In Kongtrul's presentation, the Great Madhyamaka view of the final turning, suited to meditative experience; in Mipham's sense, the unconditioned wisdom's emptiness of the adventitious, which does not exclude its also being empty of own-nature.
The true mind, like space, neither cut off nor changing, as opposed to the provisional body and deluded mind (Jinul).
The insight Linji demands: no longer seeking outside, one is not stained by birth and death.

The ground: the primordial state of all beings and phenomena prior to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, whose essence is primordially pure, nature spontaneously present and compassion all-pervading; recognized it is buddhahood, unrecognized it is the basis of delusion.
In the ground-path-fruit scheme of the Nyingma tantras, the ground is the buddha-nature present in beings, the path its recognition and cultivation, the fruit its manifestation.

cross_language.note: loose equivalent; the Dzogchen sense has no exact Sanskrit counterpart recorded

definitions.definition: The sincere mind: true in worship, praise and contemplation, without outward show and inward falsehood (Shandao).

literal: disintegratedness; the state of having ceased

definitions.definition: In Tsongkhapa's Prāsaṅgika, the disintegratedness of a thing is itself a functioning thing (dngos po) able to produce effects — how past karma connects to its result without an ālaya.
The tradition and practice of pacifying suffering through the realization of the Perfection of Wisdom, named after the Heart Sūtra's mantra that 'pacifies all suffering'.

cross_language.note: the Heart Sūtra's epithet

definitions.definition: Conceptual understanding mistaken for awakening; Huineng calls Shenhui 'a follower of intellectual understanding' (Zongbao).
Seongcheol classes Jinul's understanding-awakening under this head.

Ground-appearances: the display that arises from the ground when its compassion stirs, through the eight gateways of spontaneous presence; recognized as self-display they are liberation (Samantabhadra), not recognized they become the basis of delusion.

term: zhizhi renxin (pointing directly at the human mind)

definitions.definition: Third line of the four-line self-description.
Exclusive practice: 'ten of ten are born'; mixed practice rarely succeeds (Shandao; Huaigan).
A phrase that turns delusion into awakening; e.g. Baizhang's 'not obscuring cause and effect'.
The three tastes after digestion (sweet, sour, bitter) that determine a food's or medicine's later effect.

equivalents.note: Āyurvedic post-digestive effect

definitions.definition: The thirteen Indian treatises at the core of the Rimé-influenced monastic curriculum, annotated by Khenpo Shenga.
Assisting recitation: companions recite the name for and with the dying so that ten recitations are completed (Daochuo; Yinguang).
The auxiliary acts: the four right practices other than calling the name.
The originally pure, unborn, complete and unmoving nature of one's own mind that produces all dharmas (Huineng's awakening); delusion and awakening are its states.
One's own nature, the Dharma body, recognised in sudden awakening (Jinul).

equivalents.note: Same Chinese word as the svabhāva that Madhyamaka refutes; in the Platform Sūtra it names the empty, originally pure nature of mind, not an inherent own-being of dharmas; Madhyamaka would object to any reading of zixing as svabhāva.

definitions.definition: 'Amitābha of one's own nature': in the Chan-inflected reading every buddha is Amitābha of the original nature (Tianru); held together with birth in the West.

term: zixing zidu (saving oneself by the self-nature)

definitions.definition: The inward meaning of the four vows: the deluded beings of one's own mind are saved by one's own prajñā.
Redefined in the Platform Sūtra: not attaching to mind or purity nor mere immobility; 'sitting' is thoughts not arising toward objects, 'meditation' is seeing the unmoving self-nature.
Just sitting as the enactment of buddhahood; 'not learning meditation but the Dharma gate of ease and joy' (Dōgen).
The seat of kōan introspection and of samādhi-power (jōriki).
